In this verse God reports that the hypocrites, when told not to spread corruption on earth through disbelief, disobedience and alliance with the disbelievers, claimed to be reformers. God rejects their claim: it is they, and they alone, who are the corrupters, though they are unaware of it. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir explain corruption as disbelief, disobedience and neglect of duties, with Ibn Kathir also including alliance with unbelievers; he reports from Ibn Abbas that the hypocrites meant to reconcile the believers with the People of the Book, while Mujahid held that they saw deference to unbelievers as righteousness and guidance. Al-Mawardi lists three meanings of corruption: disbelief, transgressing what is forbidden, and aiding the disbelievers, and notes that some take the verse as referring to people who would come later, as Salman said. Al-Razi asks who speaks the warning, God, the Prophet or some believers, and gives three meanings of corruption: turning people from obedience, flattering the disbelievers, or sowing doubt in secret. Al-Zamakhshari takes corruption to mean stirring up wars and strife. For the phrase "it is they who are the corrupters", most commentators see a strong, emphatic rebuttal, reinforced by the particles of emphasis and the separating pronoun. Ibn Kathir, Ibn Ashur and Ibn Sa'di explain that they are unaware because they take their corruption for good, out of ignorance or because disbelief has taken hold of their hearts. Al-Razi, al-Qurtubi and al-Jaza'iri read the lack of awareness more as failing to grasp that their acts are corrupt, or not knowing that God will expose them.

This verse describes the hypocrites when they are urged to believe sincerely, as the people believed, that is, as the Companions believed with heart, tongue and deeds. They reply with a scornful question: shall we believe as the foolish believed? Most commentators, including al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Jalalayn, identify the people as the Prophet's Companions, both emigrants and helpers, and the foolish as those same believers, whom the hypocrites considered lacking judgment. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir explain that the sufaha are the ignorant and weak in judgment, who cannot tell what benefits from what harms. Ibn 'Atiyya and Ibn 'Ashur report that the insult was also meant to belittle believers who were often poor or freed slaves, while the hypocrites were men of standing. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Baydawi note that the hypocrites may have said this only among themselves, and that the phrase admits two readings, one of outright rejection and one of feigned belief. In God's reply, the commentators agree that He confines foolishness to the hypocrites, using the emphatic particles alla and inna and the separating pronoun, and that they do not know their own state. Al-Razi, al-Baydawi and Ibn 'Ashur explain that the verb 'know' is used here rather than 'perceive' as in the previous verse, because foolishness requires reflection, whereas corruption is readily perceived. Ibn al-Qayyim sees the verses as a debate in which God settles the matter by marking the hypocrites with four charges. Al-Sha'rawi highlights the contradiction of people who call believers fools while claiming to believe themselves.

This verse describes the hypocrites who, when they meet the believers, say with their tongues that they believe, but when they are alone with their leaders in disbelief and evil, they declare that they remain upon their own religion and are only mocking the believers. The commentators agree that the 'believers' are the sincere faithful among the Emigrants and the Helpers, and that the hypocrites' profession of faith was only outward, not held in the heart. On the meaning of 'shayatin', opinions differ. Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn Mas'ud, Qatada and al-Suddi understood them as their chiefs and leaders in disbelief; Mujahid and al-Rabi' ibn Anas took them to be their companions among the polytheists and hypocrites; al-Kalbi held they were jinn devils, and several scholars said they were soothsayers. Ibn Jarir and Ibn Kathir favoured the view that the word can apply to both humans and jinn. Grammarians also differ on the preposition 'ila': some read it as meaning 'with' or 'bi', while Zamakhshari and others understood the verb 'khalaw' as implying a sense of returning or withdrawing, and Ibn Jarir preferred to keep 'ila' in its literal sense. The commentators note the contrast in style: the statement made to the believers is unemphasised, whereas the one made to their leaders is emphasised with 'inna', since its purpose is to affirm genuine allegiance. The word 'istihza'' means mockery and scorn.

This verse describes the hypocrites who, when they meet believers, display faith, but when they are alone with their leaders in disbelief, claim they are with them and only mock the believers. The reply is: God mocks them and lets them remain in their rebellion, wandering blindly. The commentators agree that the mockery attributed to God is not play or futility, but a requital for their own mockery, named by the same word as the act, as in the verse about the recompense of an evil being a similar evil. In this world it appears as applying the rules of Islam to them outwardly while God knows their inner state, and as respite that lets them sink deeper. In the hereafter, Ibn Abbas reports that a gate of Paradise is opened for them and then shut in their faces. Al-Hasan explains that God makes the believers aware of their hypocrisy. Al-Zamakhshari notes that the present tense signals a renewal of this mockery over time.

As for the verb yamudduhum, opinions differ. Ibn Mas'ud and Ibn Abbas, followed by al-Tabari, take it to mean that God leaves them and grants them respite, while Mujahid takes it to mean that He increases them. Al-Tabari judges that both meanings can be combined, since the increase comes through the respite granted. Tughyan means exceeding the limit in disbelief and defiance, and 'amah means going astray, hesitating, and being unable to find the way out.

The Mu'tazilites read the increase as abandonment, permission to disobey, or mere delay, and Sunni scholars replied that attributing the act to God as creator does not exclude its acquisition by the human being, as al-Razi, al-Baydawi and al-Zamakhshari explain.

In this verse God describes the hypocrites who exchanged disbelief for faith and misguidance for right guidance, saying that their trade brought them no profit and that they were not rightly guided in what they did. The commentators differ on the meaning of the buying. Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn Mas'ud and Mujahid, followed by al-Tabari, explain that they took misguidance and left guidance, that is, they replaced faith with unbelief. Qatada and others understand it as preferring misguidance over guidance. Al-Tabari prefers the ordinary sense of exchange, while al-Mawardi, al-Nasafi and al-Razi explain that guidance was within their reach, so abandoning it amounts to selling it. Al-Zamakhshari, Ibn 'Atiyya and Abu Hayyan treat the word for buying as a metaphor, and the mention of profit and trade that follows as a sustained image meant to portray their loss. Regarding the words that their trade brought no profit, al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Jalalayn take them to mean a real loss, and Ibn Kathir notes that the Arabic idiom assigns profit to the trade rather than the merchant. As for not being rightly guided, some read it as their choice of misguidance, others as a judgment in God's prior knowledge. Several commentators say the verse concerns the hypocrites in general, others the People of the Book or unbelievers in general, and most hold it refers to the hypocrites.

In this verse God describes the hypocrites with a vivid image: a man in the darkness of night kindles a fire that lights up what is around him, so he sees what to avoid and feels safe. Then his fire goes out and he is left in darkness, unable to see. The commentators explain the light as the profession of faith that the hypocrites utter with their tongues while concealing disbelief, by which they benefit in this world: their blood, property, women, marriages and inheritance are protected. When they die, or when their hypocrisy is exposed, God takes away that light and they remain in the darkness of disbelief, hypocrisy and punishment. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir agree that the verse concerns the hypocrites, and that the light lost is their outward faith, the darkness being their disbelief and hypocrisy. Some, such as Ibn Zayd as quoted by Ibn Kathir, apply the image to those who believed and then apostatised, their light being their earlier faith and their darkness their later disbelief, in line with the verse about believing and then disbelieving. Al-Tabari, however, holds that these people never truly believed, and that the faith meant is a verbal acknowledgement from which they benefited without conviction. Qatada takes the light to be the words 'There is no god but God', and the darkness to be the hypocrite's fate after death; Mujahid sees it as their shifting towards the believers and guidance, then towards the unbelievers and error.

Opinions also differ on when God removes the light: in the hereafter according to some, in the grave according to others, or in this world when their hypocrisy is laid bare. Al-Razi and al-Baydawi stress that the image shows a light that goes out after shining, which makes their misguidance more painful than that of someone who never knew the light. Al-Zamakhshari notes that the word 'light' rather than 'brightness' implies the complete extinction of light. As for the phrase 'deaf, dumb, blind', commentators explain it as an inability to hear the truth, speak it, or see it, and therefore to return to guidance.

In this verse God describes the hypocrites as deaf, mute and blind: they gain no benefit from their hearing, speech or sight in reaching the truth. They do not listen to the truth with acceptance, do not speak it, and do not see the signs of guidance, so they do not turn back from their misguidance. The commentators agree that the verse refers to the hypocrites and that the description is figurative, meaning that these faculties yield no benefit rather than that they are actually lost, since they could hear, speak and see. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir explain that they will not return either to Islam or to the guidance they exchanged, while others take the negation as general and not tied to a particular time. Al-Tabari reports an explanation from Ibn Abbas that limits the lack of return to the time they remain in hypocrisy, but he rejects it because the verse is absolute. Al-Razi and al-Zamakhshari hold that the verse concludes the parable: their error leaves them frozen, not knowing whether to advance or retreat. Ibn Kathir considers that the verse shows they first believed and then disbelieved, which al-Tabari disputes. Rhetoricians see an eloquent comparison here rather than a metaphor, since the thing compared, the hypocrites, is explicitly mentioned.

In this verse God draws a further image of the hypocrites: they are like people caught in a violent rain falling from the sky, wrapped in the darkness of clouds and of night, with thunder that terrifies and lightning that flashes and fades. Overcome with dread, they put their fingers in their ears for fear of the thunderbolts that could kill them, yet God encompasses the disbelievers on every side so that they cannot escape Him. The commentators agree that the sayyib is the rain, and that the darkness, thunder and lightning stand for what the Qur'an contains of warning and proof, or for the bewilderment and fear that seize the hypocrites. Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid and most exegetes take the thunder to be the voice of an angel driving the clouds and the lightning a whip or mallet in his hand, whereas Abu al-Jald and those who follow him say the thunder is wind and the lightning water, a view many consider weak. The scholars differ on the scope of the two images. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir see two distinct kinds of hypocrite, one who mixes belief with unbelief and one who wavers between truth and doubt, while al-Zamakhshari and al-Baydawi read them as a single group. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir also relate a report from Ibn Mas'ud and Ibn 'Abbas about the occasion of revelation, concerning two hypocrites who fled to the polytheists and then returned, but al-Tabari himself doubted its chain and did not regard it as certain. On the phrase hadhar al-mawt, Sibawayh takes it as an object of purpose, while al-Farra' takes it as a specification. The word sawa'iq means thunderbolts, a fire that falls with the roar of thunder, and some say a cry powerful enough to kill.

God describes the hypocrites through the image of a man who kindles a fire in the dark, benefits from it briefly, then sees it extinguished and is left in darkness unable to see. They profess faith and gain from it, their blood and property being protected, but at death lose that light and remain in gloom. The commentators agree that these are hypocrites who showed Islam and then turned away. Deaf, dumb and blind means they are closed to truth and gain nothing from their senses. The second image, a downpour in darkness with thunder, lightning and bolts, shows them stopping their ears from fear of death, the lightning nearly taking their sight, walking in its light and halting when it fades. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir explain that the sayyib is rain, the thunder a sound from the clouds or, for some, an angel driving them, and the lightning a flash of light; al-Zamakhshari and al-Razi treat these as a composite comparison without detailed correspondence. Ibn Abbas and Qatada report that the image may describe the hypocrite whose faith wavers with prosperity or hardship. Some interpreters restrict it to a particular group, others see it as general. The verse concludes that God could take away their hearing and sight, for He is powerful over all things.

This verse addresses all people, calling them to worship their Lord, who created them and those before them, so that they may attain piety. The commentators explain that worship here means monotheism and obedience, and that the address is general: the believer is asked to persevere and grow in worship, and the disbeliever is asked to begin it. On the meaning of la'alla (perhaps, so that), al-Tabari, al-Qurtubi and Ibn Kathir note that it may mean 'so that', while Sibawayh, al-Zamakhshari and Ibn 'Atiyya take it as a hope placed in the addressees, and others read it as a rhetorical device. Ibn Kathir and al-Tabari recall that God made the earth a bed and the sky a roof, and sent down water to bring forth fruits as provision, so there is no ground to set up rivals to God when they know He is the Creator. Al-Razi observes that the verse establishes the existence of the Creator and the duty of reflection, and that the following verses lead to the challenge of the Qur'an and the warning of the Fire. Several scholars, including al-Baydawi and al-Nasafi, stress that the verse joins the command to worship with proofs drawn from creation, and that the Creator alone deserves worship.

This verse reminds people of God's visible favours: the earth made as a spread bed on which they rest, the sky raised like a sound roof over them, and water sent down from the clouds through which fruits are brought forth as provision for them. From this the commentators draw the command to worship God alone and to set up no equals to Him. They explain that "firash" means a level, spread surface, and "bina'" a firmly raised structure; "sama'" may mean the clouds or the height above, according to the commentators.

On the word "andad" (equals), al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir report that Ibn 'Abbas and Qatada take it to mean likenesses or partners in worship, while Ibn Mas'ud takes it to mean powerful men whom people obey in disobedience to God, and Ibn Zayd takes it to mean the idols. Al-Mawardi and Ibn al-Jawzi note that al-Mufaddal and Abu 'Ubayda took it to mean opposites. On the phrase "while you know", al-Tabari gives the view of Ibn 'Abbas and Qatada that people know God created them, and the view of Mujahid that they know He has no equal in the Torah and the Gospel; al-Tabari himself holds that the address is general to all who received the message.

al-Razi and Ibn Kathir stress that the verse joins lordship and worship: whoever admits that God creates and provides must single Him out in worship. Ibn Kathir cites the hadith of Ibn Mas'ud about the gravest sin, and the hadith rebuking the phrase "what God and you wish". Ibn 'Ashur and Ibn Juzayy take "min" before "the fruits" as explanatory rather than partitive.

Modern commentators such as Sayyid Qutb and al-Sha'rawi stress hidden forms of association, and Ibn 'Uthaymin links the expression "so that you may be mindful" to piety.

This verse states that the Qur'an was revealed to His servant Muhammad ﷺ, and God challenges those who doubt it to produce a sura like it. Most commentators take the pronoun in 'like it' to refer to the Qur'an, meaning a sura comparable in eloquence, arrangement and foretelling of the unseen, and that the purpose is to show their inability. Al-Tabari concludes that if the Arabs, masters of eloquence, cannot do it, others are even less able. Al-Razi and Ibn Atiyya specify the aspects of this likeness: its inimitability, its composition, its knowledge of the unseen and its truthfulness. As for the 'witnesses', Ibn Abbas understands them as helpers, Mujahid as people who would attest that their production is similar, and al-Farra, al-Wahidi and al-Baghawi as their gods. Al-Tabari finds Mujahid's reading weak, since believers would not testify for them. Ibn al-Jawzi reports that the verse answers the Jews who said the Qur'an did not resemble revelation. Scholars debate the particle 'in': some keep its conditional sense, others see a note of reproach toward a weak doubt. On 'and you will never do it', many read a prophetic announcement and a sign of inimitability, while others read a mere denial of ability. Finally, the fire whose fuel is men and stones is prepared for the disbelievers; Ibn Mas'ud and Ibn Abbas take the stones to be sulphur, others the idols worshipped, and the verb 'has been prepared' leads some to hold that Hell already exists.

This verse issues a challenge to those who doubt the Qur'an: let them produce a chapter like it, and then declares they will never do so. If they fail, they should guard themselves against the Fire whose fuel is people and stones, prepared for the disbelievers. Al-Tabari explains the sense as: if you do not do it, and it has become clear to you that this is God's speech, then beware of burning by denying His messenger. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir take the likeness to refer to the Qur'an itself, while some others read it as likeness to Muhammad in being unlettered. Al-Razi, al-Baydawi and others elaborate on its inimitability, and all agree the verse contains a prediction that they will never match it. On the stones, Ibn Mas'ud and Ibn Abbas, followed by most exegetes, say they are sulphur stones, very hot when kindled; others say they are the idols they worshipped, citing the verse that you and what you worship are fuel for Hell. Ibn Kathir favours the first reading without excluding the second. The Mu'tazilites deny that the Fire has already been created, but the majority hold it exists now, as the word prepared indicates. As for the disbelievers, some hold that this particular fire is for them and other fires for others, while the majority say the mention of disbelievers identifies the audience, since their conduct is disbelief. Common to all is that faith is the way to be saved from the Fire.

This verse announces to those who believe and do righteous deeds that they will have gardens beneath which rivers flow. The commentators explain that "beneath them" means beneath their trees and dwellings, not beneath the ground. Ibn Kathir cites a hadith that these rivers flow without a trench, a point also noted by Mawardi and others.

On the fruits, al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir report that when the people of Paradise are given a fruit they say "this is what we were given before." Al-Tabari, following Mujahid and Qatada, takes this to mean the provision of the worldly life, while Yahya ibn Abi Kathir and Abu Ubayda explain that a picked fruit is immediately replaced by a similar one, so they think it is the same. Ibn Abbas understood it as an expression of wonder at the fruit's excellence, and Zamakhshari says the resemblance is so strong that the one is the other.

The word "mutashabihan" is also debated. Ibn Abbas, Mujahid, Rabi ibn Anas and others say the fruits resemble each other in colour and differ in taste. Hasan al-Basri, Qatada and Ibn Jurayj say they resemble one another in excellence, with nothing inferior among them. Ibn Abbas is also reported to have said that nothing in Paradise matches what exists in this world except the names.

The spouses are described as purified from menstruation, from bodily impurities, and from blameworthy traits, according to Ibn Abbas, Mujahid and Qatada. Most commentators, including Razi, Qurtubi and Ibn Ashur, understand "khalidun" as lasting endlessly, which completes the bliss. The verse thus links the promise to faith and righteous action, and encourages believers to persevere.

The commentators explain that God is not restrained by shyness from setting forth any comparison, even one as small as a gnat or smaller, so long as it makes the truth clear. As al-Suddi and al-Tabari report, the verse answers hypocrites who mocked the parables; other reports say it answers polytheists or Jews who scoffed at the mention of the fly and the spider. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir give most weight to the account about the hypocrites, while Ibn Kathir also records the other views without firmly choosing among them. They agree that believers recognise the parable as the truth from their Lord, while disbelievers ask mockingly what God meant by such an example. Al-Razi and al-Qurtubi note that the phrase about God misguiding many and guiding many can be understood in several ways: al-Razi reads it as a test, al-Zamakhshari as causation, and Sunni scholars as God's creation and decree. Nearly all define the defiantly disobedient as those who step outside obedience to God, and many hold that here the word means disbelievers. On the covenant of God, al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir explain it as the pledge made to people and the revelation that the Jews concealed, and Ibn Kathir adds that severing family ties is also among these wrongs. The commentators conclude that such people are the great losers, who forfeit good and face punishment.

The commentators explain that this verse describes the sinners who leave obedience to God: they break God's covenant after it has been confirmed, sever what God commanded to be joined, and spread corruption on earth, and they are the losers. They differ on what the covenant is. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn al-Jawzi take it to be the pledge God took from the descendants of Adam when He brought them out of his loins, or the obligation in the earlier scriptures to believe in Muhammad ﷺ and to make known his description. Al-Baghawi and al-Baydawi understand it as the proofs God placed in human reason confirming His oneness and the truth of the messengers, while Ibn 'Atiyya defines it as a solemn charge to believe and obey. As for who is addressed, al-Tabari holds that it was revealed about the Jewish rabbis and the hypocrites, and that its judgment applies to anyone who shares their characteristics. On what must be joined, al-Tabari and Qatada cite family ties, al-Hasan names the Prophet ﷺ, and most exegetes, including Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Razi, take it to mean whatever God has commanded to be maintained. Ibn 'Abbas explains the corruption on earth as calling people to disbelief, while al-Sudi takes it as practising sins. Al-Tabari reads the loss as the forfeiting of a share of God's mercy, others as perdition, and Ibn 'Abbas adds that applied to non-Muslims the word means disbelief, and applied to Muslims it means sin.

In this verse God rebukes those who disbelieve in Him although they witness His power. They did not exist, then He gave them life by creating them and breathing the spirit into them; He will cause them to die when their term ends, will bring them back to life, and they will then return to Him for judgement. The commentators agree that the interrogative "how" expresses astonishment, reproach and denial, and that the "wa" in "wa kuntum" introduces a circumstantial clause. They differ on the meaning of the two deaths and two lives. Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn Mas'ud, Mujahid, al-Tabari, Ibn 'Atiyya and Ibn Kathir explain that the first death is the non-existence before creation, the first life is the creation itself, the second death is the ordinary death, and the second life is the resurrection; al-Tabari and Ibn 'Atiyya prefer this reading. Qatada holds that they were dead in their fathers' loins before being brought to life. Others count several deaths and lives: Ibn al-Qayyim does not treat the fainting at the trumpet blast as an additional death, while al-Tabari criticises Ibn Zayd, who speaks of three deaths and three lives, as contrary to the apparent sense of the text. On whether calling inert matter "dead" is figurative or literal, al-Razi and al-Qurtubi report that most take it as a metaphor, whereas Qatada takes it literally. Some have drawn from the verse a denial of the punishment of the grave, but others reply that the absence of a mention does not mean the absence of a thing. Al-Razi also reports the Mu'tazilite argument that disbelief comes from the servants themselves, and refutes it. The common thread is that the One who creates, causes to die and revives does not deserve to be disbelieved, and that the return to Him is certain.

This verse tells us that Allah created for you everything on earth, a blessing to be used in this life and to be reflected upon for faith. Then He turned toward the sky and made it into seven heavens, straight and without flaw, and He is all-knowing. The commentators agree that the verse shows that the basic principle regarding useful things is permissibility, a view many scholars hold, while others explain that the verse speaks of blessing and of God's power rather than giving a legal ruling, and that for certain matters the principle is suspension of judgment or prohibition.

On the meaning of istiwa' toward the sky, the exegetes differ. Ibn Abbas and most of the early scholars, such as al-Rabi ibn Anas, take it to mean rising high, without description or limitation, a view al-Tabari chose. Al-Farra, Ibn Kaysan and several grammarians, followed by al-Zamakhshari and al-Baydawi, read it as intending or turning toward the creation of the sky. Others understand it as dominion and sovereignty, and some report that the pronoun refers to smoke. Most agree, however, that the meaning is tied to the creation of the heavens.

They also differ on the order of creation of earth and sky. The majority, including Mujahid and Ibn Kathir, hold that the earth was created before the sky and spread out after it, while Qatada and others hold that the sky was created first. Ibn Abbas and others explain the spreading (dahw) as the bringing forth of water and pasture from the earth, which reconciles the verses. The number seven is stated explicitly; some say it does not exclude further heavens, while others keep to its literal sense.

This verse recounts God's address to the angels before creating Adam: He announces that He will place a khalifa, a successor, on earth to govern it. The angels ask, with some astonishment, how He can appoint one who may spread corruption and shed blood, while they glorify and sanctify Him. God replies that He knows what they do not know. The commentators agree that the khalifa is Adam, and some include his descendants. Al-Tabari suggests the angels may have reasoned by analogy with the jinn who had earlier corrupted the earth, while others hold they learned of this by revelation or from the Preserved Tablet. Scholars differ on the meaning of tasbih and taqdis: some take them as prayer, others as glorification, exalting God above imperfection, and purification. Most agree the angels' question was not a challenge to God but a request for understanding of His wisdom. Ibn Kathir notes that the angels knew God dislikes the shedding of blood. Some jurists, such as al-Qurtubi, derive from the verse the obligation to appoint a leader for the community, while others argue the verse does not address that question. The verse thus reminds believers that divine wisdom often exceeds human knowledge, and that when the reason is hidden, one should submit to God's perfect knowledge.

This verse shows the superiority of Adam: God taught him the names of all things, then presented their realities to the angels and asked them to name them if they were truthful in their claim. The commentators broadly agree that Adam was given knowledge of names, but differ on the scope. Ibn Abbas, Mujahid, Qatada and Sa'id ibn Jubayr hold that it covered the name of everything, down to the smallest bowl, while al-Rabi' ibn Anas restricts it to the names of the angels and Abd al-Rahman ibn Zayd to the names of Adam's offspring. Al-Tabari favours the angels and the offspring together, reasoning from the pronoun 'them', which refers to rational beings. On the presentation, Ibn Mas'ud takes it as the persons themselves and Ibn Abbas as the names. The command to inform is, for most, a test meant to humble the angels, whose claim to be more knowledgeable would be refuted. Some read 'if you are truthful' as 'if you are truthful in your claim that the successor will cause corruption'. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Baydawi treat Adam's knowledge as a sign of his fitness to rule. The common thread is that knowledge is a great distinction, and the angels confess their limits: 'We have no knowledge except what You have taught us.'

In this verse the angels glorify God, declaring Him free of any deficiency, and admit that they have no knowledge except what He has taught them, affirming that He alone is the All-Knowing and the All-Wise. Commentators explain the glorification (tasbih) as a declaration that God is exalted above ignorance and that no one else knows the unseen. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir read the verse as the angels' acknowledgment of their inability to answer when God presented the creatures and asked them to name them, and as a retraction of their earlier objection. Al-Razi offers two readings: either an admission of incapacity, or a statement that God had informed them of the matter of the khalifa. Al-Qurtubi and Ibn Kathir draw from it the lesson that one should say "God knows best" when one does not know an answer, citing reports from the Companions to that effect. Al-Baydawi stresses humility and entrusting all knowledge to God. On the meaning of "the Wise", opinions differ: most take it as the one who does everything with wisdom, al-Mawardi and al-Nasafi mention the judge and the one who prevents corruption, and Ibn Atiyya and others combine the meanings. Ibn 'Ashur notes that the angels do not deny all knowledge but acknowledge that their knowledge is limited to what God makes available to them. The common message is humility before divine knowledge and submission to His wisdom.

This verse describes how God commanded Adam to tell the angels the names of the creatures shown to them, which they could not know. When Adam told them, God rebuked them: did I not tell you that I know the unseen of the heavens and the earth, and what you reveal and what you conceal? The commentators agree that the passage shows Adam's superiority through knowledge, that knowledge is a condition of the caliphate on earth, and that knowledge of the unseen belongs to God alone. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn Atiyya report that the names cover all things, whereas al-Rabi' ibn Anas and Ibn Zayd take them to be the names of the angels or of Adam's descendants; al-Mawardi and al-Nasafi keep to the names of the things named. On what the angels revealed and concealed, opinions differ. Ibn Abbas, Sa'id ibn Jubayr and al-Tabari say the revealed part was the angels' words, 'will You place in it one who causes corruption', and the concealed part was Iblis's hidden pride; al-Hasan and Qatada say the concealed part was their inner belief that God would create no creature more honoured than them. Al-Tabari prefers Ibn Abbas's reading, while al-Zamakhshari and Abu Hayyan note that the plural refers in fact to a single person, Iblis. Al-Razi lists several readings, including one that the concealment was a secret among the angels themselves. Ibn al-Qayyim stresses that knowledge raises its possessor above other creatures, and al-Qurtubi notes that no one knows the unseen except what God reveals.

This verse recalls the honour given to Adam when God commanded the angels to prostrate before him: all obeyed except Iblis, who refused and grew arrogant, and so became one of the disbelievers. The commentators agree that the prostration was an act of honour and obedience to God's command, not worship of Adam. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and most scholars hold that Iblis was among the angels, so the exception is a continuous one, while al-Zamakhshari, Ibn 'Atiyya and Abu Hayyan judge that he was a jinn, making the exception disconnected. Al-Mawardi and al-Wahidi also record differing views on the nature of the prostration, some describing it as a bowing and others as placing the forehead on the ground. On the phrase "he was among the disbelievers", al-Tabari and others take it as known to God in advance, while others hold that he became a disbeliever by his refusal. The exegetes also explain the name Iblis, derived by some from the root meaning despair, and debate whether it is foreign or Arabic. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir cite many narrations about the creation of angels and jinn, which Ibn Kathir notes are weak. The common lesson is that pride and envy led Iblis into disobedience.

God tells Adam and his wife to dwell in the Garden and eat from it freely and abundantly, but not to approach that particular tree, lest they be among the wrongdoers. The commentators agree that the prohibition implies that eating from it is forbidden, and that disobedience is wronging oneself. As for the Garden, al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baydawi hold that it is the Garden of Eternity in the heavens, while Abu Muslim al-Isfahani and the Mu'tazila say it was a earthly garden; al-Razi and others refrain from deciding. On raghadan, Ibn Abbas and Ibn Mas'ud take it to mean pleasant living, Abu 'Ubayda ample provision, and Mujahid lawful provision without reckoning. The tree is disputed at length: Ibn Abbas, Sa'id ibn Jubayr and as-Suddi say it was the grapevine, others the wheat or ear of grain, Ibn Jurayj the fig, and others the palm. Al-Tabari, followed by al-Razi and Ibn Kathir, considers it best not to specify it since no sound proof exists. On how the disobedience occurred, some say Adam forgot the prohibition, others that he interpreted it narrowly, and Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab that he ate while intoxicated, a view Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi find weak. As for Satan, Ibn Abbas and most exegetes say he seduced them face to face, citing the oath, whereas Ibn Ishaq says he whispered without appearing. The addressees of the command to descend are variously identified as Adam, Eve, Iblis and the serpent, or Adam and his descendants, with descent to earth being the majority view.

The verse describes the fall from Paradise: Satan caused Adam and his wife to slip after urging them to eat from the forbidden tree, and they were removed from the state of ease they had been in. They were then told to descend to earth, where they would be enemies of one another, with a dwelling place and enjoyment for a time. The commentators agree that Iblis was the cause of the lapse but differ on how he brought it about. Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn Mas'ud and most scholars, including al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi, hold that he addressed them directly, citing the verse 'And he swore to them, I am surely a sincere advisor to you.' Ibn Ishaq holds that he only planted the temptation in their souls, while al-Razi reports several positions. As for why Adam disobeyed, some say he forgot the prohibition, others that he disobeyed deliberately, and others that he understood it as applying only to one tree. Sa'id ibn al-Musayyib reports that Eve gave him wine, but Ibn Kathir and al-Baydawi find this doubtful since the wine of Paradise does not intoxicate. The scholars also differ on who is addressed by the command to descend: Adam, Eve and Iblis, or their descendants according to al-Zamakhshari. On the word mustaqarr, Abu al-'Aliya and Ibn Zayd take it as a place of settlement, while al-Suddi takes it as graves. The word hin is mostly understood as death, though Mujahid takes it as the Last Day. Many Israelite narrations about the serpent are cited, but what the tradition keeps is that the verse shows Satan's enmity toward humans and the temporary nature of life on earth.

The commentators explain that Adam received words from his Lord, which he accepted and acted upon, and through them God turned to him, for He is the Oft-Returning, the Most Merciful. Most of them identify these words as the supplication, "Our Lord, we have wronged ourselves; if You do not forgive us and have mercy on us, we will surely be among the losers." This is the view of Ibn 'Abbas, al-Hasan, Mujahid, Qatada, Sa'id ibn Jubayr and Ibn Zayd, and al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn 'Atiyya adopt it, al-Tabari judging it the reading the verse itself points to. Mujahid and Muhammad ibn Ka'b al-Qurazi, however, report a prayer beginning "There is no god but You, glory be to You, and praise; I have wronged myself." In another narration from Ibn 'Abbas, Adam reminded his Lord of His favours and then asked to be allowed to return to Paradise, while 'Ubayd ibn 'Umayr reports that Adam asked whether his sin had been decreed before his creation and was told it had, and then asked for forgiveness. Other opinions mention weeping, modesty or supplication in general. The verse names only Adam, since Eve followed him, as al-Razi, al-Qurtubi and Ibn 'Atiyya explain. Al-Razi and al-Ghazali describe repentance as resting on knowledge of the harm of sin, then regret, then the resolve not to return to it. On the nature of the offence, some treat it as a minor sin, since Adam was protected from major ones, while others see it as a corrective disobedience in a world without full obligation. Al-Alusi adds that God's turning includes acceptance, pardon, and the grace of enabling repentance.

The commentators explain that God commanded Adam, Eve and Iblis to descend from the Garden to the earth, and that the address extends to Adam's descendants. God promises that guidance (huda) will come to them from Him, namely the Books, the messengers and clear explanation, and whoever follows it will have no fear regarding what lies ahead nor grief over what is past. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi and al-Qurtubi broadly agree on this meaning. Abu al-'Aliya took guidance to mean the prophets, messengers and clarification; Muqatil identified it with Muhammad (peace be upon him), and al-Hasan with the Qur'an. Ibn Kathir considered these views sound, with Abu al-'Aliya's the more comprehensive. On the repetition of the command to descend, al-Zamakhshari and al-Qurtubi see emphasis and stress, while al-Razi and Ibn 'Atiyya explain it by the difference in its objects: enmity linked to the first command, the coming of guidance linked to the second. Al-Jubba'i held that there were two real descents, from the Garden to the heaven and then to the earth, and Ibn 'Ashur held that the second was a fresh command to Adam. On the nature of the Garden, opinions differ: some say it is the Garden of eternity, others an earthly garden, and al-Razi lays out several positions without deciding. The Qur'an distinguishes fear, which concerns the future, from grief, which concerns the past. Ibn Kathir cites a hadith about the people of the Fire who are purified there, and al-Zamakhshari sees in the verse a refutation of the view that faith needs no sending of messengers.

The commentators explain that this verse stands in contrast to the promise given to those who follow guidance, describing the fate of those who disbelieved and denied God's signs. Disbelief is understood as denial and concealment, and the signs as proofs, revealed books and the Quran. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi, al-Baydawi and al-Nasafi hold that the companions of the Fire are its constant inhabitants, who remain in it without dying or leaving. In this context al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir cite the hadith of Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, that the people of the Fire who are its people neither die nor live in it, while some are caused to die by it and later intercession is granted. Ibn 'Ashur reads the clause as a continuation of the conditional sentence, covering all of Adam's offspring and implicitly addressing the polytheists. Al-Razi and al-Nasafi understand the abiding as endless, while al-Alusi and Ibn 'Ashur take it as the permanence agreed upon by consensus. Ibn 'Uthaymin notes that other verses confirm absolute eternity. Al-Zamakhshari, followed by al-Qurtubi and Ibn al-Jawzi, explains that companionship here means constant attachment, and applies to the inhabitants of the Fire. On the main meaning the commentators agree, and their differences concern the details of wording and context.

God commands the Children of Israel to remember His favours, to fulfil their covenant with Him, so that He fulfils His covenant with them, and to fear Him alone. The commentators give various details. Ibn 'Abbas, al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir explain that these favours include what God bestowed on their forefathers: deliverance from Pharaoh, the parting of the sea, the manna and quails, the sending of prophets and the revelation of scriptures. Ibn Zayd holds that the favours are general and that the greatest is Islam. As for the covenant, most, including al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn al-Jawzi, take it to be all of God's commands, prohibitions and instructions, including faith in the Prophet Muhammad, whom they find described in the Torah. Al-Hasan reads it as the pact mentioned in Surat al-Ma'ida, and Qatada and Mujahid also link it to that passage. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Razi note that the promised reward is Paradise or God's pleasure. On the fear, all agree it means reverential awe, and al-Zamakhshari observes that placing the object first gives exclusivity. On not mixing truth with falsehood, most read it as distorting the description of the Prophet or claiming he was sent only to the Arabs, while Muqatil says they acknowledged some of his traits and concealed others. The commentators do not choose among these readings and treat them as compatible, the passage combining promise and warning.

In this verse God commands the Children of Israel to believe in the Qur'an that He sent down to Muhammad ﷺ, which confirms what they already have, the Torah and the Gospel. He forbids them to be the first to reject it, to trade God's signs for a small price, and commands them to fear Him alone. The commentators agree that the Qur'an confirms the Torah in matters of monotheism, prophethood and the accounts of the prophets, and that differences over certain rulings reflect the variation of times and interests. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir explain that the Qur'an agrees with the good tidings about the Prophet found in their scriptures, so that believing in it confirms those scriptures and rejecting it denies them. The pronoun in "to it" refers, according to al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir, to the Qur'an, while al-Razi and Ibn 'Atiyya mention other readings that point to the Prophet or to the Torah. As for "the first to reject it", Abu al-Aliya, Ibn Juraij and al-Tabari take it as the first among the People of the Book, whereas al-Razi and al-Baydawi see a rebuke: they should have been the first to believe, since they knew his description. Others read it as a warning against hasty rejection. The "small price" is understood by Abu al-Aliya as payment for teaching, by al-Suddi as greed for worldly gain, by al-Hasan as the entire world, and by others as leadership, bribes or the perquisites of the rabbis. Some jurists derive from it a prohibition on paid teaching of the Qur'an, but the majority permit it, relying on the hadith of Ibn 'Abbas, and Ibn Kathir limits the prohibition to someone for whom teaching is an obligation. The verse also forbids mixing truth with falsehood and concealing the truth: according to Ibn 'Abbas this means mixing truth with lies, and according to Mujahid, mixing Judaism and Christianity with Islam.

In this verse God forbids the Children of Israel to mix truth with falsehood and to conceal the truth while they know it. The commentators read the truth in closely related ways. Ibn 'Abbas, al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir take it to be the description of the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ as written in the Torah and the Gospel, which they recognised and then hid. Mujahid understands the forbidden mixing as blending Judaism and Christianity with Islam, a view also reported from Qatada and al-Hasan al-Basri. Ibn Zayd holds that the truth is the Torah and the falsehood is what they altered in it concerning the Prophet, while Abu al-'Aliya sees the confusion in their claim that Muhammad was sent to other peoples than them. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Nasafi and Abu Hayyan discuss the grammar of the conjunction in «wa takتumu». It may be a plain coordination with the prohibition, so that both the mixing and the concealment are forbidden, or it may mean «together with», so that the combination is what is forbidden. Most prefer the first reading. The commentators stress that mentioning their knowledge makes the fault graver, since wrongdoing with full awareness is worse than doing it in ignorance. The command to establish prayer, pay zakat and bow with those who bow is taken by Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi to mean praying with the Muslims and paying the alms. Al-Razi and al-Nasafi note that naming bowing stands for prayer as a whole, and they take it as an instruction to pray in congregation. In short, whoever knows the truth must make it known and is forbidden to conceal it, and mixing truth with falsehood misleads people.

This verse commands the Children of Israel to establish the prayer, give the zakat, and bow down with those who bow, meaning to pray along with the Muslims, pay the obligatory alms, and submit heart and body to God and His Messenger. Al-Tabari explains that it addresses the Jewish rabbis and hypocrites who ordered people to pray and give alms without doing so, and that ruku' here means submission to God through obedience. Al-Wahidi, al-Baghawi, Ibn Kathir and al-Baydawi agree that the prayer means the prayer of the Muslims and the zakat means the obligatory alms. They note that ruku' is mentioned alone because Jewish prayer had no bowing, so the sense is: pray a prayer that includes bowing. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Razi observe that ruku' may stand for the whole prayer, or for submission. Several commentators, including al-Qurtubi and Ibn Juzayy, take the phrase 'with those who bow' as an invitation to pray in congregation, though some do not regard this as a decisive proof. Al-Razi and al-Qurtubi draw from it that disbelievers are addressed by the rules of the law, a view al-Qurtubi links to the hadith of Mu'adh on the order of invitation. Ibn 'Ashur connects prayer and zakat to faith and sees them as evidence of a believer's sincerity. The commentators do not choose between these readings.

This verse rebukes the scholars of the Children of Israel for ordering people to righteousness while forgetting themselves, even though they recite the Book that warns against this. God asks: 'Will you not then use your reason?' Most commentators agree that the address is to the rabbis and that the verse condemns the gap between speech and conduct, not the act of enjoining good as such. The exact meaning of 'al-birr' divides the exegetes. Ibn 'Abbas took it as adherence to the Torah or to the Prophet ﷺ, whom the rabbis recognised in their scriptures yet advised others to follow without doing so themselves; he also, in another report, understood it as entering the religion of Muhammad. Al-Suddi and Qatada read it as obedience to God and piety, Ibn Juraij as prayer and fasting, and al-Zajjaj as almsgiving, which they withheld. Ibn Zayd reported that the rabbis urged a questioner towards the truth without giving it themselves. Al-Mawardi, al-Baghawi and Ibn al-Jawzi transmit these views without choosing among them. On forgetting oneself, al-Tabari and al-Razi explain it as neglecting oneself in what is good. al-Zamakhshari, al-Baydawi and al-Nasafi read the interrogative as rebuke and wonder. Some jurists drew from the verse that a sinner should not command good; al-Razi, Ibn Kathir, Ibn Sa'di and Ibn 'Uthaymin answer that the rebuke falls on neglecting one of the two duties and that a person must both exhort others and correct himself. Ibn Kathir, citing the hadith of Usama about the man whose entrails spill out in the Fire, observes that a scholar who contradicts his knowledge is more blameworthy than the ignorant.

This verse tells the Children of Israel, and by extension the believers, to seek help in their affairs through patience and prayer. It describes prayer as a heavy burden, yet one that becomes light for the humble, those who fear God and submit to Him. Most commentators, including al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi, understand patience as restraining oneself from sin and persisting in obedience. Mujahid and al-Hasan al-Basri took it to mean fasting, and several note that Ramadan is called the month of patience. The prayer is generally understood as the obligatory prayer, and it is reported that the Prophet turned to prayer whenever a matter distressed him, as Ibn Abbas related when he received news of his brother Qutham's death. Opinions differ on what the pronoun in "and it is" refers to: most say prayer, while others take it to refer to the act of seeking help or to the whole set of commands given to the Children of Israel. On the meaning of humility (khushu'), Ibn Abbas and Qatada speak of faith and fear, Muqatil ibn Hayyan of modesty, and al-Zajjaj of the visible trace of submission in the body. Regarding "those who expect to meet their Lord", most exegetes take the verb to mean certainty, whereas al-Zamakhshari and Ibn Atiyya understand it as hoping for reward, which makes the hardship easier. Al-Razi and al-Alusi stress that prayer turns the heart from this world toward the next, and Ibn Ashur presents patience as the basis of all virtues. Ibn Uthaymin adds that only prayer offered with humility restrains from indecency. The commentators agree on the call to combine patience and prayer, and on the point that humility lightens the effort of worship.

In this verse God tells the Children of Israel to seek help through patience and prayer, and says that prayer is burdensome except for the humble (khashi'in), those who are certain that they will meet their Lord and return to Him. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi and al-Qurtubi agree that the verb "zanna" (to think) here means "to be certain", and they cite Arabic poetry and the verse "I thought that I would meet my reckoning" (69:20). Mujahid, Abu al-'Aliya and al-Suddi report that every "zann" in the Quran means certainty.

The meaning of "meeting their Lord" divides the commentators. Al-Razi, al-Baydawi and al-Nasafi take it to mean seeing God, while the Mu'tazilites deny that the word implies vision. Ibn 'Atiyya understands it as receiving God's reward, and Abu Hayyan notes that vision is the view of most Muslims. As for "returning to Him", al-Tabari, al-Mawardi and Ibn Kathir apply it to resurrection, while others apply it to death, and al-Tabari prefers the first reading.

On patience, Mujahid identifies it with fasting, while others take it as restraint from sin, perseverance in duties and endurance of hardship. Regarding the pronoun in "it is indeed burdensome", commentators suggest it refers to prayer, to the act of seeking help, or to all the commands mentioned earlier; al-Zamakhshari and al-Alusi favour the last view. Ibn Sa'di explains that the believer who hopes for reward finds the effort light.

God reminds the Children of Israel of the blessings He bestowed on them and of His preferring them above the worlds of their time. Most commentators, including al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi, Ibn al-Jawzi and al-Nasafi, understand "the worlds" as the people of their own era rather than all creation, relying on the verse calling this community the best of nations and on the hadith of Mu'awiya ibn Haydah that this community is the best. Al-Tabari explains that the preference applied to their forefathers in the time of Moses and after him, before they changed, and that the honour of the fathers reaches the sons. Al-Wahidi, al-Sam'ani, al-Baydawi and Abu al-Su'ud follow the same reading. Al-Razi raises the objection and answers that the preference may hold in one respect only. Ibn 'Atiyya and Ibn al-Jawzi describe the phrase as a general term meaning a particular group. Ibn Zayd holds that only their believers are meant, since their disobedient ones were turned into apes and swine.

The commentators agree that recalling a blessing calls for gratitude through obedience, and that the mention of preference, the greatest of blessings, is a warning to those who neglect it. Ibn al-Qayyim separates absolute grace, reserved for believers, from general grace shared by all creation, and holds that each side is right on its own point. Ibn 'Uthaymin adds that the plural does not mean that their era was the best of all eras.

This verse warns the Children of Israel, and those addressed with them, about the Day of Judgment, a day when no soul can avail another in anything, when no intercession is accepted, when no ransom is taken, and when no one is helped against God's punishment. Al-Tabari explains that the Jews claimed their prophetic ancestors would intercede for them, and God dispelled this hope. Al-Tabari reads 'not avail' as not discharging another's debt, and cites the hadith of Abu Hurayra about wronging a brother, settled by transferring good and evil deeds. Al-Mawardi, al-Wahidi and others explain 'jaza' as sufficing or substituting, and 'adl' as ransom, while grammarians such as al-Farra' and al-Zajjaj distinguish between the two vowelings of the word. On intercession, al-Razi, Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi report that most scholars restrict the negation to unbelievers, since the hadiths affirm the Prophet's intercession for sinning believers, while the Mu'tazilites, relying on the verse's generality, deny it for grave sinners, an opinion their opponents reject. Ibn Kathir stresses that on that day every usual means of escape, whether favour, power or wealth, is cut off, and only God's just judgment remains.

God reminds the Children of Israel of His favour in rescuing them from the family of Pharaoh, who subjected them to the worst torment: slaughtering their sons and sparing their women. The commentators generally agree that this suffering was a severe trial from their Lord. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and others explain that the family of Pharaoh means his followers, agents and those who shared his religion, not only his relatives, and that Pharaoh was a title given to the Amalekite kings of Egypt. They differ on the name of Moses' Pharaoh: Ibn Ishaq and most others name him al-Walid ibn Mus'ab, while others give different names. The verb yasumunakum means to subject, impose on or inflict upon you. Al-Tabari and others take the "evil torment" to be the slaughter of sons and the sparing of women, whereas Ibn Atiyya and al-Qurtubi read it more broadly, including forced labour and the poll tax. As for the reason for the killings, Ibn Kathir and al-Razi mention a dream or the warnings of soothsayers that a boy from Israel would end Pharaoh's rule, while al-Tabari restricts the killing to boys. The word bala' is read by some as a trial and a hardship, and by others as a blessing, following Ibn Abbas and Mujahid. Ibn Ashur holds that the rescue of the forefathers counts as a rescue of their descendants, and al-Razi explains that recalling a blessing magnifies it and strengthens the argument against them.

God reminds the Children of Israel of the favour He bestowed when He split the sea for them, rescuing them from Pharaoh's people while they watched their enemies drowned. The commentators agree that the sea parted by Moses' staff, and that the particle in « bikum » may express cause (« because of you »), accompaniment (« with you passing through ») or benefit (« for you »). Al-Tabari and al-Sam'ani report that the sea split into twelve paths, one for each tribe. Ibn Kathir and Ibn al-Jawzi note that the event took place on the day of Ashura. Al-Tabari, al-Wahidi and others narrate that Pharaoh, reaching the shore, hesitated before his horse until Gabriel, mounted on a mare, led the way into the water, after which the sea closed over the army. Al-Razi, al-Qurtubi and Ibn 'Ashur point out that « you are looking » may mean seeing with the eyes, reflecting and taking warning, or simply knowing, as al-Farra' says. Ibn 'Ashur notes that the rescue came in two stages: escaping the pursuit, then crossing the sea. Ibn Kathir explains that the address is to the contemporaries of the Prophet, since they are the descendants of those who lived these events, and Ibn 'Uthaymin adds that God's favour to the first generation is a favour to the last. The phrase « the family of Pharaoh » refers to his army and followers rather than only his relatives. Ibn 'Ashur cautions that many detailed accounts of the episode lack a sound basis.

This verse recalls God's appointment with Moses for forty nights, during which he was to receive the Torah, and the fact that the Israelites took the calf as a god in his absence, and were wrongdoers in doing so. The commentators explain that the forty nights were Dhu al-Qa'da and the first ten days of Dhu al-Hijja, and that the appointment came after the deliverance from Pharaoh. Al-Tabari, Ibn 'Atiyya and Ibn Kathir note that the reading 'wa'adna' (without alif) makes the promise purely God's, while 'wa'adna' with alif implies mutual agreement, since Moses accepted the command; al-Tabari holds both readings correct and equivalent in meaning. Several, including al-Zamakhshari and al-Baydawi, take all forty nights to be included in the appointment, whereas some Basran grammarians read it as the end of the period. All name al-Samiri as the maker of the calf, but the detailed accounts of how he fashioned it from ornaments borrowed from the Copts come mainly from traditions whose chains al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir report without deciding, and al-Qurtubi and Ibn 'Ashur regard them as uncertain. Most understand the calf as an image whose lowing was produced by wind, while al-Hasan held that it became living flesh and blood, a view the majority rejected. Al-Razi, Ibn 'Ashur and others see the whole sequence as a lesson in Israel's ingratitude. The phrase 'then We pardoned you' is linked by commentators to the repentance that followed, with Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi reporting that seventy thousand were killed, a detail others do not accept. The reminder is meant to call for gratitude.

This verse recalls that God pardoned the Children of Israel after they took the calf as a god during Moses' absence from his people. Al-Tabari explains the pardon as God withholding immediate punishment, while Ibn Kathir presents it as a reminder of the favour granted once the appointed forty nights had ended. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Baydawi understand the pardon as the erasure of the offence through repentance. They agree that the phrase 'that you may be grateful' expresses hope, but differ on what kind of hope it is; al-Zamakhshari reads it as an intention, which al-Razi and later Sunni commentators reject. On gratitude, Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi define it as obedience with all the limbs, while al-Junayd says true gratitude is the admission of one's inability to thank God fully. On the length of the appointment, most hold that all forty nights were part of the promise, while some Basran grammarians take it to mean the completion of forty nights. The commentators also report that the Israelites killed one another as an act of repentance, which al-Razi, al-Qurtubi and Ibn Kathir mention. Al-Razi notes that the Mu'tazilites link the pardon to this repentance, a view he rejects. The commentators do not settle these readings, and the shared point is that the verse speaks of God's mercy after a grave offence.

This verse reminds the Children of Israel of the blessing God gave Moses in granting him the Book and the Furqan, so that they might be guided. The commentators agree that the Book is the Torah, and that the guidance intended is the guidance that comes from knowing it and acting on it. The meaning of Furqan, however, is discussed in several ways. Al-Tabari, Ibn Abbas, Abu al-Aliya and Mujahid take it as a description of the Torah itself, since it separates truth from falsehood, while al-Zamakhshari and al-Nasafi present it as a book that is also a criterion. Al-Zajjaj and al-Farra' regard the repetition as an emphatic restatement of the same thing. Others, including al-Shinqiti and Ibn Ashur, understand the Furqan as the miracles given to Moses, such as the staff and the hand, which divided truth from falsehood. Ibn Abbas and Ibn Zayd took it to mean the victory that separated Moses from Pharaoh, which is why the Day of Badr is called the Day of the Furqan, while others read it as the parting of the sea. Al-Razi and Ibn Atiyya object to that reading, since guidance fits the Book better. Some scholars, such as Ibn Juzayy, also report that the Furqan is the Quran given to Muhammad, though they consider this view weak. The particle la'alla is read by the commentators as expressing hope and purpose, and guidance is understood both as knowledge and as success in acting upon it.

God reminds the Children of Israel of what happened when they worshipped the calf in Moses' absence. Moses tells his people that they wronged themselves by taking the calf as a god, and orders them to turn in repentance to their Creator (bari'), to kill one another as the means of that repentance, which he says is better for them with their Creator. They obey, and God accepts their repentance. The commentators agree that the command did not mean each person killing himself with his own hand, but that some killed others. Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, Sa'id ibn Jubayr and Ibn Jurayj report that in a thick darkness or cloud they slew one another until about seventy thousand had fallen. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir hold that it was martyrdom for the slain and repentance for the living, and al-Tabari reports that Moses and Aaron pleaded with God to spare the remnant, whereupon the killing stopped. Al-Razi and al-Baydawi read the first fa' as causal and the second as sequential, with the killing completing the repentance. Al-Zamakhshari and Ibn 'Atiyya widen repentance to a series of acts whose last is the killing. Al-Qurtubi takes it that the worshippers of the calf were to be killed. Al-Qadi 'Abd al-Jabbar, as cited by al-Razi and Abu Hayyan, considers the command to kill oneself impossible on rational grounds. The verse closes by affirming that God is the Ever-Returning, the Most Merciful.

This verse recounts that the Children of Israel told Moses they would not believe him until they saw God openly, "jahratan", face to face, and that they were then struck by a thunderbolt while they looked on. The commentators agree that "jahra" means plain and open sight. Most of them, following Ibn 'Abbas, Qatada and Anas, identify the speakers as the seventy men Moses chose, while Ibn Zayd holds that it was the whole nation. On the nature of the thunderbolt they differ. Al-Sudi, al-Nahhas and Ibn al-Jawzi describe a fire sent from heaven that burned them. Al-Hasan and Qatada take it to be death itself. Marwan and some narrators speak of a cry from the sky, and Wahb of heavenly troops whose sound killed them for a day and a night. Al-Razi, al-Baydawi and Ibn Kathir prefer that the thunderbolt was the cause of death rather than death itself, citing the verse on the "raj fa" quake and the phrase "while you were looking". Al-Tabari adds that Moses was stunned but not killed, since he later recovered. The commentators explain that the revival afterwards was a blessing so that they would give thanks, and that the verse rebukes their boldness and warns the contemporaries of the Prophet. The Mu'tazila cited the verse to deny that God can be seen; the Sunni scholars answered that the punishment was for obstinacy and bad manners, not for the request itself, which al-Qurtubi and Ibn Kathir regard as permissible in the hereafter. Al-Zamakhshari, by contrast, draws from it the impossibility of such vision.

The commentators explain that God brought the Children of Israel back to life after the thunderbolt had caused them to die, so that they would give thanks. Almost all agree that the death was a punishment for asking to see God openly, and that the "raising up" was the return to life that followed. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn al-Jawzi report, following Qatada and al-Rabi' ibn Anas, that God revived them so that they could complete their appointed lifespans.

They differ on who was struck. Ibn Mas'ud, Ibn 'Abbas and most exegetes say it was the seventy men chosen by Moses, while Ibn Zayd holds that it was the Children of Israel as a whole, except those whom God protected.

The meaning of "raising" is also debated. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Abu al-Su'ud take it as a return to life after death. Al-Sudi, cited by al-Mawardi, Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Razi, reports that they then asked to be made prophets, and God granted this. Others, such as al-Razi, al-Baydawi and al-Alusi, hold that the death was a swoon rather than real death, or that "death" is a metaphor for ignorance and "raising" for teaching.

Finally, the scholars differ on whether religious duty continued after the return to life. According to al-Qurtubi, who cites al-Mawardi, most hold that it did, pointing to the fact that the Israelites, having seen the mountain hanging over them, were compelled to believe while remaining accountable. Ibn 'Ashur holds that the request to see God came after the pardon for worshipping the calf, without settling the matter further.

God reminds the Children of Israel of the favours He gave them during their wandering in the wilderness: He shaded them with clouds against the scorching sun, sent down manna and quails, and told them to eat of the good things He had provided. They did not give thanks, yet they did not wrong God; they wronged themselves. The commentators differ on the cloud. Ibn 'Abbas and most exegetes take it as a thin white cloud, while Mujahid describes a cloud colder and purer than ordinary clouds, the one in which God will come on the Day of Resurrection and in which the angels came at Badr, and others take it as any white cloud. On the manna, opinions vary: Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid and the majority say it fell on trees, Mujahid calls it a gum, al-Rabi' ibn Anas a drink mixed with water, Ibn Zayd honey, Wahb ibn Munabbih a thin bread, al-Suddi ginger, and many the terengabin. Most agree the quails are a bird resembling the common quail, though some say honey in the dialect of Kinana. The exegetes place these gifts during the wandering between Egypt and Syria. Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi cite an authentic hadith that the mushroom is part of the manna, understood either as a gift to the Children of Israel or as food obtained without toil. As for the phrase 'they did not wrong Us', al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir read it as disobedience and rejection of the blessing, while al-Zamakhshari reads it as ingratitude whose harm falls on themselves alone.

God reminds the Children of Israel of a favour: they are ordered to enter the town, which most commentators identify as Jerusalem (Bayt al-Maqdis), while some say it is Jericho near it. They may eat its produce freely and abundantly wherever they wish, enter its gate in humble prostration, and say « Hitta », meaning remove our burdens from us. In return God will forgive their sins and increase the reward of the good-doers. Most commentators understand the prostration as bowing, lowliness or submission, and the gate as the gate of the town, which some report was called the gate of Hitta. The meaning of Hitta varies: al-Hasan, Qatada and Ibn Zayd take it as a request to have sins removed; Ibn 'Abbas, al-Suddi and al-Dahhak take it as seeking forgiveness or acknowledging the truth of the command; 'Ikrima takes it as the declaration that there is no god but God; al-Zajjaj reads it as simply a request. They agree that the people disobeyed: they entered dragging themselves on their buttocks and spoke other words, as the authentic hadith reports, saying « a grain in a hair ». God then sent down a rijz from heaven, which most explain as punishment in general, while Ibn Zayd and others identify it as a plague that killed many of them. Ibn 'Uthaymin notes that doing good brings increased reward, and that altering God's words is a blameworthy distortion.

This verse of al-Baqara recalls that after the fathers of the Children of Israel were commanded to enter a city, most commentators identifying it as Jerusalem, they were told to enter its gate humbly and to say "Hittah", meaning "remove our sins", in exchange for forgiveness and increased reward for the good-doers. Those among them who did wrong changed both word and deed: they entered dragging themselves on their backsides and said "a grain in a barley-corn", mocking the command, so God sent down a punishment from heaven because of their defiance. The commentators agree that rijz means punishment and that the change was a deliberate disobedience rather than a mistake. Al-Tabari, Ibn Zayd and Muqatil, and Ibn Kathir who leans the same way, understand it as a plague that killed many of them; Ibn 'Abbas speaks of darkness and sudden death, Wahb of a plague lasting forty nights, Sa'id ibn Jubayr of hail or snow, and Abu al-'Aliya of divine wrath. The place and gate are disputed: the majority, including Qatada, al-Suddi, Ibn Kathir and al-Razi, identify Jerusalem and the Gate of Hittah, while Ibn 'Abbas and Ibn Zayd propose Jericho. Some read prostration as bowing or humility, others as literal. Several works note that the phrase fa-baddala refers to disobedience rather than mere replacement of words, and that repeating "those who did wrong" serves to condemn them more sharply.

God reminds the Children of Israel of the favour of watering them in the wilderness when they were thirsty. Moses asked his Lord on their behalf, and God commanded him to strike the rock with his staff; twelve springs gushed forth, one for each tribe, and each tribe knew its own spring so that they would not quarrel. They were then told to eat and drink of God's provision and not to spread corruption on earth. The commentators agree that this happened in the wilderness of wandering, and that the rock was carried with them and that the springs flowed when struck and ceased when no longer needed. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Qurtubi take the rock to be a specific known stone, while al-Hasan, Ibn 'Atiyya and Abu Hayyan hold that any stone would do, which they consider a greater proof of the miracle. They differ on its description: Ibn 'Abbas says it was square and the size of a man's head, 'Ata compares it to an ox's head, and others mention marble or a stone from Paradise. Al-Razi and al-Baydawi distinguish between infajara, a strong outflow, and inbajasa, a slighter one. On the verb 'atha, al-Zamakhshari and Ibn Kathir take it as the utmost corruption, while al-Tabari and Ibn Zayd read it as transgression. Ibn Kathir, Ibn 'Ashur and Ibn 'Uthaymin note that the manna and quails were a single food for them, and that choosing lesser foods instead was a sign of poor judgment. Several commentators conclude by stressing the gratitude this favour calls for.

The verse recalls the complaint of the Israelites in the wilderness, who tired of the manna and quails sent to them and asked Moses to pray that God bring forth from the earth herbs, cucumbers, garlic or wheat, lentils and onions. Moses rebuked them for exchanging what is lower for what is better, and told them to go down to a city where they would find what they asked for. The commentators agree that the 'single food' means the manna and quails, even though they were two, either because they were eaten together or because they never changed. They differ on the meaning of 'fum': Ibn Abbas, Qatadah, al-Suddi and most exegetes say wheat, while Mujahid, 'Ata' and Ibn Zayd say bread, and al-Kisa'i, al-Nadr ibn Shumayl, and Ibn Mas'ud's reading (thawmiha, with a thaa) point to garlic. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir favour wheat, while Ibn 'Ashur explains the request as a sign of their preference for the earth's produce. As for 'Misr', most read it with tanwin as any city, while Abu al-Aliyah, al-Rabi' and Abu Hayyan's sources take it as the land of Pharaoh; Ibn Kathir prefers the general sense. The verse then says that humiliation and poverty were struck upon them and they returned with the anger of God, because they disbelieved in the signs of God and killed the prophets unjustly, and because they disobeyed and transgressed. Al-Razi and al-Baydawi discuss whether the request was itself a sin, and Ibn 'Ashur and Ibn Kathir see the story as an example for later generations."}

This verse states that God rewards whoever believes in Him and the Last Day and does righteous deeds, whether he belongs to this community, to the Jews, the Christians or the Sabians: they will have their reward with their Lord, with no fear and no grief. Ibn 'Abbas and most exegetes understand 'those who believed' as the believers of Muhammad's community, 'those who became Jews' as the Jews, and the Christians as the followers of Jesus. The Sabians have drawn many views. Mujahid describes them as a people between the Jews and the Magians, without a religion; al-Suddi as a group among the People of the Book; Qatada as worshippers of angels who pray toward the qibla and recite the Psalms; Ibn Zayd as a people who only affirm that God is one, with no works or book; al-Khalil as worshippers of the stars. Ibn Kathir reports that the most likely view is that they are a people who never received the call of a prophet.

Scholars also differ on the meaning and occasion of revelation. According to al-Tabari and others, the verse was revealed about Salman al-Farisi and his Christian companions who lived in the Prophet's time; others take it to cover anyone who died faithful to his prophet's religion before the mission. Ibn 'Abbas holds it abrogated by the words 'whoever seeks a religion other than Islam, it will not be accepted from him'; Mujahid and al-Dahhak consider it unabrogated, referring to those who believed in the Prophet. Al-Tabari understands faith as steadfastness in belief, so whoever recognised the Prophet and followed him receives his reward. Al-Razi distinguishes the outward faith of the hypocrites from true faith in the two occurrences of the word.

Most explain the reward as that of the Hereafter, 'with their Lord' as a sign of its certainty, and the absence of fear and grief as safety from the terrors of the afterlife and the regrets of this world.

God reminds the Children of Israel of the solemn covenant He made with them, and of how He raised the mountain above them until they agreed to act upon what is in the Torah. He commands them to hold fast to what He has given them with determination and to remember what it contains, so that they may become God-fearing. The commentators agree that the covenant refers to a firm pledge to act by the Torah's rulings, and that 'strength' means earnest effort and resolve, though some take it as obedience, practice or sincerity. 'Remember what is in it' means study, memorization, and not neglecting its promises, threats and rulings. On the word 'al-Tur', they differ: Ibn Abbas, Ibn Jurayj, Mujahid, Qatada, 'Ata', and 'Ikrima take it to be the mountain where God spoke to Moses, or a mountain in Palestine; Mujahid says it is the Syriac term for any mountain, and al-Dahhak reports from Ibn Abbas that it means only mountains that bear vegetation. Most exegetes report that the mountain was lifted above them when they refused the Torah, that they accepted it out of fear, and that their prostration was on one side of the face. Many note that the phrase 'then you turned away' shows they broke the pledge, and that God's grace and mercy kept them from ruin, some understanding this as respite and repentance and others as the sending of messengers.

This verse reminds the Children of Israel that after accepting the covenant to act upon the Torah, while the mountain was raised above them, they turned away from it. Had it not been for God's grace and mercy, they would have been among the losers. The commentators generally understand the address as directed originally at their ancestors, and turning away as breaking the covenant and abandoning what the Torah contains. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir explain that al-Tur is the mountain on which God spoke to Moses, while al-Tabari, Mujahid and Qatada hold that the word applies to any mountain, and Ibn Abbas specifies that it is one that bears vegetation. The word 'strength' is read by Ibn Abbas and Qatada as diligence and determination, by Abu al-'Aliya and al-Rabi' as obedience, and by Mujahid as acting upon it. Al-Razi and al-Baydawi report that grace means Islam and mercy the Qur'an according to Abu al-'Aliya, whereas Ibn Juzayy understands it as the acceptance of repentance and pardon. On the meaning of 'you turned away', al-Tabari sees a reference to the worship of the golden calf, while al-Razi mentions a series of later transgressions. Al-Tabari also records the view that the address to the contemporaries of the Prophet is framed through their ancestors, which he regards as an accepted Arabic usage.

This verse recalls to the Children of Israel what their forebears experienced: some of them transgressed the sabbath prohibition on fishing, devising a trick by digging pools and channels to trap the fish until Sunday. God then told them: be apes, cast out and humiliated. The commentators agree that only a part of the people was involved, that the punishment was real, and that a ruse to bypass a prohibition is of no use. They differ, however, on the nature of the transformation. Al-Tabari, al-Wahidi, Ibn Kathir, Ibn al-Jawzi, al-Qurtubi and Ibn 'Atiyya take it as a literal change into apes, who lived no more than three days and did not reproduce, relying on a hadith reported by Muslim. Mujahid holds that only their hearts were transformed, and that the ape is a parable, as the donkey is in the Surah of Friday. Al-Razi discusses the question at length and defends the possibility of a bodily change. As for the pronoun in 'fa-ja'alnaha', Ibn Kathir and Ibn 'Atiyya favour the town, while al-Razi and al-Farra' refer it to the punishment or to the apes.
