On the meaning of 'nakalan' and 'ma bayna yadayha wa ma khalfaha', opinions differ: a deterrent for contemporaries and successors according to Ibn 'Abbas, past and future sins according to Qatada. Ibn al-Qayyim draws from this passage the prohibition of legal stratagems, a view Ibn 'Ashur partly shares. Most commentators agree that the verse offers a moral warning, especially for the God-fearing.

The verse reminds the Children of Israel of the people of the Sabbath, who broke God's prohibition on fishing that day, and God turned them into despised, banished apes. The commentators differ on what the pronoun in "fa-ja'alnaha" refers to. Ibn 'Abbas, Abu al-'Aliya and al-Rabi' take it to mean the punishment or the transformation, while another report from Ibn 'Abbas relates it to the town itself, and Mujahid and al-Farra' offer similar readings. "Nakal" means a punishment severe enough to deter anyone who sees it or hears of it. On "limа bayna yadayha wa ma khalfaha", opinions vary: Ibn 'Abbas, al-Dahhak and 'Ikrima say it means the neighbouring towns and those that will come after; Qatada and Mujahid say it means their sins before and after; al-Sudi says it means earlier and later nations; al-Hasan says it covers all their wrongdoing before and after this act. al-Tabari holds that the pronoun refers to the punishment itself. On "maw'iza lil-muttaqin", Ibn 'Abbas and Qatada take it as a lesson for every God-fearing person until the Day of Judgement, al-Sudi restricts it to the community of Muhammad, and al-Zajjaj reads it as a warning to that community against violating God's sacred limits. Some commentators hold the transformation was literal, others that it was spiritual; Ibn Kathir cites Mujahid's view that hearts were transformed, but prefers that it was both physical and spiritual.

God reminds the Children of Israel of how their forefathers reacted when Moses told them that God commands them to slaughter a cow. The cause was a murder committed among them whose perpetrator was unknown, which led to disputes that nearly erupted into fighting. When Moses ordered them to strike the corpse with part of the slaughtered cow so that it would come back to life and name its killer, they replied with scorn, asking whether he was mocking them. Moses sought refuge in God from being among the ignorant. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir report that this episode led to a tightening of the command: they kept asking about the cow's age, then its colour and its use, and God made the matter stricter for them. According to a tradition cited by several commentators, any cow would have sufficed had they not argued. The exegetes differ on the details of the story and on the identity of the killer: al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn al-Jawzi describe a nephew or relative seeking inheritance, while al-Razi and al-Qurtubi focus on the sign of God's power. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Baydawi explain that seeking refuge from ignorance means guarding against mockery and answering out of place. Ibn 'Ashur holds that the Qur'anic account differs from the Torah's version. On the meanings of fariḍ (an aged cow), bikr (a young cow) and 'awan (one of middle age), the commentators agree. Several of them warn against Israelite narratives whose authenticity cannot be verified.

The Qur'an reports that after the Israelites were commanded to sacrifice a cow, they asked Moses to request from his Lord a description of it. He replied that it should be neither an aged, worn-out cow nor a young one that has not yet calved, but one of middle age. The commentators agree that this passage exposes the Israelites' obstinacy and their endless questioning, and that they should have obeyed at once. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and others report, citing Ibn Abbas, that any cow would have sufficed, but they made the matter strict and God made it strict for them. As for the meaning of 'fari\d', the majority, including Mujahid, Qatada and Ibn Zayd, take it to mean an old, decrepit cow, while others take it to mean one that has borne many offspring. 'Bikr' is a young cow that has not yet calved or been covered, and 'awan' is one of middle age. On the colour, most exegetes, including Ibn Abbas, Qatada and Ibn Kathir, hold that it was bright, pure yellow; al-Hasan al-Basri held that 'safra' meant black here, a view that Ibn Kathir and al-Razi considered weak. Said ibn Jubayr held that the yellow applied only to the horns and hooves. On the phrases 'dhalul', 'musallama' and 'la shiyata fiha', the commentators agree that the cow had never been used for ploughing or irrigation, was free of defects, and bore no other colour. Some, such as al-Razi and Ibn 'Atiyya, debated whether the command implies generality, which would mean that the order to sacrifice any cow was later restricted; some accepted this and others disputed it. Finally, the commentators note that immediate obedience would have sufficed, and that the accumulation of qualities was a rebuke for their behaviour.

This verse reports that the people of Moses asked him to ask his Lord about the colour of the cow they had been ordered to slaughter, and God answered that it was a bright, pure yellow that delights those who look at it. The commentators, including al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi, al-Qurtubi and al-Baydawi, generally take yellow in its ordinary sense and explain fāqi' as meaning intense and unmixed, while the phrase “pleasing to the beholders” conveys admiration for its striking beauty. Ibn Abbas, Mujahid, Sa'id ibn Jubayr and Ibn Zayd hold that the cow was yellow all over, including its horns and hooves. Al-Hasan al-Basri, however, said that yellow here means very dark black, citing a line of al-A'sha; Ibn Qutayba, al-Zajjaj and al-Qurtubi rejected this, noting that the Arabs do not describe black as fāqi' but as ḥālik. On the meaning of fāqi', Ibn Abbas says it means very yellow, to the point of almost whitening, Qatada and Abu al-'Aliya say it means pure, and Qutrub says unmixed. Ibn 'Ashur observes that fuqū' applies to all colours, and that attributing the delight to the cow rather than to its colour suggests it was a particularly fine animal. Several commentators add, on the authority of Ibn Abbas and others, that the Israelites' persistent questioning made the command harder for them, which is why they are cited as a lesson against excessive questioning.

The verse recounts the Israelites asking their prophet to ask his Lord to specify the cow they were commanded to slaughter, since the cows looked alike to them, and they add that they will be guided if God wills. The commentators, from al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir to al-Zamakhshari, al-Qurtubi, al-Baydawi and Ibn 'Ashur, agree that any cow would have sufficed, but that by repeated questioning they imposed hardship on themselves, and God made the matter harder for them. They cite hadiths and reports from companions and successors on this; Ibn Kathir notes that the hadith traced to the Prophet is weak and at best may be a saying of Abu Hurayra. On the terms fariḍ, bikr and 'awān, the majority take them as an old barren cow, a young cow that has not yet borne, and one of middle age; al-Mawardi mentions another view of fariḍ as a cow that has borne many times. On the colour safra', most take it as bright yellow, while al-Hasan al-Basri understood black, a view Ibn Qutayba and al-Qurtubi reject, and Sa'id ibn Jubayr limited the yellow to horns and hooves. Several readings of tashabaha are recorded, and al-Tabari preferred the lighter form. Some exegetes, including Ibn Sa'di, warn against Israelite narratives about the cow's owner. Al-Zamakhshari and Abu Hayyan see the phrase 'if God wills' as an expression of humility, while al-Razi draws from it an argument about divine will.

This passage tells how Moses described to his people the cow God commanded them to slaughter: one not broken to plough or to draw water for the crops, sound and free of defects, with no mark of a colour other than its own. They said: now you have brought the truth; and they slaughtered it, though they had almost not done so. The commentators, including al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi, Ibn al-Jawzi and al-Qurtubi, agree that the requirements were made stricter because of the Israelites' persistent questioning, and that any cow would have sufficed had they not pressed the matter. On the meaning of 'without a mark' (shiya), opinions differ: Mujahid understood no white and no black, Qatada and Abu al-'Aliya no white, Ibn Zayd a pure yellow, and al-Sudi no red. On 'unblemished' (musallama), Ibn 'Abbas and Qatada said free of defects, Mujahid free of marks, and al-Hasan free of labour. As for the high price, accounts differ: Muhammad ibn Ka'b and Ibn 'Abbas say they bought it for the weight of its hide in gold, 'Ikrima says it cost only three dinars, and Wahb attributes their reluctance to fear of exposure. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir lean towards a combination of reasons without deciding between them. Some exegetes note that the verb 'kada' here expresses difficulty and reluctance rather than a plain negation, and that grammarians have debated its sense.

This verse reminds the Children of Israel that they killed a soul and then disputed about it, each party pushing the blame away from itself, and that God would bring out what they were concealing. The commentators explain that the verb fa-ddara'tum means to quarrel and to repel one another, from the root daraʾa, its original form being tadara'tum with the t assimilated into the d. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi take it to mean disagreement and dispute, while al-Zamakhshari and al-Baydawi also understand it as each side throwing the killing onto the other. Al-Tabari explains that the bringing forth means making manifest what was hidden, namely the killing and the identity of the killer. Ibn Kathir adds that God left vague which part of the cow struck the dead man, since no religious benefit depends on knowing it. The scholars agree that this verse comes first in meaning, though it is placed after the command to slaughter the cow in the order of recitation. Al-Razi notes that the statement that God will bring forth what is concealed is stated in the present tense to describe a past situation. Al-Qurtubi and Ibn Kathir connect the story to the rule that a killer does not inherit and to the procedure of collective oaths, although the verse itself does not settle these questions. Ibn Kathir and others draw the general lesson that God does not leave hidden deeds unrevealed.

God reminds the Children of Israel of the murder whose culprit they disputed among themselves. He ordered them to slaughter a cow and strike the dead man with part of it; he came back to life, named his killer, and died again. Commentators see in this a proof that God can resurrect the dead on the Day of Judgment, and a display of His power so that people may reason and refrain from sin. On which part of the cow was used, opinions differ: al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and others leave it unspecified, Mujahid, Qatada and Ikrima mention the thigh, as-Suddi the flesh between the shoulders, Abu al-Aliya a bone, Ibn Abbas the bone next to the cartilage, al-Dahhak the tongue, and Ibn Jubayr the tip of the tail. Al-Tabari holds that knowing the exact part neither harms nor benefits. All agree the man rose, spoke, and died again, and that the killer was barred from inheritance. Al-Qurtubi and Ibn Juzayy report that Malik relies on this story to accept the victim's own accusation, a view most scholars reject. Al-Zamakhshari explains that the narrative follows the order to sacrifice to rebuke two separate offences: mocking God's command and the killing itself.

God reminds the Children of Israel that after the signs they had witnessed, their hearts hardened until they became like stones, or even harder. The commentators agree that this hardness means a heart that is closed to reflection and refuses to submit to God, even though the preceding miracles should have softened it. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi take the particle « or » as offering a choice or as an imprecision meant for the listener; al-Tabari also cites readings in which it means « and » or « rather », but he ultimately favours the view that some hearts are like stone and others harder than stone. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Baydawi note that the form « harder » is stronger than « hardest » and that whoever knows their state might liken them to stone or to something harder still, such as iron.

The verse then names what stones do that these hearts do not: some burst forth with rivers, some split and release water, and some fall from the mountain out of fear of God. The exegetes differ on the meaning of « falling » and of « fear ». Mujahid, Ibn Jurayj and al-Tabari read it as an image of obedience to God's command, while al-Razi, Ibn Kathir and others accept that God may give some stones a measure of perception, citing the hadith of the trunk that wept and the stone that greeted the Prophet; the Mu'tazilites reject this, as al-Razi reports. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir also mention the view that the falling refers to the mountain that crumbled at the theophany.

The verse closes with a warning that God is not unaware of what they do, and that He will recompense them for it.

God rebukes the believers for hoping that the Jews would accept their message, when a group among their forebears heard the word of God and then distorted it after understanding it, knowing what they did. The commentators disagree about who this group was. Mujahid, al-Suddi and Ibn Abbas, followed by Ibn Kathir and most scholars, identify them as Jewish scholars who altered the Torah, changing its rulings, the description of the Prophet ﷺ and the verse on stoning. Al-Rabi ibn Anas and Ibn Ishaq hold that they were the seventy men chosen by Moses, who heard God's speech on the mountain and then misreported it to their people. Al-Tabari prefers this second view and argues that the verse refers to those who directly heard God's word; al-Qurtubi and Ibn al-Jawzi reject the claim that the seventy heard God Himself. On the manner of distortion, Ibn Abbas speaks of altering meaning through interpretation while the words remained, whereas most scholars hold that words were changed. The commentators agree that the Jews of the Prophet's time followed the path of their ancestors, which makes their belief unlikely. Ibn Kathir reports that Jewish hypocrites told the believers they had faith, then privately urged one another not to reveal what their Book contained, lest they be condemned before God. The verse ends with a rebuke: their ignorance is not from lack of knowledge, since they know that God knows both their secrets and their public words. Al-Zamakhshari and Abu al-Su'ud note that the knowing character of the scholars' sin makes it graver than that of the ignorant.

This verse describes the conduct of some hypocritical Jews in Medina. When they met the believers they professed faith, but when they were alone some of them rebuked others for having told the Muslims what their scripture says about the Prophet ﷺ, fearing the believers would use it as evidence against them before their Lord. Most commentators, including al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Qurtubi and al-Baydawi, take 'what God has revealed to you' to mean the description of the Prophet ﷺ in their Scripture. Al-Tabari gives 'fath' the sense of judgment and decree, and understands it as what God had ordained for them, including the covenant to believe in Muhammad. Ibn Kathir also cites Qatada and Abu al-Aliya, who share this reading. Al-Suddi and Ibn Zayd offer another reading: some Jews related to the believers the punishments inflicted on their forebears, and others reproached them for it. Mujahid reports that the phrase refers to the Qurayza Jews, whom the Prophet ﷺ had called 'brothers of apes and swine'. On 'that they may argue against you before your Lord', al-Hasan takes it as a matter of religion, al-Asamm places it on the Day of Resurrection, and al-Razi records Abu Bakr al-Qadi's view that it may mean argument aimed at sincere admonition and establishing proof. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Nasafi take 'Will you not reason?' as part of the speech of those who rebuked, while Ibn 'Ashur and al-Baydawi also allow that it is God addressing the believers. The verse ends with 'Do they not know that God knows what they conceal and what they reveal?', which the commentators read as a rebuke for supposing that their hidden thoughts could escape God.

This verse rebukes believers who hope that the Jews will accept their faith, since a group of them heard God's word and then distorted it after understanding it, knowingly. It then states that God knows what they conceal and what they reveal, and it rebukes those who think their hidden matters are hidden from God. Commentators differ on who the pronoun refers to. Al-Tabari, Qatada and Abu al-Aliya explain that the Jews conceal their disbelief in the Prophet ﷺ and display faith in front of the believers, a view Ibn Kathir follows. Ibn 'Atiyya holds that what the rabbis concealed was the description of the Prophet and their knowledge of him, while the wording covers everyone. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Baydawi report that the hypocrites tell the believers they have faith, and then, when they are alone, those who did not dissemble reproach the others for telling the Muslims what God had revealed in their scripture about the Prophet, fearing the believers would use it as proof before their Lord. The meaning of God having 'opened' this to them also varies: the description of the Prophet in the Torah, the punishment imposed on them according to as-Suddi, or what God taught them. Ibn Kathir reports that this verse concerns hypocritical Jews, and that the Prophet ﷺ had said that no one but a believer should enter the town. As for the unlettered among them, Ibn Kathir and others take them as common people who know the Book only by recitation without understanding its meanings. The word 'amani' is read in two ways; for many it means recitation, and for others lies or fabrications. Abu Hayyan takes 'they only conjecture' to mean wavering between two options.

This verse describes a segment of the Jews, the common people, who are unlettered (ummiyyun): they cannot read or write and do not understand the Torah. What they have of it is recitation without comprehension, or 'wishes' and falsehoods received from their leaders. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir explain that the unlettered here means one who cannot write, and that the exception in 'except wishful thinking' is disjunctive, meaning 'but'. Al-Farra', al-Kisa'i and al-Zajjaj take 'amani' to mean mere recitation. Ibn 'Abbas and Mujahid understand it as lies, while Qatada, al-Hasan and Abu al-'Aliya take it as the wishes the Jews formed about God: forgiveness without accountability, intercession by their forefathers, a limited term of punishment. As for 'they only conjecture', Mujahid explains it as lying, whereas al-Tabari, al-Rabi' and Qatada take it as doubt or assumption without certainty. Al-Razi notes that these ordinary people follow their scholars by imitation. Ibn Kathir reports a different view attributed to Ibn 'Abbas, that the unlettered are those who rejected a book and a messenger, but he questions the soundness of that transmission. Most commentators see the verse as referring to the mass of the Jews and their followers, mentioned after other groups, which makes hope for their faith unlikely.

This verse threatens severe punishment for certain Jewish scholars who altered the Scripture with their own hands and then attributed what they had written to God, in order to gain a small worldly price. The commentators agree that "wayl" means ruin and intense punishment, but they differ on its nature. Al-Tabari, citing Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, describes it as a valley in Hell into which the disbeliever falls for forty autumns, while others relay from 'Uthman ibn 'Affan that it is a mountain of fire, and Sufyan al-Thawri and Abu 'Iyad describe it as the pus flowing from the damned. Ibn 'Abbas explains it simply as severe torment, and al-Khalil as extreme evil. The phrase "with their own hands" is understood by al-Razi, Ibn 'Atiyya and Abu Hayyan as an emphasis, excluding the idea that they merely ordered others to do it. As for the alteration itself, Ibn 'Abbas, al-Suddi and al-Rabi' say it concerned the description of the Prophet ﷺ in the Torah, while al-Tabari stresses false doctrines presented as revelation. Regarding the "gain" mentioned, al-Tabari and Ibn al-Jawzi take it to mean bribes and illicit profit, whereas others take it to cover all sins. The repetition of "wayl" is read by many as a way of stressing its gravity, and al-Razi notes that lying about God, misleading others and loving this world together make the offence even greater.

In this verse God quotes the claim of the Jews that the Fire would touch them only for a number of counted days. The commentators differ on the length of these days. Ibn 'Abbas, Qatada, 'Ata', al-Suddi, Abu al-'Aliya, al-Hasan and others hold that they were forty days, the number of days during which the Israelites worshipped the calf, or a period sufficient to fulfil an oath of God. Another report from Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid and Ibn Jurayj says that the Jews believed the world would last seven thousand years and that they would be punished one day for each thousand years, which makes seven days. Ibn 'Abbas also reports that they found written in the Torah that the distance between the two edges of Hell was forty years' journey, and that they would cross one year each day. Al-Kalbi alone mentions the idea that God swore to punish them for forty nights. Many exegetes say the verse was revealed as a rebuttal of this claim. God tells His Prophet to ask them whether they have made a covenant with God, for God does not break His covenant, or whether they are saying about God what they do not know. Most read this as rebuke and reproach. The verse then gives a general rule: whoever earns an evil deed that his sin surrounds will be a companion of the Fire, where he will abide forever, while those who believe and do righteous deeds will be companions of Paradise, where they will abide forever. Ibn 'Abbas, al-Dahhak, 'Ata', Abu al-'Aliya and al-Rabi' take the evil deed to mean associating partners with God, while others take it to mean a major sin, and some understand being surrounded by one's sin as persisting in it until death without repentance. The people of the Sunna take from the verse that only the disbeliever abides forever in the Fire, whereas the Mu'tazilites cite it to affirm the eternal punishment of the grave sinner. Al-Razi also notes that the verse shows that God is free from lying in His promise.

This verse answers the claim of the Jews that the Fire will touch them only for a few counted days. God declares that the reality is otherwise. Most commentators agree that whoever commits an evil deed, which for Ibn Abbas, Mujahid and Qatada is shirk, and whose wrongdoing surrounds him so that he dies without repentance, belongs to the Fire and remains in it forever. Those who believe and do righteous deeds are the people of Paradise, where they abide eternally. All agree that to be surrounded means to be overwhelmed on every side with no way out. They differ on the meaning of sayyi'a and khati'a. Ibn Abbas, Abu al-'Aliya and al-Rabi' ibn Anas take both to mean shirk, al-Hasan and al-Suddi take the evil deed to be a major sin, al-Rabi' ibn Khuthaym takes the wrong to be a sin one dies holding without repenting, and Qatada and Ikrima describe persistence in sin until death. Mujahid reports that sins rise over the heart until they cover it. Al-Zamakhshari and the Mu'tazila take the verse to mean that the perpetrator of a grave sin dwells forever in the Fire, whereas al-Tabari, al-Baydawi and Ibn Kathir, following the Sunni position, hold that eternal abiding applies only to disbelievers, since being surrounded by sin applies only to the unbeliever. Al-Razi lays out the arguments of both sides without deciding. Nafi' reads the plural khati'atuhu, the others the singular.

This verse from al-Baqara states that those who believe in what the Prophet ﷺ brought and do righteous deeds, meaning they obey God, perform His obligations and avoid what He forbids, are the people of Paradise, where they will remain forever. It answers the claim of the Jews that the Fire would touch them only for a few days. Al-Tabari takes it to refer to believers of this community and earlier ones, and reports from Ibn 'Abbas that whoever believes in what his people rejected and acts on what they abandoned will have Paradise, while Ibn Zayd takes it to refer to the Prophet and his companions. Ibn Kathir compares it to the verse saying that salvation comes neither from wishes nor from the wishes of the People of the Book. Al-Razi explains that God pairs threat with promise to show His justice and mercy and to keep the believer's fear and hope balanced. The commentators agree that good deeds accompany faith and require sincerity and following the Sunna, as Ibn Sa'di notes. Regarding eternity, most exegetes apply it to disbelievers and associators. Al-Razi and al-Baydawi say the verse offers no decisive proof about the fate of one who commits a major sin, while al-Zamakhshari and al-Alusi observe that the conjunction introduces a contrast. Al-Baydawi holds that the conjunction shows that deeds lie outside the definition of faith. Nearly all the commentators see the verse as a reply to the Jewish claim and a reminder of divine justice founded on faith and action.

God reminds the Children of Israel of the covenant He made with them, as set out in the Torah: to worship God alone, to be good to parents, relatives, orphans and the needy, to speak good words to people, to establish prayer and to give zakat. The commentators see this pledge as a foundation of religion that does not change from one revelation to another. Al-Tabari explains that the verb 'not worship' may be read in the second or third person, since taking a covenant is like making someone swear, and he links kindness to parents with gentle speech and humility. Ibn Kathir notes that God joins the rights of parents to His own right. On the reading of 'hasanan', Hamza and al-Kisa'i read it with a fatha, while most read it with a damma and sukun; al-Tabari prefers the fatha, whereas Ibn 'Atiyya and Abu Hayyan consider the two forms to have the same meaning. Ibn 'Abbas takes the good word to mean the testimony of faith and calling to good, Sufyan al-Thawri takes it as ordering what is right and forbidding what is wrong, and al-Hasan as gentleness and good conduct. As for 'except a few of you', al-Tabari, al-Nasafi and Ibn Kathir understand it as those who believed or remained faithful, such as Abdullah ibn Salam. Some relate the rebuke to the contemporaries of the Prophet, others to their ancestors. Al-Qurtubi notes that some scholars held the command to speak well to be abrogated, a view Ibn 'Atiyya does not accept for the Children of Israel.

God reminds the Children of Israel of the solemn covenant He made with them in the Torah: that they should not shed each other's blood, nor expel one another from their homes. They acknowledged this and bore witness to it. al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi and al-Razi understand shedding blood as killing, and hold that members of one community are like a single soul, so that killing another is in effect killing oneself. They cite the hadith that believers are like one body. al-Zamakhshari and al-Baydawi add that killing a kinsman may be treated as killing oneself when it brings retaliation. Ibn 'Atiyya and others read the verse more broadly as forbidding any acts that make blood lawful or lead to exile. On the phrase 'then you acknowledged, while you were witnesses', al-Tabari and Ibn Juzayy take it as addressed to the Jews of the Prophet's time, who are the heirs of their forefathers, while others read it as addressed to the forefathers with the witnessing emphasised. al-Qurtubi and Ibn Kathir report that the verse concerns the Aws and Khazraj and their Jewish allies, who fought one another and then ransomed captives although the Torah forbade killing, so they were rebuked for believing in part of the Book and rejecting the rest. The commentators agree that this breach was gravely condemned, though they differ on how many clauses the covenant contained and on the exact meaning of al-ithm and al-'udwan.

In this verse God addresses the Children of Israel and rebukes them for their contradictions. In the Torah they had pledged not to shed each other's blood, not to expel one another from their homes, and to ransom their captives. Yet they broke the first two while keeping the third. The commentators relate that this happened in pre-Islamic times between al-Aws and al-Khazraj: Qurayza were allies of the Aws and al-Nadir allies of the Khazraj, so they fought, destroyed each other's houses, and then ransomed those taken captive once the fighting ended, which earned them the scorn of the Arabs. The exegetes agree that the verse censures this inconsistency of believing in part of the Book and disbelieving in another. Ransoming is the part they accepted, while killing and expulsion are the part they rejected. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir identify the worldly disgrace as the killing of the Banu Qurayza and the exile of the Banu al-Nadir, while al-Hasan takes it to be the poll tax, and al-Razi understands it as a general and unrestricted great shame. The readings of tadahharun, asra and tufadduhum differ, and al-Tabari notes they are close in meaning, though Abu 'Amr distinguished between asra and usara, a distinction many scholars did not accept. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Nasafi report that the covenant had four undertakings, including not aiding the enemy, and that they kept only the ransoming. All conclude that the recompense is disgrace in this world and the most severe punishment on the Day of Resurrection, and that God is never unaware of what they do.

This verse describes those who traded the life of this world for the Hereafter: the Jews who, in violation of the Torah's commands, killed some of their own people and drove others from their homes, yet ransomed captives when they were taken. The commentators explain that the Aws and Khazraj fought each other in Medina, each tribe supported by a Jewish allied clan, so the Jews slaughtered and expelled one another, then paid ransom to free prisoners, which the Arabs mocked as inconsistent. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi agree that the disgrace in this world refers to the killing of the Banu Qurayza and the exile of the Banu Nadir, while the punishment of the Hereafter is the greatest. Al-Tabari and al-Zamakhshari read 'bought' as a figure of speech for preferring the lower to the higher. Al-Razi notes that most scholars restrict the words 'nor will they be helped' to the Hereafter, since the verse describes a recompense for their deeds, while al-Wahidi applies the denial of lightening to both worlds. Ibn Atiyya and Abu Hayyan focus on grammar and recitation, while Ibn Juzayy and al-Qasimi concentrate on the reasons for the revelation. Modern commentators such as Ibn Sa'di and Ibn Ashur draw the lesson that choosing one's obligations according to one's interest brings the same fate.

The verse recalls God's favours to the Children of Israel: He gave Moses the Torah, sent messengers one after another after him, gave Jesus son of Mary clear proofs, and strengthened him with the Holy Spirit. It then rebukes them for how they responded: whenever a messenger brought them what their desires did not favour, they grew arrogant, denying some and killing others. The commentators largely agree that the Book is the Torah, that the verb 'qaffayna' means to follow or send after, and that the 'clear signs' are miracles such as raising the dead and healing the blind and the leper, though some also take them to mean the Gospel. On the Holy Spirit, al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Qurtubi and al-Baydawi mostly identify it with Gabriel, while others take it to be the Gospel, the Greatest Name by which Jesus raised the dead, or Jesus's own soul. The meaning of 'holiness' is given as purity, blessing, or a name of God. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Razi explain that the present tense 'you kill' depicts a past scene to make its horror vivid, whereas others read it as pointing to the plot against the Prophet ﷺ. All agree the verse is a rebuke and that desire drives the rejection of truth, but they differ on who the two groups are, with many linking the denied to Jesus and Muhammad and the killed to Zechariah and John. They set out these views without judging between them.

This verse reports that the Jews said, "Our hearts are wrapped," meaning they cannot grasp what the Prophet calls them to. Commentators differ on the meaning of "ghulf." Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, Qatada, Abu al-'Aliya and al-Suddi understood it as hearts covered by coverings or sealed, unable to understand; al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn al-Qayyim favoured this reading. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Baydawi related it to the uncircumcised. Others, including Ibn 'Abbas in another report, 'Ata' and al-Kalbi, took it to mean vessels full of knowledge that need nothing further. A minority reading, plural of "ghilaf" (sheath), is attested, and al-Tabari discusses it. God answers with "Nay, Allah has cursed them for their disbelief": the verse presents their closedness as the result of their disbelief, not of the nature of their hearts, a point all the commentators share. On "fa-qalilan ma yu'minun," al-Tabari, Qatada and Abu Muslim understood that few of them believe; Ma'mar took it to mean they believe only in part of what they have; al-Waqidi and al-Kisa'i read it as outright negation, as in the Arab saying that a land hardly grows anything. Al-Tabari treats "ma" as an emphasis, while Ibn 'Ashur allows that scarcity may denote absence. The verse thus describes a refusal attributed to disbelief rather than an original closedness of heart.

This verse describes how the Jews, when the Quran came to them from God confirming what they already had, rejected it, although before his coming they had sought victory through this prophet against the Arab polytheists and had threatened them that a prophet was near whom they would fight alongside. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir explain istiftah as seeking victory, and both relate, through Ibn Ishaq, that the verse was revealed concerning the Jews of Medina who lived beside the Aws and Khazraj, and that they rejected him because he came from the Arabs rather than from the children of Israel. Al-Tabari understands that they knew the truth and denied it. Abu Hayyan, al-Shawkani and Ibn Ashur give other senses of istiftah, such as informing others of the nearness of a prophet. On grammar, al-Farra' takes the second lamma with its answer as the answer, al-Mubarrad holds that kafaru bihi answers both and the second lamma was repeated because the sentence is long, while al-Zajjaj and al-Akhfash posit an omitted answer. Al-Razi attributes their disbelief to fear of losing leadership and wealth, while al-Zamakhshari and Abu Hayyan point to envy and the desire for dominance. All agree that the curse means being removed from God's mercy, and that the Jews are the first addressed by it since they had recognised the truth. Ibn al-Qayyim gives several arguments showing the contradiction in rejecting him after seeking victory through him. Ibn Uthaymin notes that anyone who rejects the truth because it conflicts with his desires resembles them.

This verse describes some Jews who sold their souls for disbelief in what Allah revealed, out of envy and defiance, because Allah was bestowing His grace, meaning revelation and prophethood, on whomever He willed among His servants, namely Muhammad ﷺ, who was from the Arabs rather than the Children of Israel. The commentators agree that 'ishtaraw' means 'they sold' here, that 'bi'sa ma' is a rebuke, and that 'baghyan' means envy, which al-Baghawi, al-Wahidi and Ibn Kathir link with injustice and the coveting of what is not theirs. On the two wraths, opinions differ. Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn Ishaq and one report of al-Tabari hold that the first wrath was for losing the Torah or worshipping the calf and the second for rejecting Muhammad ﷺ, while Qatada, Abu al-'Aliya, al-Hasan, al-Sha'bi and 'Ikrima hold that the first was for rejecting 'Isa and the Gospel and the second for rejecting Muhammad and the Qur'an. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Razi mention other views, including that the second wrath merely reinforces the first. Al-Tabari notes that intense anger need not come from a single cause but from several. On 'muhin', most exegetes understand it as humiliating and degrading, while al-Tabari and Ibn 'Uthaymin add that the punishment of sinful Muslims is a purification rather than a humiliation. Grammarians differ on the role of 'ma' after 'bi'sa', as subject, specifier or relative pronoun, and most commentators take 'an yakfuru' as the object of the reproach.

This verse reports the reply of the Jews when they were called to believe in what Allah had sent down, namely the Qur'an. They said they would believe only in what had been sent down to them, the Torah, and would reject whatever came after it. Al-Tabari, Qatada, Abu 'Ubayda and al-Farra' explain that "what lies behind it" means what came after the Torah, or whatever else was revealed. All agree that the Qur'an is the truth and confirms what they already possess.

Ibn Kathir, al-Sa'di and al-Tabari show that God exposes their contradiction: whoever believes in the Torah must believe in what confirms it. Al-Razi and al-Qurtubi add that believing in some scriptures while rejecting others is not genuine faith. The question "why did you kill the prophets of Allah?" is taken by most commentators, including al-Tabari, al-Baghawi and Ibn Kathir, as addressed to the present Jews because they approved their ancestors' deeds, and as a rebuke. Al-Tabari also reports that as-Suddi understood it as a reproach aimed at them.

On the verb tense, al-Tabari, al-Razi and al-Qurtubi note that it refers to the past, since the words "before" clarify this. Some grammarians see it as describing a habitual conduct. The conditional "if you are believers" is read by several commentators as an emphasis on the contradiction, with its answer implied or placed earlier in the sentence.

This verse states that Moses came to the Children of Israel with clear signs proving his truth, such as the staff, the hand, and the splitting of the sea, and that they then took the calf as a god after he had gone or after his coming, depending on what the pronoun 'after him' refers to. In doing so they were wrongdoers, worshipping what does not deserve worship. The commentators agree that the verse rebukes the Jews of the Prophet's time, who claim to believe in what was revealed to them, and that its purpose is to refute that claim by showing what their ancestors did. They differ on what the 'clear signs' are. Ibn 'Abbas and Ibn al-Jawzi understood them as the content of the Tablets, the lawful and the unlawful, while Muqatil, Ibn Kathir and others took them to be the nine signs, which Ibn Kathir extends to include the cloud, the manna and the quails. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Baydawi hold that repeating the episode of Mount Sinai binds the present-day Jews to their ancestors' conduct, while al-Razi sees the repetition as emphasis and as establishing the argument. Ibn 'Ashur judges that the passage moves the debate on to a stronger argument. For Ibn 'Atiyya and Ibn Kathir, the word 'then' indicates a delay after considering the signs, which makes the offence greater. On the question of wrongdoing, al-Tabari, al-Baghawi and al-Nasafi explain it as placing worship in the wrong place, and Ibn Kathir adds that they knew there is no god but God. Most take the final clause as a circumstantial phrase, while some take it as a parenthetic remark meaning that wrongdoing is their habit.

God reminds the Children of Israel of the covenant He took from them to act upon what is in the Torah, when He raised Mount Sinai above them as a warning. He commanded them to hold fast to the Book with determination and to listen with obedience and acceptance. They answered, "We hear and we disobey," setting their disobedience against the command, whether in words or in deeds. As for the phrase "and the calf was made to soak into their hearts," the commentators agree that it means the love of the calf penetrated and took root in their hearts. Al-Tabari, al-Mawardi, Ibn Kathir and others take it as a metaphor for deep attachment, like water seeping into the body, while al-Zamakhshari and al-Baydawi compare it to dye soaking into cloth. Al-Suddi and Ibn Juraij report that Moses burned the calf, scattered its dust on water, and that those who loved it had gold residue on their lips; yet al-Tabari, Ibn 'Atiyya, al-Qurtubi and Abu Hayyan argue that the words "in their hearts" rule out this literal reading.

The commentators also agree that the verse "Say: how evil is what your faith commands you!" is a rebuke and a mocking irony. Attributing the command to their faith is sarcastic, since true faith does not order the worship of a calf or the killing of prophets. Al-Razi, al-Baydawi and al-Nasafi see the phrase "if you are believers" as casting doubt on their claim to faith. Ibn 'Atiyya and Abu Hayyan note that it may also function as a denial, or as a conditional whose answer is implied.

Scholars differ on whether the words "we hear and we disobey" were actually spoken. Ibn Kathir, Ibn Juzayy and al-Qasimi take them as spoken, while al-Mawardi, al-Razi and Ibn 'Ashur read them as figurative speech, with their conduct standing in for the statement. Ibn 'Ashur also notes that the mention of the mountain here adds a rebuke aimed at the Jews contemporary with the Prophet, who share the attitude of their ancestors.

God commands His Prophet ﷺ to confront the Jews with a decisive challenge: if the Last Abode, meaning Paradise and its blessings, is theirs alone to the exclusion of other people, as they claim, then let them wish for death so that they may reach it, if they are truthful. The commentators agree on the main purpose, which is to refute their claim, since whoever is certain of Paradise longs for death to escape the abode of troubles. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir report that the verse also carries the sense of mutual imprecation (mubahala), each side calling for death upon the liar, as transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas, Qatada, Abu al-'Aliya and al-Rabi'. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Baydawi and al-Razi understand the wish as a desire of the heart expressed in words, whereas Ibn 'Abbas takes it to mean simply asking for death with the tongue. Al-Razi and al-Qurtubi rely on the phrase 'they will never wish for it', which they read as a prophecy of the unseen, since no Jew is recorded to have made such a wish, and they cite the hadith that had they wished it they would have died on the spot. Ibn Kathir finds the mubahala reading more convincing, because wishing for death does not necessarily signal righteousness, while Ibn 'Uthaymin prefers the apparent meaning. Al-Biqa'i and Ibn Juzayy report the explanation attributed to Ibn al-Zubayr for the use of 'lan' here and 'la' in the Friday sura, namely that the condition is future here and present there. The commentators draw no legal ruling from the verse; it remains an argument of theological and linguistic refutation.

God states that the Jews will never wish for death, because they know that what their hands have sent forward, namely disbelief and sins, bars them from Paradise, and that God knows the wrongdoers well. The commentators differ on the command to wish for death in the preceding verse. Ibn 'Abbas, Qatada, Abu al-'Aliya and al-Rabi', as transmitted by al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir, understand it as calling down death on the liar of the two parties, a mutual invocation (mubahala). Al-Tabari, Ibn al-Jawzi, al-Zamakhshari, al-Razi and al-Baydawi take it as a real call to desire death, issued as a challenge. All agree that the Jews refrained, and that this refusal exposes the falsity of their claim that the Hereafter belongs to them alone, since whoever is certain of Paradise longs for it.

Al-Tabari and al-Zamakhshari explain that "what their hands have sent forward" is a figure for deeds, the hand being the instrument of most sins; al-Baydawi and al-Nasafi specify disbelief in the Prophet, distortion of the Torah and the killing of prophets. Ibn 'Atiyya, al-Sam'ani and Ibn Kathir count the verse among the signs of prophethood, since the prediction of their refusal came true. Al-Razi answers the objection that wishing is an inward act: in the Arabic usage, a wish is known only through speech, and no one reported that they had uttered one.

Ibn 'Ashur notes that the verse challenges the Jews of the Prophet's time, and that its force extends to later generations, since no Jew is known to have wished for death. The verse closes with a warning that God, who knows the wrongdoers, will hold them to account.

This verse states that the Jews are the most eager of all people for life, even more than the polytheists, so that one of them would wish to live a thousand years, yet a long life will not remove him from punishment, and God sees what they do. The commentators broadly agree that the verse addresses the Jews, and that their attachment to life stems from their knowledge of what awaits them in the Hereafter because of their disbelief and deeds. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn Juzayy report that the wish for a thousand years is hyperbole for a very long life rather than an exact number, and Ibn Kathir cites the Persian greeting wishing a thousand years to the sneezer. As for the polytheists meant, Ibn Abbas, Ibn Qutayba, al-Zajjaj, Abu al-'Aliya and al-Rabi' identify the Magians, Muqatil identifies the Arab polytheists, while al-Razi and al-Qurtubi take it to include anyone who denies the resurrection. On the phrase 'ma huwa bi-muzahzihihi', al-Tabari and al-Baydawi explain that a long life does not distance its bearer from punishment, while some grammarians treat 'huwa' as a pronoun of support, and others as an ambiguous pronoun clarified by what follows. The commentators also differ on how to parse 'wa min al-ladhina ashraku': some attach it to 'the most eager', others take it as a new sentence. Most conclude that the subject is the Jews and that the mention of the polytheists serves to stress the extent of their eagerness.

This verse answers the Jews who claimed that Gabriel was their enemy because he brings punishment and war, and said they would have believed if the revelation had come through Michael. The commentators explain that Gabriel sent the Qur'an down upon the heart of the Prophet ﷺ by God's permission, that it confirms earlier scriptures, and that it is guidance and good news for believers. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi and Ibn al-Jawzi agree that the verse was revealed concerning the Jews. On the occasion of revelation, al-Tabari and others report two accounts: some hold that it was a debate between the Prophet and Jews about prophethood, including the story of Ibn Sawriya transmitted from Ibn Abbas and Ikrima; others hold that it was an exchange between Umar ibn al-Khattab and Jews, reported by al-Sha'bi, al-Suddi and Qatada, whose chain Ibn Kathir notes is broken. The scholars agree that Gabriel and Michael are named after the general term for angels to honour them. They explain that revelation descends upon the heart because it is the seat of understanding and memory. Opinions differ on the meaning of the word 'permission': some say command, others knowledge or facilitation. There is also debate about the answer to the conditional: al-Zamakhshari, Ibn 'Atiyya and most scholars take 'he has sent it down' as the response or its justification, while the authors of the Jalalayn supply an omitted response. The commentators note many forms and readings of Gabriel's name, and Ibn Abbas and Ikrima explain it as 'servant of God'. The verse concludes that whoever is an enemy of God, His angels, His messengers, Gabriel or Michael, God is the enemy of the disbelievers.

This verse states that whoever is an enemy of God, His angels, His messengers, Gabriel and Michael, then God is an enemy to the disbelievers. The commentators, including al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir, report that it responds to Jews who claimed Gabriel was their enemy because he brings punishment and war, while Michael was their friend because he brings rain and fertility. The verse answers that enmity toward either one amounts to enmity toward the other and toward God. Al-Tabari explains that enmity toward God means disobeying Him and fighting His allies, and that the explicit repetition of God's name at the end avoids any ambiguity about what the pronoun refers to. Several exegetes explain that Gabriel and Michael are named separately after the angels to honour them, while al-Razi and others discuss their relative rank. All agree that Gabriel is the one who brought the Quran down upon the Prophet's heart, confirming earlier scriptures and offering guidance and good news to believers, so hostility toward him has no basis. The commentators also record many readings of the names Gabriel and Michael, and Ibn 'Abbas and 'Ikrima gave the meaning 'servant of God' for their components. Scholars differ on how the condition connects to its answer: some take the answer to be 'it was he who sent it down', while others hold the answer is implied. The verse thus remains a warning against hostility toward the angels and messengers, which the commentators treat as disbelief.

God tells His Prophet Muhammad ﷺ that He sent down to him clear signs that attest to the truth of his prophethood, and that only the defiant, those who depart from obedience to God, reject them. The commentators largely take these signs to be the Qur'an, with its disclosures about things hidden from the People of the Book and about the distortions of the Torah. Al-Tabari, followed by Ibn Kathir, reports that the occasion of revelation was Ibn Sawriya's words to the Prophet: 'You have brought us nothing we recognise,' and the verse answers him. Al-Razi adds that the signs also include other miraculous proofs. Most commentators understand 'kufr' here as denial and 'fisq' as departure from obedience. Opinions differ on the article in 'al-fasiqun': al-Zamakhshari, al-Nasafi and Abu al-Su'ud see it as generic or as referring to the Jews, while Ibn 'Atiyya takes the word to mean disbelievers. Al-Hasan al-Basri notes that when 'fisq' is used for a type of sin, it denotes the gravest of that type. The following verses speak of the Jews breaking their covenants and casting aside God's Book, which al-Tabari explains as throwing away and breaking. The commentators diverge on the passages about Harut and Marut and Solomon's sorcery: al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir incline to the view that the two angels did not send down magic, while others report that they were sent as a trial, and Ibn Kathir notes that many of these accounts come from Israelite traditions. Overall, they agree that the signs are clear and that rejection stems from corruption and departure from the religion, not from any weakness in the proof.

This verse rebukes the Children of Israel for breaking their covenants: every time they made a pact, a group among them cast it aside. The commentators agree on the condemnation of breaking one's word, but differ on which covenant is meant. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir take it to be the pledge to believe in Muhammad ﷺ found in the Torah, citing the report about Malik ibn al-Sayf who denied that any such pledge had been taken from them. 'Ata' instead understands the agreements made between the Prophet ﷺ and the Jews, which they broke as the Banu Qurayza and Banu al-Nadir did, a view also given by al-Baghawi and al-Qurtubi. Al-Razi widens the covenant to cover all the proofs and promises made to God. On the phrase 'a group among them', al-Zamakhshari and al-Baydawi explain that it does not necessarily mean a minority, since some did not break the covenant, and al-Razi adds that the following words 'but most of them do not believe' rule out the idea that the breakers were few. Al-Tabari defines faith as sincere acceptance of the truth, and notes the verse is read as meaning that most do not believe in God or His messengers. Ibn Sa'di draws from the phrase 'every time' that breaking covenants had become their habit, and that lack of faith is the cause. Ibn 'Ashur observes that the verb 'cast aside' evokes the image of throwing away what one was holding, a picture of abandoning the pact.

This part of the verse says that a messenger from Allah came to the People of the Book, confirming what they already had of the Torah, and that a group among them cast the Book of Allah behind their backs as if they knew nothing. Al-Tabari and most commentators identify the messenger as Muhammad ﷺ and the Book as the Torah, since rejecting the Prophet who confirms it amounts to rejecting it. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Qurtubi and al-Nasafi also hold that the Book of Allah may mean the Qur'an, which they rejected after having been bound to accept it. Al-Razi, al-Biqa'i and Abu al-Su'ud favour the Torah, because rejection can only apply to what one first held to. The phrase 'behind their backs' is a metaphor for turning away from something and neglecting it completely. Al-Sha'bi reports that they read the Torah without acting on it, and Sufyan al-Thawri that they wrapped it in silk and brocade and adorned it with gold without following its rulings. As for 'as if they did not know', most take it as a comparison with the ignorant, although their knowledge was firm and they feigned ignorance out of obstinacy; Ibn 'Ashur reads the denied knowledge as knowing that the Qur'an is the speech of Allah. Al-Tabari holds that they acted with knowledge and stubbornness, and Qatada that they concealed and denied what they knew. Commentators differ on who cast it aside: some say their scholars, others the people as a whole. Ibn Kathir links this rejection to their subsequent turn toward the sorcery taught by the devils.

The Quran reports that some Jews rejected God's Book and followed what the devils recited during the reign of Solomon. The commentators agree in clearing Solomon of disbelief: it was the devils who disbelieved, teaching people sorcery. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir relate that the devils eavesdropped on the heavens, added lies to what they heard, and buried their writings beneath Solomon's throne; after his death they dug them up and attributed them to him. On the two angels Harut and Marut, opinions differ. Most early scholars hold that they were angels sent to Babylon as a trial: they warned whoever came to learn from them, saying, 'We are only a test, so do not disbelieve.' Mujahid and others take what was sent down to them to be what separates a man from his wife. Some make them two men or two clans of jinn, while others reject the stories told about them, and several regard the accounts linking them to the planet Venus as Israelite lore. On the nature of magic, the Sunnis hold it has a real effect by God's permission, whereas the Mu'tazila and Abu Hanifa see it as illusion. All agree that learning and practising it is disbelief, while learning it only to guard against it is not sinful. The text stresses that magic harms only by God's leave and profits no one. It then condemns those who sold their faith for it, and opens the door of repentance through faith and piety. The verse forbidding the words 'ra'ina' warns believers against a word the Jews twisted into an insult, and tells them to say 'unzurna' instead; God adds that the disbelievers wish no good for the believers, and that He grants His mercy to whom He wills.

This verse contrasts what the Jews chose, namely learning the sorcery that the devils recited, with the reward God gives to those who believe and fear Him. The commentators explain the plain meaning: had the Jews believed in the Prophet ﷺ and the Qur'an, and guarded themselves against sins such as sorcery, God's reward would have been better for them than what they gained through magic. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi explain that mathuba means reward and recompense. Al-Akhfash holds that the answer to the conditional is implied, while al-Zamakhshari and al-Baydawi see the nominal sentence as conveying the permanence and firmness of that reward. Abu Hayyan mentions the possibility that the phrase expresses a wish, and Ibn Ashur reads it as a rebuke. The commentators agree that the verse belongs to a passage condemning the Jews who cast aside God's Book and followed what the devils recited during the reign of Solomon. Solomon was not an unbeliever; it was the devils who disbelieved by teaching magic. Several scholars, including al-Qurtubi and Ibn Kathir, note that the accounts of Harut and Marut rest largely on Israelite narrations with no sound prophetic chain, so many prefer to keep to the Qur'an's wording. Opinions differ on who the two angels were. Most commentators conclude that the verse calls to faith and piety as the path to the better reward.

This verse forbids believers from saying « rā'inā » to the Prophet ﷺ and orders them to say « unzurnā » instead, while listening attentively, and it warns the disbelievers of a painful punishment. For most commentators, « rā'inā » means: give us time and watch over us until we understand, or: lend us your hearing. They agree that the Jews twisted their tongues when saying it, intending an insult or to call the Prophet foolish, so the Muslims were forbidden to use it to block this route of mockery. Ibn 'Abbas, Qatada, al-Baghawi and Ibn Kathir report that the word was an insult in the Jewish language, whereas al-Tabari and 'Atā' hold that the Ansar used it in pre-Islamic times. « Unzurnā » is explained by al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Razi as « wait for us » or « turn your gaze toward us ». Ubayy and al-A'mash read « anzirnā », meaning « grant us respite ». Al-Tabari prefers the reading with the hamza of connection. Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Alusi understand « listen » as listening in obedience and acceptance, not mere hearing. Al-Razi and al-Zamakhshari offer other reasons for the prohibition, such as the fact that the verbal form suggests equality with the Prophet. Al-Tabari judges that the harshness of the expression was the cause of the prohibition and that the verse condemns every lapse of courtesy. As for the painful punishment for the disbelievers, most read it as the Jews who mocked the Prophet, while some take it in general terms. The following verse adds that the People of the Book and the polytheists do not wish any good to descend upon the believers from their Lord, and that God grants His mercy to whom He wills, as al-Jaza'iri and Ibn Sa'di put it.

This verse states that those who disbelieve among the People of the Book and the polytheists do not wish any good to be sent down upon the believers from their Lord, and that God singles out whom He wills for His mercy, for His grace is immense. The commentators generally agree that the good here refers mainly to revelation and prophethood, and that mercy refers to prophethood, the Qur'an or Islam. Al-Tabari, al-Baghawi and Ibn Kathir explain that the verse exposes the envy of the Jews and the polytheists toward the Muslims, and forbids the believers to rely on them or to listen to their words. Al-Razi and Abu Hayyan discuss the grammar: the first min clarifies, the second is an added particle that stresses generality, and the third indicates origin. Ibn Atiyya holds that mercy covers every favour God gives His servants. Al-Zamakhshari notes that God's choice of whom to make a prophet is itself a great grace. Ibn Kathir links the verse to the preceding prohibition against saying 'ra'ina', and commentators also connect it to the abrogation verse that follows. Ibn Ashur adds that envy, not attachment to their own religion, prevented the Jews from accepting Islam. Ibn Uthaymin draws the lesson to beware of the community's enemies and not to entrust them with its affairs.

The commentators explain that God states that whatever verse He abrogates, altering its ruling or removing its wording, or whatever He causes the Prophet to forget without abrogating it, He will replace with something better for the servants in benefit and reward, or with its like. Ibn 'Abbas, Qatada and Mujahid tie the superiority to ease and benefit, while others understand it as greater reward. The scholars agree that abrogation is rationally possible and has occurred in the law, and that rulings follow interests that change with circumstances. Abu Muslim al-Isfahani denied that it had occurred and treated the cases as specification, though many regard this as a verbal disagreement. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir note that nunsiha may mean causing to forget, leaving, or delaying, and that several readings are transmitted with their justifications. Concrete abrogations are cited, such as the change of prayer direction from Jerusalem to the Kaaba, the abrogation of the one-year waiting period for widows, and the replacement of the 'Ashura fast by Ramadan. Regarding the interrogative in 'Did you not know', most read it as a confirmation, reminding the listener of God's power and sovereignty over the heavens and earth so that no one contests what He legislates. Accounts of the occasion differ: some report that Jews or polytheists criticized his commanding then forbidding, while others link the verse to the change of qibla. The commentators agree that the verse explains the wisdom of abrogation and answers those who reject it.

This verse teaches that abrogation (naskh) belongs to God's wisdom and to His complete dominion: when He abrogates a verse or causes it to be forgotten, He brings something better for the believers in benefit or reward, or one equal to it in effort and merit. The commentators agree that abrogation exists, is lawful, and serves the interests of the servants. Al-Tabari defines naskh as the transfer of a ruling from one state to another, and notes that it may concern the ruling alone, the wording alone, or both. Ibn Kathir and al-Zamakhshari report that some verses were abrogated in both their text and their ruling. The readings differ: most read “nunsikha” meaning “We cause it to be forgotten or set aside,” while Ibn Kathir and Abu 'Amr read “nunsa’ha” meaning “We postpone it.” Al-Tabari and Ibn al-Jawzi add that “better” may mean lighter for the people or more rewarding, depending on the case. Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Baydawi stress that “better” does not imply that one verse is superior to another, since all of God's speech is good. Al-Razi and al-Qurtubi explain that the question is rhetorical and serves as an affirmation, that the address to the Prophet is meant for his community, and that God's dominion over heaven and earth grounds His right to command. Ibn al-Qayyim and Ibn Kathir read the passage as a rebuttal of the Jews who denied abrogation, while Abu Muslim al-Isfahani rejected it, and al-Shawkani notes that this dispute is largely verbal. The exegetes also agree that excessive questioning should be avoided, and that whoever exchanges faith for disbelief has strayed from the right path.

This verse warns believers against challenging their Messenger with demands and questions as the Children of Israel challenged Moses, and states that whoever exchanges faith for disbelief after the truth has become clear has strayed from the straight way. The commentators differ on who is addressed. Abu Muslim, al-Asamm, al-Jubba'i and al-Razi take the believers as the audience, while al-Razi, Ibn Kathir and others prefer the Jews, and Ibn Abbas and Mujahid identify the Quraysh. The occasions of revelation vary: according to Ibn Abbas, Rafi' ibn Huraymila and Wahb ibn Zayd asked for a book sent down from heaven and rivers made to flow, Mujahid reports that the Quraysh asked that Safa be turned into gold, and Abu al-'Aliya relates a story about the expiations of the Children of Israel. Nearly all agree on the core meaning: the verse forbids the spiteful and demanding question put after proofs have been established, not the question asked by one who wishes to learn, which the text does not condemn. The word sawa' is explained as the middle and the direct line of the path, so going astray means veering from that line. Al-Tabari and others take kufr here as denial and iman as affirmation, while Abu al-'Aliya reads the pair as hardship and ease, an interpretation most do not adopt. Ibn 'Ashur sees the final clause as a general conclusion that reinforces the prohibition. Ibn Kathir and Ibn 'Uthaymin add that excessive questioning is blameworthy unless there is a real need.

This verse reports that many People of the Book wish to turn the believers back into disbelief after their faith, out of envy that comes from their own selves, even though the truth about the Prophet ﷺ has become clear to them. Commentators explain that this envy springs from their own inclinations and not from a command in their scriptures. Al-Tabari, al-Baghawi and Ibn Kathir understand the verse as telling the believers to pardon and overlook the harm and disputes from the People of the Book until God's command arrives, which they interpret as the fighting, the killing of the Banu Qurayza and the expulsion of the Banu al-Nadir. Ibn Abbas, Qatada, al-Suddi and Abu al-'Aliya hold that the verse was abrogated by the verse of fighting in Surat al-Tawba, while al-Razi and Abu Hayyan argue that since the deadline is known only through revelation, the abrogation still applies. Ibn 'Ashur explains that the wish for the Muslims to return to polytheism is stated in general terms, and that the closing phrase reminds that God is powerful over all things. On the occasion of revelation, opinions differ: some mention Hudhayfa and 'Ammar facing the Jews after Uhud, others Huyayy ibn Akhtab and his brother Abu Yasir, others Ka'b ibn al-Ashraf. Al-Tabari finds it unconvincing that the plural refers to a single man. The verse ends by affirming God's complete power.

In this verse God commands the believers to establish the prayer and give the zakat, and assures them that whatever good they send forward for themselves they will find with God, who sees all that they do and loses none of their deeds. The commentators connect the verse with the preceding passages about the envy of many People of the Book toward the Muslims and their wish to turn them back to disbelief, so the command to pray, give alms and do good is presented as the right response in that situation. All agree that 'good' means every act of obedience and righteous deed, and that 'you will find it with God' means you will find its reward. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir link the verse to a correction of certain words addressed to the Prophet, a reading Ibn 'Atiyya considers weak. The verse also contains a promise to the doers of good and a warning to others, since God's seeing is a form of knowledge of everything. Most scholars read the command to pardon and overlook as a call to patience until God permits fighting. Ibn 'Abbas, Qatada and al-Suddi held this command to be abrogated by the verse of the sword, while al-Razi and al-Baydawi discuss the abrogation depending on how the final clause is understood. Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi cite occasions of revelation involving Huyayy ibn Akhtab and Ka'b ibn al-Ashraf. The commentators generally conclude that the verse urges steadfastness in worship and good works, with the certainty that the reward is safeguarded with God.

The Quran reports the claim of Jews and Christians that no one will enter Paradise except one who follows their own religion. The two claims are merged into a single phrase for brevity, then God replies that these are mere wishes without foundation, and commands His Prophet to ask them to produce proof if they are truthful. The commentators, including al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Qurtubi, al-Baydawi and Ibn 'Ashur, agree that the verse refutes this exclusive claim, that hud is the plural of ha'id, meaning one who returns to the truth, and that amaniyy are wishes pursued without the action needed to attain them. Al-Tabari and others say the verse addresses any group claiming salvation for itself alone, and that burhan means a clear proof. Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi see the real answer in God's words 'Nay', meaning the reality is otherwise: whoever submits his face to God while doing good enters Paradise. Several explain that submission means sincerity toward God, and goodness means deeds that conform to the revealed law; Ibn Kathir stresses that a deed is accepted only when it combines sincerity with following the Prophet's way. Al-Baghawi and al-Tabari take 'face' to mean the self or intention, singled out for its nobility. As for 'those who do not know', some identify them as Arab polytheists, others as peoples earlier than Jews and Christians; al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir hold that the verse may include all of them. Most report that the revelation was occasioned by the delegation of Najran and the Jews of Medina, who quarrelled in the Prophet's presence. Several conclude that the final judgment belongs to God on the Day of Resurrection, who will decide between truth and falsehood in what they disputed.

This verse answers the claim of the Jews and Christians that only those who follow their religion will enter Paradise. God replies that this is not so: whoever submits his whole self to God and does good will enter it. Al-Tabari, al-Wahidi, al-Baghawi and al-Nasafi explain that submitting the face means devoting oneself sincerely to God, and the face is named because it is the noblest part of the body and the place of prostration, so the rest of the body follows it. Most commentators agree that ihsan means acting in line with the revealed law. Al-Zamakhshari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn Sa'di note that a deed is accepted only when it is both sincere and in accordance with the Sunna, and Ibn Kathir cites the hadith that whoever does a deed not based on our command will have it rejected. Al-Razi adds that ihsan means worshipping God as if you see Him. The reward is with the Lord, and there is no fear or grief for these believers: al-Tabari and al-Razi explain that fear concerns the future and grief the past. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Baydawi observe the shift between singular and plural pronouns, caused by the word man, and consider the singular more elegant at the start. The commentators also report the occasion of revelation, a dispute before the Prophet between the Jews of Medina and the Christians of Najran, in which each group said the other had nothing. Ibn Kathir, al-Tha'alibi and al-Qurtubi, citing Ibn 'Abbas, note this, and Ibn Kathir holds that the text blames each side for speaking so while knowing the truth. As for « those who do not know », some identify them as the pagan Arabs and others as earlier peoples. Al-Tabari, quoted by Ibn Kathir, judges that the verse covers all these groups at once, since no proof singles out one of them.

This verse describes how the Jews and the Christians each denied the other any standing in religion, even though both recite the Book. The commentators agree that the verse condemns this mutual rejection, and that the phrase 'while they recite the Book' is a rebuke: their own scriptures contradict what they say. Ibn Abbas, transmitted by al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn Ishaq, reports that the revelation came after a quarrel between Jewish rabbis and a Christian delegation from Najran in the presence of the Prophet, in which each side denied the prophet and scripture of the other.

Scholars differ on who 'those who do not know' are. The majority, including Ibn Abbas, al-Zamakhshari and Ibn Kathir, understand them to be the pagan Arabs, who had no scripture. Ata' takes them to be earlier nations such as the people of Noah and Hud, while Mujahid takes them to be ordinary Christians. Al-Tabari judges that no decisive proof singles out one group, so the verse may be read as covering all of them, a view Ibn Kathir also favours.

As for 'God will judge between them on the Day of Resurrection', al-Tabari and al-Razi explain it as a separation between the one who is right and the one who is wrong. Al-Hasan holds that God will declare them all liars and cast them into the Fire, whereas al-Zajjaj says that God will show them with their own eyes who enters Paradise and who enters the Fire. Al-Razi adds that the same dispute recurs within the Muslim community whenever each sect declares the others to be unbelievers.

In this verse God declares that there is none more unjust than one who prevents the name of God from being mentioned in the mosques, through prayer, recitation and the like, and who strives to ruin them. The commentators differ on who is meant. Ibn 'Abbas, Qatada, al-Suddi and Mujahid say it refers to the Christians, or the Romans, who helped Nebuchadnezzar destroy the sanctuary of Jerusalem, threw filth into it and stopped people praying there. Al-Tabari prefers this view because the surrounding verses address the People of the Book. Ibn Zayd, 'Ata' and Abu Muslim hold that it refers to the Quraysh polytheists who barred the Prophet and the Muslims from the Sacred Mosque at Hudaybiyya. Ibn Kathir favours this view and answers al-Tabari that barring the remembrance of God from the Ka'ba is itself a ruin of it. Al-Razi and others argue the ruling is general, covering anyone who blocks access to a mosque, since the plural does not prevent a single case being the occasion. As for the phrase "they would enter only in fear", some read it as a description of Christians who entered Jerusalem only in disguise and fear, others as a promise to the Muslims that the unbelievers will be humbled and will enter the Sacred Mosque only in dread, and others as a prohibition on letting them in. Most identify the disgrace in this world with killing, the poll tax or humiliation, and the great punishment in the Hereafter with the Fire. Jurists differ, as al-Razi and al-Qurtubi report, on whether a non-Muslim may enter a mosque: Abu Hanifa permits it, Malik forbids it, and al-Shafi'i distinguishes the Sacred Mosque from others.

This verse states that the East and the West, meaning the whole earth, belong to God, who owns and directs them. Wherever the believer turns his face, by God's command or out of necessity, there is the face of God, meaning His chosen direction, and God is vast and all-knowing. The commentators explain that the verse was revealed in the context of the change of qibla from Jerusalem to the Ka'ba, which the Jews criticised, according to al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir.

Other commentators report different occasions. Ibn 'Umar, followed by several scholars, links the verset to the voluntary prayer of a traveller on his mount, while Mujahid and Ibn Zayd take it to mean that the Ka'ba is the qibla that the believer faces from anywhere on earth. Others connect it to people who prayed in a dark night without knowing the direction, or to the funeral prayer for the Negus, as Qatada and Ibn Juzayy report.

Most agree that the prayer of one who sought the direction through ijtihad and later discovered his mistake remains valid, a view noted by al-Qurtubi and which Ibn Juzayy considers the soundest. The word "wajh" is understood by most as direction, qibla, or God's approval, while Ibn Qayyim and al-Razi reject any reading that would place God in a location. As for "wasi'", al-Tabari understands it as generosity and providence, Ibn Kathir as knowledge and mercy, and al-Qurtubi as the facility God grants His servants. Some regard the verse as abrogated by the command to face the Sacred Mosque, while al-Tabari holds it to be unabrogated.

In this verse God declares Himself exalted above the claim, made by Jews, Christians and polytheists, that He has taken a son. He affirms that everything in the heavens and the earth belongs to Him and submits to His command and governance. Commentators agree that a son must be of the same nature as his father, and that a created being owned by its Creator cannot be His offspring. They give the word "qanitun" closely related meanings: Mujahid, Qatada, al-Suddi and Ibn 'Abbas understand obedience, 'Ikrima and Muqatil understand acknowledgment of servitude, al-Rabi' understands standing before God on the Day of Resurrection, and Ibn Kaysan understands standing firm in testimony. Some also read a compelled submission of the whole cosmos. Most agree on several arguments: ownership contradicts sonship, the creation of the heavens and the earth shows that God can create without needing a son, and the phrase "Be, and it is" shows that nothing can resist Him.

The commentators differ on who is meant by "they said". Some point to the Jews who said 'Uzayr is the son of God, others to the Christians who said the Messiah is the son of God, and others to the Arab polytheists who said the angels are God's daughters. Ibn 'Atiyya and Abu Hayyan note that the verse may include all three groups. They also differ on the scope of "all": Ibn 'Abbas and al-Farra' take it to mean only the obedient believers, while the majority take it as general, including disbelievers whose shadows prostrate unwillingly. al-Tabari prefers the meaning of obedience and of the creation's acknowledgment of its Creator.

Some commentators also cite the hadith in al-Bukhari in which God says that the son of Adam calls Him a liar and insults Him by claiming He has a son, which shows how grave this claim is.

This verse states that God is the Originator of the heavens and the earth, meaning their Creator without any prior model, and that when He decrees a matter, He only says to it "Be!" and it is. Al-Tabari explains that "badi'" means one who brings into being what no one has done before, and he links this to the sense of a blameworthy innovation in religion. The commentators agree that the verse answers those who ascribe a son to God, whether Christians, Jews, or Arab polytheists. If God originates the heavens and the earth and can create by a single word, He has no need of a child and can create a being without a father. Al-Mawardi, al-Baghawi and al-Razi develop this argument, and Ibn Kathir adds that a son must be of the same nature as his father, whereas God has no equal and no consort. On the meaning of "Be!", opinions differ. Al-Tabari holds that the command neither precedes nor follows existence; others see a general statement of the immediate effect of divine power; al-Zamakhshari and al-Baydawi read it as a picture of the speed of creation rather than a real utterance; and some theologians take it as a real, eternal word. As for the reading, Ibn 'Amir reads "fayakuna" in the accusative while the majority read it in the nominative, and Ibn 'Atiyya considers the accusative weak. The commentators agree on God's complete power and transcendence, while differing on how creation takes place.

This verse reports the demand of those who lack knowledge: why does God not speak to us directly, or why does no sign come to us? The commentators differ on who they were. Mujahid, followed by al-Tabari, identifies them as Christians; Ibn Abbas says they were the Jews of the Prophet's time; Qatada, al-Suddi, al-Rabi' and most exegetes say they were the pagan Arabs, and some combine these views into one group. Here 'law la' carries the sense of an urging 'why not', as al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Zamakhshari and Abu Hayyan explain.
