The phrase 'so said those before them' consoles the Prophet ﷺ, since earlier peoples said the same. All agree the request reflects stubbornness rather than a search for truth, and that the Quran itself is a sufficient sign. On 'their hearts are alike', opinions vary: Mujahid and Qatada speak of the Jews, Christians and pagans sharing unbelief; al-Tabari sees the shared obstinacy and demand for the impossible; Ibn Kathir and al-Sa'di see blindness and obstinacy. The verse concludes that the signs have been made clear, yet only those who are certain benefit from them, while the doubtful gain nothing however clear they are.

This verse states that God sent His Prophet Muhammad with the truth, as a bringer of good news to believers and a warner to those who reject, and that he will not be questioned about the people of the blazing Fire once he has delivered the message. The commentators broadly agree that his duty is only to convey, announce and warn, that guidance belongs to God alone, and that the verse consoles him for the stubbornness of his opponents. They differ mainly over the reading of the word 'tus'alu'. Al-Tabari, Ibn 'Atiyya, al-Razi, Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi prefer the majority reading in the indicative, meaning 'you will not be asked', that is, you are not held accountable for their disbelief. Al-Zamakhshari, Abu Hayyan and Ibn 'Ashur also read it as consolation and a warning. The jussive reading, attributed to Nafi' and Ya'qub, is taken by several scholars as a prohibition, though Abu Hayyan and al-Zamakhshari note that it can also express the enormity of their punishment, as when one says of someone who has fallen into calamity: do not ask about him. Some link this reading to a weak, unconnected report from Muhammad ibn Ka'b al-Qurazi that the Prophet wondered what had become of his parents; al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn 'Ashur reject this report as weak, while al-Qurtubi and al-Baydawi mention it. Al-Wahidi and al-Baghawi record another occasion of revelation, in which the Prophet said that if God sent His punishment on the Jews they would believe.

This verse states that the Jews and Christians will never be pleased with the Prophet ﷺ until he abandons his creed and follows theirs. Most commentators explain that the aim is to make him despair of their conversion. God tells him to reply that the guidance of God, meaning Islam, is the true guidance and not what they follow, and then warns him against following their desires after knowledge has come to him, for he would then have no protector or helper against God. At-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi, Ibn 'Atiyya and Ibn al-Jawzi agree that the address is to the Prophet while its scope includes his community, and that the guidance is Islam. Az-Zamakhshari and al-Nasafi hold that what these two communities call to is mere desire and innovation rather than guidance. On the occasion of revelation the reports differ: Ibn 'Abbas links it to the change of the qibla, when Jews and Christians gave up hope that he would adopt their direction; Muqatil links it to their invitation to join their religion; Ibn 'Atiyya and Abu Hayyan report that they sought a truce while promising to follow him later. Al-Baydawi, al-Alusi and others explain that the negation with 'la' is for emphasis and that each group's satisfaction is separate from the other's. Ibn Kathir, al-Qurtubi and Abu Hayyan record a legal debate on whether unbelief is one religion for inheritance purposes, with Malik and one narration of Ahmad holding that it comprises several. For the following verse, most commentators take 'those whom We gave the Book' to be the believers among the People of the Book or the Muslim community, and true recitation to mean reading correctly, acting on its rulings and following its guidance, as reported from Ibn Mas'ud, Ibn 'Abbas and al-Hasan.

This verse speaks of those given the Book who recite it as it should be recited and truly believe in it, while whoever rejects it is among the losers. Commentators differ on who is meant. Ibn 'Abbas, 'Ikrima, Qatada, Muqatil and Ibn al-Jawzi take it to mean believers among the People of the Book, or even the Companions of the Prophet, with the Book being the Qur'an or the Torah depending on the view. Al-Tabari and Ibn Zayd hold that it refers to the scholars of the Children of Israel and those among them who embraced Islam, the Book being the Torah; al-Tabari prefers this view because of the context of the surrounding verses. On the phrase 'recite it as it should be recited', Ibn Mas'ud, Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, Qatada and al-Hasan mostly explain it as following the Book, making lawful what it makes lawful and unlawful what it forbids, and acting on it; others understand it as reading it as it was revealed, without distortion. Al-Hasan adds that one should act on its clear verses and entrust the obscure ones to God. Scholars also differ on the pronoun 'in it', which refers to the Book according to al-Zamakhshari, al-Baydawi and Ibn 'Atiyya, but may refer to the Prophet or to the guidance mentioned earlier. Ibn Kathir and Ibn al-Qayyim stress that true recitation combines reading, understanding and practice. As for the occasion, Ibn 'Abbas links the verse to the people of the ship who came with Ja'far ibn Abi Talib, while others apply it to the Companions of the Prophet.

This verse calls the Children of Israel to remember God's favour and His preference of them over the peoples of their time. To remember means to give thanks, that is, to believe in God and His messenger and follow him. Al-Tabari reads it as an admonition to the Jews of Medina in the Prophet's time, reminding them of the blessings granted to their ancestors: deliverance from Pharaoh, manna and quails in the wilderness, settlement in the land, and prophets raised among them. Ibn Kathir and al-Biqa'i hold that the repetition of the verse, already given at the start of the surah, serves to emphasise and to urge following the unlettered Prophet whose description they find in their scriptures. Abu Hayyan and Ibn 'Ashur see it instead as a summary conclusion of the discourse, and Ibn 'Ashur regards the change of order between ransom and intercession as a matter of stylistic variety. On the meaning of the 'worlds', Ibn 'Atiyya explains that it refers to their contemporaries, since the community of Muhammad is superior to them, while others take it as a general term covering all creation. For the second passage, Ibn Kathir and al-Jaza'iri explain that on the Day of Judgement no soul can avail another, no ransom will be accepted, and no intercession will benefit, and that whoever rejected the Book will be among the losers. Ibn 'Uthaymin notes that this negation concerns the intercession of disbelievers, without excluding the intercession God permits.

This verse warns the Children of Israel to be mindful of a day when no soul can avail another in anything, when no ransom will be accepted, when no intercession will benefit, and when no one will be helped. The commentators explain that it repeats a warning already given at the beginning of the surah, and that the repetition serves as emphasis and as a summary closing the account of the Children of Israel. Al-Tabari, al-Zamakhshari, Ibn Kathir, Ibn 'Atiyya and Abu Hayyan agree that the passage calls the People of the Book to follow the unlettered Prophet, whose description they find in their scriptures. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir take the warning to address those who distorted the Book, while al-Zamakhshari explains that the preceding verse concerns the believers among the People of the Book. On intercession, al-Sam'ani, al-Shawkani and Ibn 'Uthaymin note that the negation is general but is qualified by the intercessions established in the Sunnah, and that any intercession requires God's permission and approval. Ibn 'Ashur reads the negation of intercession as meaning that no authorised intercessor exists. Several scholars observe that the order of ransom and intercession differs between the two passages, and al-Biqa'i and Ibn 'Ashur present this as a stylistic variation suited to each context. The commentators set out these views without judging between them.

This passage recounts how God tested Abraham with commands and prohibitions, which he fulfilled completely, and how God made him an imam for mankind. The commentators agree that the 'words' were demanding obligations Abraham carried out, but they differ on what they were. Ibn 'Abbas, in one transmission, al-Sha'bi, Tawus and Ibn Kathir link them to the practices of natural purity such as rinsing the mouth, sniffing water into the nose, circumcision, trimming the moustache and the nails; Mujahid, Abu Salih and al-Rabi' take them to be the trials mentioned after the verse, namely the appointment as imam, the building of the House and the rites of pilgrimage; Qatada limits them to the rites of pilgrimage; al-Hasan lists the stars, the fire, the emigration and the sacrifice of a son. Al-Tabari declines to fix one meaning and considers that several may be correct together, while Ibn Kathir leans toward including all of them. An imam is one who is followed in religion. Abraham asked that his descendants receive this office, and God answered that His covenant does not reach the wrongdoers. Commentators read 'covenant' variously as prophethood (al-Suddi), leadership (Mujahid), mercy ('Ata'), religion (al-Rabi' and al-Dahhak) or security from the Fire (Qatada). Al-Zamakhshari, al-Razi and al-Qurtubi conclude from this that a sinner may not be an imam, whereas Ibn Kathir notes the ruling concerns religious leadership, and al-Shinqiti and Ibn 'Uthaymin separate legitimate religious office from executive authority. The differing readings of the name and of the covenant do not change the core meaning.

The commentators explain that God made the Kaaba a place of return to which people come back again and again without ever tiring of it, and a sanctuary in which whoever enters is safe. God commanded people to take the station of Abraham as a place of prayer, meaning the stone on which Abraham stood while raising the walls of the House. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir report that it was Umar ibn al-Khattab who proposed this, and that the verse was revealed in agreement with his view. God then charged Abraham and Ishmael to purify the House from idols, from polytheism and from whatever is unfitting, so that it would serve those who circumambulate it, those who stay in it and those who pray. Scholars differ on the meaning of the station of Abraham: Ibn Abbas and Mujahid take it to mean the whole pilgrimage or the entire sanctuary, Ata' takes it to mean the rites of Arafat, Muzdalifah and the pillars, while the majority, including al-Tabari, al-Razi and al-Qurtubi, identify it with the stone known in the Sacred Mosque. They also disagree about praying beside it: many link it to the two rak'as after the tawaf, al-Shafi'i considers them recommended and Malik considers them obligatory. Opinions likewise differ on the terms 'those who circumambulate' and 'those who remain': Ata' takes the first to be those who perform the tawaf and the second those who stay without circling or praying, while Ibn Jubayr understands the first as strangers and the second as the people of the city. As for the safety of the sanctuary, commentators understand it variously as protection from raids, from killing, or as forgiveness in the hereafter, and they debate whether a punishment may be carried out on a wrongdoer within it, a question on which Abu Hanifa and al-Shafi'i differ.

This verse recounts Abraham's prayer for Mecca, that Allah make it a secure land and provide its people with fruits, and he first restricted this provision to those among them who believe. The reply extends worldly provision to the disbelievers as well, who will enjoy it briefly before being driven to the Fire. The commentators differ on the security requested. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir report that the sanctuary has been secure since its creation and that Abraham asked for protection from famine and want, while Ibn Kathir also notes that its sanctity may have been declared by Abraham, citing hadiths on Medina to show the analogy. Al-Razi mentions protection from tyrants, sinking and famine, and considers that it may mean safety from killing. As for the restriction to believers, Ibn Juzayy and al-Nasafi see it as courtesy towards God, while al-Zamakhshari explains that Abraham had compared provision to the imamate, which God distinguishes from it. On the reading of 'fa-umatti'uhu' and 'thumma adtarruhu', al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir take them as God's own words, while Ibn Abbas and Mujahid take them as the continuation of Abraham's prayer. Al-Tabari understands the brief enjoyment as the present life and the compulsion towards the Fire as being driven forcibly, whereas Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Baydawi add that the brevity may refer to the short span of life or to the smallness of worldly goods compared with the Hereafter.

The verse describes Abraham and Ismail raising the foundations of the House while praying that God accept their work, for He is the All-Hearing and the All-Knowing. Commentators explain that the qawa'id are the foundations on which the walls rise, and that raising them means building upon them. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir report that Abraham built while Ismail handed him the stones, whereas Ibn 'Atiyya and Ibn Juzayy hold that both raised the structure together, Ismail being at least a helper. Al-Razi notes that the verb is in the present tense to make the scene vivid, and that Ismail was already grown, while a report attributed to Ali that he was still a small child is judged weak by Abu Hayyan and Ibn 'Atiyya. On the origin of the House, the reports differ: some attribute an earlier building to Adam, others to angels or to a foundation that existed before Abraham, and al-Tabari declines to choose among them because no sound proof settles the matter. Al-Razi, Ibn Kathir and al-Baydawi agree that the prayer for acceptance means God's pleasure and reward, and that the believer's fear of rejection is itself an act of devotion. Ibn Kathir adds that the two prophets repeated this prayer as they walked around the building.

As Ibrahim and Isma'il raise the foundations of the House, they pray that God make them submissive to Him, and that from their offspring He raise up a community that is also submitted. They ask to be shown their rites (manasik) and for their repentance to be accepted. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn Atiyya report that the rites are the pilgrimage rituals and its landmarks, as Qatada and al-Suddi say, while Mujahid, Ata and Ibn Jurayj take them to be the places of sacrifice, and others take them to mean all acts of worship. Al-Tabari holds that the verb means seeing with the eyes, whereas az-Zamakhshari and al-Razi understand it as teaching or making known. As for the repentance requested, al-Tabari explains it as a return to obedience. Many commentators, including Ibn Kathir, identify the offspring as the Arabs and the messenger raised among them as Muhammad, citing his saying that he is the answer to his father Ibrahim's prayer. Ibn Atiyya and most exegetes agree that asking for repentance does not imply that the prophets sinned, but rather expresses humility and teaches their descendants. Al-Razi takes islam here to include both faith and surrender, and he uses the verse in the debate on whether God creates human acts.

In this verse, Ibrahim and Isma'il ask God to raise up among their descendants, within the Muslim community, a messenger from among them who will recite God's signs to them, teach them the Book and wisdom, and purify them from polytheism and sin. The commentators identify this messenger as the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ, since no other messenger with the Book came from the descendants of both patriarchs, and the Prophet himself said he was the answer to Ibrahim's prayer and the good news foretold by Jesus. Al-Tabari and most exegetes take the "signs" to be the verses of the Qur'an, though al-Tabari also notes they may mean the signs that point to God's existence and attributes. Scholars differ on the meaning of "wisdom": Qatada and al-Shafi'i take it to be the Sunna of the Prophet, Malik takes it as knowledge of the religion, its understanding and following it, Mujahid as understanding the Qur'an, and Muqatil as the Qur'an's admonitions and rulings, while al-Tabari holds it to be knowledge of God's rulings that only the Messenger's explanation makes known. Ibn 'Abbas and Ibn Jurayj explain purification as deliverance from polytheism and sincerity in obedience, and Ibn Kaysan adds that the community will testify on their behalf on the Day of Judgment. The verse closes with "You are the Mighty, the Wise": the Mighty is the one nothing can overpower, and the Wise the one who places everything in its proper place. Al-Razi and others note that these two attributes suit the request for a messenger. Taken together, the verse combines a prayer for guidance with a description of the qualities of the prophetic mission.

This verse states that no one turns away from the religion of Abraham, meaning his upright, submissive monotheism, except one who foolishly wrongs himself. It adds that God chose Abraham in this world, making him a friend and a leader, and that in the hereafter he is among the righteous. The commentators agree that Abraham's religion is Islam founded on pure monotheism, and that the opening question is a rebuke and an expression of astonishment. Al-Tabari, Qatada and al-Rabi' understand that the verse addresses Jews and Christians who abandoned this path for innovations of their own, whereas Ibn Atiyya and al-Razi apply it to those who reject the law brought by Muhammad, peace be upon him, which they regard as the same religion in its essentials. On the meaning of 'safiha nafsahu', al-Zajjaj, al-Sam'ani and Ibn al-Jawzi take it to mean 'ignored his own soul', Abu 'Ubayda 'ruined his soul', al-Farra' sees a specification, al-Akhfash a verb whose preposition was dropped, and al-Zamakhshari a sense of 'debasing and despising oneself'. Some relate the occasion of revelation: Abdullah ibn Salam invited his two nephews to Islam, one accepted and the other refused. For 'istafaynahu', Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi explain it as choosing him for prophethood, while al-Jalalayn includes both mission and divine friendship. Most commentators understand the phrase about the hereafter as meaning he is counted among the prophets or the blessed, and some take it as an encouragement to follow his path.

This verse reports that when his Lord told Abraham, "Submit," he answered at once, "I have submitted to the Lord of the worlds." The commentators connect it to the preceding verses that praise Abraham: whoever turns away from his creed has foolishly wronged himself, since God chose him in this world and counted him among the righteous in the next. On the meaning of "safiha nafsahu," opinions differ. Al-Akhfash, Abu 'Ubayda, Ibn Kaysan and al-Zajjaj take it to mean he ignored or destroyed his own soul, while al-Farra' and his followers treat the accusative as a specification or a dropped preposition, meaning his soul became foolish. As for when the command was given, most, including al-Razi and al-Baydawi, place it before prophethood, during Abraham's reflection on the stars, the moon and the sun; others place it after prophethood, so the command then means steadfastness. Ibn Kathir and Ibn 'Atiyya understand "islam" as surrender and pure monotheism. Many report that the verse was revealed about Abdullah ibn Salam and his nephews Salama and Muhajir. The readings also differ between "wassa" and "awsa" and between the nominative and accusative for "Ya'qub," and each has its supporters among the exegetes.

The commentators explain that the verse recounts first Abraham's charge to his sons, then Jacob's charge to his own sons, and that its subject is Islam, meaning devotion to God alone and submission to Him. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi take the pronoun in "with it" to refer to Abraham's words "I have submitted to the Lord of the worlds", while al-Qadi, Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Qurtubi refer it to the creed (millah) mentioned just before; az-Zamakhshari and Abu Hayyan mention other possibilities. The two readings, "wa-wassa" and "wa-awsa", are both transmitted, most scholars holding that they mean the same, with the doubled form indicating repetition. The majority hold that "do not die except as Muslims" is, outwardly, a prohibition on dying otherwise, but that its aim is to command steadfastness in Islam until death, as az-Zamakhshari and Ibn Kathir explain. As for Jacob, al-Tabari, az-Zamakhshari and an-Nasafi take him to be joined to Abraham, so that he too charged his sons; others make Jacob a separate subject or read the accusative, as recorded by az-Zamakhshari and Ibn Kathir. Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi report that some exegetes saw here a reply to the Jews who claimed Jacob had bequeathed Judaism to his sons; the answer is that he enjoined Islam. Ibn 'Atiyya and Ibn Kathir stress the eloquent brevity of the phrase and its reminder of death, whose timing no one knows.

This passage, from verse 2:133, states that the Jews who claimed that Jacob died as a Jew and enjoined that religion on his sons were not witnesses to it. The question is rhetorical and reproachful: you were not present when death approached Jacob. The verse then reports his words to his sons: what will you worship after me? They answer: we will worship your God, the God of your fathers Abraham, Ishmael and Isaac, one God, and to Him we submit. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and others explain that Ishmael, Jacob's uncle, is counted among the fathers because the Arabs call an uncle a father. Al-Tabari prefers the reading 'wa-ilaha abika', while Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Zamakhshari treat 'ilahan wahidan' as an appositive, a state, or an accusative of emphasis. On the occasion of revelation, al-Wahidi and al-Baghawi report that the Jews told the Prophet that Jacob had bequeathed Judaism to his sons; al-Kalbi mentions Jacob's fear when he saw idolatry in Egypt. Al-Razi draws from the verse the rejection of blind imitation and the principle that children gain nothing from their fathers' piety, while Ibn 'Ashur sees in it a refutation of the Jewish claim. The verse ends: That is a community that has passed away; to it what it earned, and to you what you earned.

This verse states that Abraham, Jacob and their monotheist descendants were a community that has passed away: they have what they earned, and you have what you earned, and you will not be questioned about what they did. The commentators, including al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi, al-Nasafi and al-Baydawi, agree that it rejects pride in one's ancestry: each person answers for his own deeds, no one bears another's burden, and another's merit benefits only one who follows the same path. Ibn Kathir and al-Baydawi add that benefit comes from imitating their works, not from mere descent, and they cite the hadith addressed to the Banu Hashim.

Al-Zamakhshari, al-Nasafi and Ibn 'Ashur see the verse as silencing the Jews who boasted of their forefathers, and as making reward depend on deeds rather than on lineage. Ibn Kathir connects it to the preceding passage, which denies that Jacob bequeathed Judaism to his sons, and he extends the argument to both Jews and Arabs.

The notion of kasb (acquisition) has drawn different readings. Al-Tabari, Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Baydawi use it to attribute actions to the servant. Al-Razi takes the verse as evidence against blind imitation. Al-Qurtubi and Abu Hayyan read it as a refutation of both the Jabriyya and the Qadariyya, holding that the servant acquires his acts although God creates them. Ibn 'Ashur notes that the Ash'aris rely on this word to describe human action.

Abu Hayyan and al-Shawkani observe that the fronting of the predicates signals restriction: each community's gains do not pass to another. Al-Sha'rawi holds that believing descendants may be raised thanks to their fathers' faith, through God's pure grace, without this contradicting justice.

This verse reports the claim of the Jews and Christians that guidance lies in becoming Jewish or Christian. God tells His Prophet to reply that the true path is the religion of Abraham, a hanif, meaning upright and devoted to pure monotheism. The commentators agree that a hanif is one who turns away from false religions toward the truth, and that the closing phrase, 'nor was he of the polytheists', is an indirect rebuke to the People of the Book, who claim to follow Abraham while falling into association, such as calling Ezra or the Messiah the son of God. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir record several interpretations: Mujahid says the hanif is one who follows, Ibn ‘Abbas, al-Hasan and ‘Ata’ say one who performs the pilgrimage, al-Suddi says one who is sincere, and al-Dahhak says one who is a Muslim. Al-Tabari himself holds that hanifiyya is steadfastness in the path of Abraham and following him, not the pilgrimage or circumcision alone. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Baydawi and al-Razi debate how 'milla' is parsed, whether as 'we shall follow' or 'we shall be the people of Abraham's creed', and note the nominative reading attributed to al-A'raj. Ibn Ishaq gives the occasion of revelation, when Ibn Suriya asked the Prophet to follow their faith in order to be guided. Ibn al-Qayyim notes that the argument is a counter-argument, since both sides claim Abraham. Ibn ‘Ashur explains the exclusive sense implied by the conditional form of 'you will be guided'.

This verse tells the believers to say to the People of the Book that they believe in God, in what was sent down to them in the Qur'an, in what was sent to Abraham, Ishmael, Isaac, Jacob and the tribes, and in what was given to Moses, Jesus and all the prophets from their Lord, making no distinction between any of them, and that they submit to Him. The commentators agree that the address is to the believers and that it lays down the common faith in all messengers. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir report that it was revealed in a dispute with Jews who denied the prophethood of Jesus, and that the Prophet recited it in the two units of the dawn prayer. Although the Qur'an came later, al-Razi explains that it is mentioned first because it confirms what came before it. On the tribes, al-Tabari, al-Wahidi and Ibn Kathir take them to be the twelve sons of Jacob, al-Baydawi takes them to be his descendants, and al-Shinqiti and Ibn 'Uthaymin take them to be the prophets of the Children of Israel in general. Most agree that not distinguishing means believing in all the messengers rather than rejecting some as the Jews and Christians did. Al-Razi and others separate this faith from the recognition that some prophets are more excellent than others. Zamakhshari and al-Nasafi note that the word 'ahad' carries a collective sense here, which allows it to follow 'bayn'. Ibn 'Ashur and Ibn Sa'di explain that the verse spells out the religion of Abraham, and that Islam means submission to God both inwardly and outwardly.

The commentators explain that this verse addresses the Prophet and the believers: if the People of the Book come to a faith like the believers' faith, meaning belief in God, in what was revealed to them and to the prophets without distinguishing between them, they are rightly guided; if they turn away, they are in shiqaq, meaning opposition and enmity, and God will suffice His Messenger against them. Ibn 'Abbas, 'Ata' and al-Akhfash read the word as disagreement and dispute, al-Hasan as estrangement and separation until the Day of Judgment, Muqatil and Abu 'Ubayda as misguidance, and Ibn Zayd as strife and war. On the word "mithl" (like), opinions differ. Al-Tabari, followed by Ibn Kathir and Ibn 'Atiyya, holds that the likeness lies between the two acts of faith rather than in the object of faith. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Razi see a rebuke, since the true religion is one and has no equal. Others consider the word or the particle bi to be superfluous. Ibn 'Abbas is reported to have recited "bima amantum bihi" and said that God has no like, but al-Tabari treats this as an interpretation rather than a valid reading. The commentators link the promise of sufficiency to the punishment of the Banu Qurayza, the expulsion of the Banu Nadir and the imposition of the jizya. They also note that God hears what they say and knows what they conceal.

The commentators explain that God commands the believers to answer the Jews and Christians who urged them to become Jewish or Christian in order to be guided: they follow the dye of God, meaning His religion, which leaves a visible mark on those who adopt it, as dye colours cloth. No dye is finer than God's, and the believers worship Him alone. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi report that the phrase refers to the custom of Christians immersing their children in a yellow water called the baptism, which they regarded as purification, and that God rejected this by declaring that the true dye is Islam. Most, including al-Hasan, Qatada, Mujahid and Ibn Abbas, take the dye to be the religion itself. Mujahid in one report, together with Abu Ubayda and al-Zajjaj, connects it with the natural disposition, the fitra, that God gave to humankind; others understand circumcision, which stains the body with blood. Al-Zamakhshari and Ibn Atiyya treat the word as an emphatic verbal noun confirming the faith mentioned just before, while al-Akhfash and al-Zajjaj take it as an appositive to the creed of Abraham, and some prefer a grammatical reading as an instruction to hold fast. Al-Mawardi and al-Qurtubi also mention the view that it refers to the ritual bath for one entering Islam. The exegetes do not rule between these readings, and several note that they converge, since religion and natural disposition are closely linked, and God knows best.

God tells His Prophet to answer those among the People of the Book who disputed with the believers about God: "Do you argue with us concerning God, when He is our Lord and your Lord? For us are our deeds, and for you are your deeds, and we are sincere to Him." The commentators differ on the subject of the dispute. Al-Hasan and Ibn Zayd report that the Jews and Christians claimed closeness to God as His sons and beloved, while al-Tabari and Ibn al-Jawzi mention their argument from the antiquity of their religion and scripture. Al-Razi and Abu Hayyan add that the words may also address the Arab polytheists, a reading al-Razi considers less fitting to the verse's structure. On the meaning, the exegetes agree: the Lord is one, and each person is recompensed for his deeds, not for his lineage or for the age of his religion. Al-Razi and al-Baydawi explain that prophetic honour is either a pure favour of God or the reward of those who persevere in obedience and sincerity. Ibn Kathir and al-Sa'di see here a disavowal of the opponents' deeds and a call to argue with wisdom and courtesy. Ibn 'Atiyya reports that some scholars held the verse abrogated by the verse of the sword, though the other commentators do not follow them on this. The overall sense is a rebuke of the disputants and an exhortation to believers to sincerity toward God and to abandon boasting in ancestry and priority.

In this verse God answers the Jews and Christians who claimed that Abraham, Ishmael, Isaac, Jacob and the tribes were Jews or Christians. He asks them who knows better, and then states that these prophets were upright Muslims, not Jews or Christians, since both religions arose after them. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi understand the hidden testimony as the one God placed in their scriptures, affirming that the prophets followed the hanif path and were free of Judaism and Christianity. Qatada and Ibn Zayd take it to mean the testimony about Muhammad's prophethood and the description of him found in their books, a view also favoured by al-Qurtubi and al-Razi. Ibn 'Atiyya, al-Zamakhshari and al-Baydawi combine both readings, noting that the Quran denies Judaism and Christianity to Abraham. On grammar, al-Razi, Abu Hayyan and al-Alusi discuss whether the particle 'am' is connective or disjunctive, meaning either 'or' or 'rather'. Al-Tabari considers the reading in the second person ('you say') the correct one, while others prefer the third person. The commentators agree that God is not unaware of what they do, which is a warning to them. Ibn 'Ashur adds that the verse reminds the People of the Book of a covenant recorded in their scriptures, and that lineage alone does not benefit those who do not follow the path of their forefathers.

This verse refers to the community of prophets just named, Abraham, Ishmael, Isaac, Jacob and the tribes, which has passed away, so it has what it earned and you have what you earned, and you will not be questioned about what they did. The commentators agree that the verse cuts the link between salvation and mere lineage: only one's own deeds count, and another's deeds neither harm nor benefit. Al-Tabari, Qatada and al-Rabi' take the community to be the named prophets, while al-Shawkani adds that the sentence refers to these same figures. Scholars differ on whether the sentence is a repetition. Al-Razi and Abu Hayyan hold that it is not a true repetition, because the context changes: the first comes after the prophets are mentioned, the second after the ancestors of the Jews and Christians. Al-Zamakhshari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baydawi and al-Nasafi see it as emphasis and a warning, and Ibn Kathir applies it to contemporaries who boast of their ancestors. Al-Baydawi and al-Nasafi also note the reading in which the first mention means the prophets and the second the Jewish forebears. Ibn 'Ashur explains the repetition as a way to fix the meaning firmly in the listeners' minds. Ibn 'Uthaymin and Ibn Sa'di draw the lesson that one must not rely on ancestry alone.

This verse reports something God told His Prophet before it happened: foolish people will object to the change of prayer direction from Jerusalem to the Kaaba, asking what turned the believers away from the qibla they had followed. The answer is that east and west belong to God, that no direction is sacred in itself, and that God guides whom He wills to the straight path by commanding what He wills. Commentators largely agree that the foolish are Jews, polytheists, or hypocrites, but they differ on which group is meant. Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid and al-Bara' ibn 'Azib say the Jews, as-Suddi says the hypocrites, and al-Zajjaj says the Quraysh, while Ibn Kathir and al-Tabari consider the verse to cover all of them. Ibn 'Ashur notes that this verse came before the verse of abrogation, which makes the prediction a sign of prophethood. On how long the prayer faced Jerusalem, opinions vary: sixteen or seventeen months according to al-Bara' and Ibn 'Abbas, thirteen according to Mu'adh, nine or ten according to Anas. Al-Tabari reports that the Prophet had a choice and preferred Jerusalem to win over the Jews, whereas Ibn Kathir says most scholars held that it was by divine command. The next verse describes the Muslims as a middle nation, meaning just and excellent, called to bear witness before mankind, with the Messenger bearing witness over them. The commentators explain that 'that We may know' means knowledge that brings reward or punishment, that the prayer toward Jerusalem is not lost in God's sight, and that faith here means, for most, the prayer.

These verses state that God made the community of Muhammad a middle nation, meaning upright and excellent, so that they would be witnesses over the peoples on the Day of Resurrection, and that the Messenger would in turn bear witness to their uprightness. Commentators differ on the nature of this witness. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and most others understand it as an eschatological scene in which the nations deny having been warned and the community of Muhammad testifies that the prophets delivered the message. Ibn 'Ashur also includes a worldly judgment on the conduct of past peoples. On the word wasat, most take it to mean just and excellent, while al-Tabari adds the sense of a balanced middle between the excess of the Christians and the neglect of the Jews. As for the qibla, most identify the first direction of prayer as Jerusalem, followed by the switch to the Kaaba. On the phrase 'that We may know,' al-Tabari and al-Zamakhshari speak of a knowledge that grounds reward and punishment, while others prefer 'see' or 'distinguish.' Ibn Kathir and most understand 'your faith' as the prayer facing Jerusalem, which God will not allow to be lost, a reading Malik links to the principle that prayer is part of faith. All commentators stress God's compassion toward people.

Commentators explain the verse 'We see you turning your face towards the sky' as describing the Prophet's ﷺ longing, as he looked up to heaven hoping for a revelation ordering a turn toward the Ka'ba instead of Jerusalem. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi report that God granted this wish with the words 'We shall surely turn you to a qibla you will be pleased with.' They differ on why he preferred it: Ibn Abbas holds that it was the qibla of Abraham, while Mujahid and Ibn Zayd report that the Jews said Muhammad followed their direction and that he wished to differ from them. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Razi add that the Ka'ba would draw the Arabs more readily to faith.

The commentators agree that 'the Sacred Mosque' means the Ka'ba and that the obligation is to face its direction. One who sees it must face it directly, whereas one far away may suffice with its general direction, a view Ibn al-Arabi upholds and al-Qurtubi cites. Ibn Abbas holds that the whole House is a qibla and its door is the precise point, while Ibn Umar placed it opposite the water spout. Al-Tabari and al-Qurtubi note that 'wherever you are' addresses all Muslims, not only the people of Medina.

On 'those given the Scripture know it to be the truth from their Lord,' opinions differ: al-Suddi takes it as referring to the Jews alone, while Muqatil and others include the Christians. Al-Qurtubi lists reasons for their knowledge, including the mention of the Prophet in their books and the acceptance of abrogation in their tradition.

The commentaries conclude that God is not unaware of what these opponents do, and that believers must not follow the desires of the People of the Book.

This verse tells us that God addresses His Prophet, saying that even if he brought the People of the Book every sign and proof that facing the Kaaba is the truth, they would not follow his direction of prayer. Their rejection does not come from a doubt that argument could remove, but from stubbornness and arrogance, since they know from their own scriptures who the Prophet is. God adds that he will never follow their direction, and that Jews and Christians do not follow each other's direction either: the Jews face Jerusalem and the Christians face the east. The commentators agree that the address is outwardly to the Prophet but is meant for his community, since his protection from sin makes such a deed impossible for him. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Razi and al-Baydawi note that the negated nominal sentence is stronger than a plain prohibition, and that the oath, the emphatic lam, inna and idhan intensify the warning. As for the phrase 'after the knowledge that has come to you', some understand it as revelation and proof, others as religious knowledge as a whole. Ibn Kathir and al-Sa'di draw from it that whoever knows the truth and abandons it for the sake of his desires is among the wrongdoers, whatever his rank, and that this warning applies to the whole community.

The commentators explain that this verse concerns the People of the Book, Jews and Christians, who were given the Torah and the Gospel, and that they know the Prophet ﷺ with a certain knowledge, free of doubt, just as a man recognises his own sons among other children. The commentators differ on what the pronoun "they know him" refers to. Mujahid, Qatada and most exegetes, including al-Zamakhshari, Ibn 'Atiyya, al-Qurtubi and al-Baydawi, take it to mean the Prophet ﷺ himself: they recognise his prophethood and the attributes described in their scriptures, and some cite the report of 'Abd Allah ibn Salam with 'Umar. Ibn 'Abbas, Qatada, al-Rabi' and Ibn Jurayj, and al-Tabari, understand it as their knowledge that turning to the Kaaba is the truth. Al-Razi prefers the first reading because the preceding passage concerns prophethood, while Ibn Kathir stresses the clarity of this recognition. As for the group that "conceals the truth", Mujahid and Qatada say it is the description of the Prophet ﷺ, whereas Ibn 'Abbas, al-Rabi' and Muqatil say it is the change of qibla; Ibn al-Jawzi reports both views. Ibn 'Ashur sees the verse as a digression connected with the objections of the People of the Book to the Muslim qibla. Most note that only a part of them is meant, since some believed, like Ibn Salam. The comparison with recognising one's children conveys, according to al-Razi and Abu Hayyan, complete certainty, and the choice of sons is explained by fathers' stronger attachment to them. The exegetes stress that concealing the truth while knowing it is a graver fault. Finally, the prohibition on doubt, addressed to the Prophet ﷺ, is understood as addressing his community.

The commentators explain that the verse means the truth is what God has made known to His Prophet and revealed to him, not what the Jews and Christians tell him. The address is to the Prophet ﷺ, but it is meant for his community. Most take the pronoun in 'they recognise him' to refer to the Prophet ﷺ: the learned among the People of the Book know his truthfulness as they know their own sons, and Ibn Kathir cites the exchange between Umar and Abdullah ibn Salam to illustrate this. Al-Tabari, al-Razi and Ibn 'Atiyya prefer to refer the pronoun to the change of the prayer direction, though al-Razi considers prophethood the closer antecedent since the preceding verse mentions knowledge, and Ibn 'Atiyya holds that the recognition covers both. As for the group that conceals the truth, Mujahid and Qatada identify it as the description of Muhammad ﷺ, while others take it to be the direction of the Kaaba. The commentators stress that the prohibition on doubt is an exhortation to the community and does not imply that the Prophet doubted; al-Razi and al-Baydawi develop this point. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Razi understand imtira as oscillating between certainty and doubt, while the consensus is that the mumtarun are the doubters, though Ibn 'Atiyya questions whether the verse of al-A'sha cited by al-Tabari supports this meaning. Ali's reading al-haqqa is treated by al-Kashshaf as an apposition and by Ibn 'Atiyya as an object of 'they know'.

This part of the verse says that every community, every group among the people of earlier scriptures, has a direction it faces in prayer, and it calls believers to hasten toward good deeds, because God will gather all creatures on the Day of Resurrection wherever they are, and He is able to do anything. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn al-Jawzi understand the word wijha as the qibla. Ibn Abbas, Ata and al-Suddi take it as the direction of prayer that each community accepts, while Mujahid holds that the pronoun refers to each people turning its face toward its own qibla. Al-Akhfash and others hold that God is the one who turns each people toward its direction. Ibn Amir and Ibn Abbas read the passive form mawlaha, which Farra and Zajjaj explain as meaning turned toward it. Al-Tabari and al-Samani believe the call to race ahead covers all good deeds, whereas al-Razi and al-Qurtubi emphasize praying at the beginning of the prescribed time, citing hadiths and the views of al-Shafi'i, Abu Hanifa and Malik. Zamakhshari and al-Baydawi offer another reading: the directions meant are those that face the Kaaba, even though they differ. Ibn al-Qayyim says the verse invites believers to follow the truth and not go with falsehood. Al-Sha'rawi links the passage to human free choice and the urgency of doing good before death. Zamakhshari and Ibn Atiyya explain 'wherever you are' as referring to the final gathering, and Ibn Kathir stresses that God can reassemble scattered bodies.

God instructs His Prophet to turn his face toward the Sacred Mosque wherever he sets out from, and states that this change is the truth from his Lord, since God is not unaware of what people do and will repay them for it. The commentators broadly agree that the verse confirms the change of qibla. Many explain the repetition of the command in this surah by saying that abrogation is a source of confusion and doubt, so it needs to be reinforced. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir hold that the verse covers travel as well as residence. Al-Razi and Ibn Kathir report another reading, according to which the three verses address three different situations: being inside the Sacred Mosque, being in Mecca but out of sight of it, or being in other lands. Ibn Kathir adds that the purpose of the repetition is to cut off the objections of the Jews, who knew from their scriptures that the Prophet would turn toward Abraham's qibla, and of the Quraysh. Al-Tabari treats the exception in « except those who did wrong » as a continuous exception, meaning their arguments are baseless. Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Zamakhshari read it as discontinuous, meaning the wrongdoers do raise arguments, but false ones. Ibn 'Atiyya also notes that the pronoun in « they recognise it » refers to the qibla according to Ibn 'Abbas, and to the Prophet according to Qatada and Mujahid. The commentators conclude by promising reward to the believers and warning the disbelievers in the reading with the third person.

God commands His Prophet ﷺ and the believers to turn in prayer toward the Sacred Mosque wherever they are, and the commentators explain that the change of direction from Jerusalem to the Kaaba was a truth from the Lord. They agree that its purpose was to cut off the objections of opponents, but they differ on who these were. Ibn Abbas, Qatada, al-Rabi' and al-Tabari identify them as the People of the Book, who said Muhammad had longed for his father's house and his people's religion. Mujahid, Ata' and Ibn Jurayj identify them as the Quraysh polytheists, who claimed he had returned to their qibla and would return to their religion. As for the exception "except those who did wrong", al-Tabari, al-Razi and Ibn Kathir take it as a continuous exception: only the wrongdoers have a false argument. al-Zajjaj, al-Baydawi and Ibn 'Atiyya take it as discontinuous, meaning that the wrongdoers still argue falsely. Abu 'Ubayda proposed that illa means waw, a view al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir rejected. Al-Razi and Ibn Juzayy explain the repetition as emphasis, since abrogation invites doubt, or as covering different situations: in the city, outside it, or on a journey. Most say the fear commanded is the fear of God alone. Completing the blessing is, for most, guidance to Abraham's qibla; 'Ali and Sa'id ibn Jubayr say it means death in Islam or entry into Paradise.

This verse recalls that God completed His favour upon the believers by sending them a messenger from among themselves, Muhammad ﷺ, who recites His signs to them, purifies them from polytheism and bad conduct, teaches them the Book and wisdom, and teaches them what they did not know. Most commentators understand 'the Book' as the Quran and 'wisdom' as the Sunna, while others take wisdom to mean the Quran's admonitions or knowledge of the secrets of the Law, and some add that what they did not know includes the stories of prophets, the histories of past nations and matters of the unseen. As for purification, some explain it as freeing them from polytheism, others as growth and elevation, and others as teaching them what makes them pure in God's sight. Scholars differ on the particle 'as' in 'as We sent': al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baydawi and Abu al-Su'ud link it to what precedes, meaning a completion of blessing like the sending of a messenger and an answer to Abraham's prayer, whereas al-Farra', Mujahid, 'Ata', al-Kalbi, al-Zajjaj and al-Akhfash link it to the following words, 'remember Me, and I will remember you'. Az-Zamakhshari, Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Qurtubi offer other readings. The commentators agree that the remembrance commanded involves the heart, the tongue and the limbs, that God's remembrance of the servant brings reward, forgiveness and increase, and that gratitude is the fitting response to this favour.

In this verse God commands believers to remember Him through obedience and reverence, and promises that He will remember them with forgiveness and reward. He also commands them to thank Him in word and deed, and not to deny His favours through ingratitude or disobedience. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and others explain that the servant's remembrance means obedience, and God's remembrance means His forgiveness and mercy; Ibn Kathir cites this reading from Ibn Abbas and Sa'id ibn Jubayr. Al-Tabari, with al-Rabi' and al-Suddi, takes remembrance to mean praise: God remembers whoever mentions Him with mercy and punishes whoever disbelieves in Him. Al-Razi distinguishes remembrance by the tongue, the heart and the limbs, and lists several meanings. Ibn al-Jawzi defines gratitude as acknowledging the benefactor's right together with praise, while al-Tabari links it to acknowledging the gift of Islam and guidance. Ibn 'Atiyya holds that remembrance and gratitude mean the same thing here. Al-Zamakhshari and others explain that kufr here means concealing or denying a blessing, not disbelief in the sense of rejecting the message. Al-Qurtubi, al-Baydawi and Ibn Kathir note that remembrance may include prayer, glorification and supplication, and Ibn Juzayy lists several views on its meaning. Several commentators cite the hadith 'I am as My servant thinks of Me' to show the excellence of remembering God. Al-Zajjaj and others attach the word 'as' to what follows, meaning 'as I reminded you by sending the Messenger, so remember Me'; others attach it to what precedes. The verb 'I will remember you' answers the command, hence its jussive form.

This verse calls the believers to seek help through patience and prayer, in the face of what God commands and the trials of life. Al-Tabari understands patience as steadfastness in obedience and in bearing hardships, and most commentators concur; al-Mawardi and al-Qurtubi add that it includes perseverance in obligations and fasting, while al-Razi and al-Baydawi emphasise prayer, which gathers acts of worship and restrains from indecency and wrongdoing. Nearly all agree that "God is with the patient" describes a special presence of help, support and protection, distinct from the general presence of knowledge and encompassing power, as Ibn Sa'di and Ibn Uthaymin explain. Ibn Kathir distinguishes two kinds of patience, restraining oneself from what is forbidden and persevering in acts of obedience, the second being the greater reward. The following verses, which forbid calling those slain in God's cause dead, are linked to this passage by most exegetes. Al-Baghawi, Ibn Kathir and al-Tabari report that they were revealed concerning the martyrs of Badr, whose life, according to al-Alusi, is that of their souls with their Lord, and who receive their provision, as al-Hasan and al-Baghawi relate. Ibn Atiyya, however, holds that the ruling is general and not restricted to Badr.

In this verse God tells believers not to say of those slain in His cause that they are dead, for they are alive with their Lord, though this life cannot be perceived by the senses. Most commentators say the verse was revealed about the martyrs of Badr, whom people described as dead, having lost the pleasures of this world. All agree that the martyr is alive in the intermediate state (barzakh), but they differ on the nature of that life. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi cite hadiths that the souls of martyrs are in green birds that roam Paradise and rest in lamps beneath the Throne, and al-Tabari adds that they receive provision there before the resurrection. Ibn 'Atiyya, al-Baydawi and al-Nasafi report al-Hasan's view that their provision is presented to their souls, which feel joy and comfort. Al-Razi holds that the life is in the grave and draws arguments from it for the punishment and reward of the tomb, while reporting Abu Muslim al-Isfahani's view that they will be revived on the Day of Resurrection. Al-Alusi inclines towards a spiritual life with an intermediate body, and Ibn 'Uthaymin holds that this unseen matter should be left to what revelation says. Commentators also see in the verse a consolation for martyrs' families and an encouragement to patience and jihad. A few, such as al-Qasimi, suggest that death and life may also be understood figuratively.

God tells the believers that He will test them with a measure of fear, hunger, loss of wealth, lives and crops, and commands the Prophet ﷺ to give good news to the patient. The commentators understand the trial as an examination that separates the sincere from the hypocrite, and the word 'some' as softening the test, since God's mercy surrounds the believers in every state. Al-Tabari, al-Baghawi, al-Zamakhshari and Ibn Kathir largely agree on the common reading: fear is fear of the enemy, hunger is famine, loss of wealth is its destruction or decline, loss of lives is death or martyrdom, and loss of fruits comes from blights and poor yields. Al-Shafi'i, as transmitted by al-Mawardi, al-Qurtubi and Ibn Kathir, offers a different reading: fear is fear of God, hunger is the fast of Ramadan, the loss of wealth is obligatory zakat and charity, the loss of lives is illness, and the loss of fruits is the death of children. Ibn Kathir finds this reading questionable, and al-Zamakhshari also expresses doubt. The patient are those who, when struck by a calamity, say: 'Indeed we belong to God and to Him we return', a formula which the commentators read as an acknowledgement of God's ownership, servitude and the resurrection. All see God's blessings as mercy, praise and forgiveness, and the guided as those directed to the right path. On the addressees, 'Ata' and the majority, along with Ibn 'Abbas, take them to be the community of Muhammad ﷺ or his companions, though others said the Quraysh or the believers at the end of time. Many cite the hadith of Umm Salama on invoking God at a calamity and that of Abu Musa about the 'House of Praise'.

This verse states that God will test believers with a measure of fear, hunger, loss of wealth, lives and crops, to reveal who is patient. It promises good news to the patient, who, when struck by a calamity, say: 'Indeed we belong to God and to Him we shall return.' By this they acknowledge that they are God's property, that He disposes of them as He wills, and that they will return to Him to be rewarded. The commentators, including al-Tabari, al-Baghawi, Ibn Kathir, al-Qurtubi and al-Baydawi, agree that this formula is a refuge for the afflicted, that it affirms both divine ownership and resurrection, and that 'calamity' covers anything that harms the believer. They read the 'prayers' from God as praise and forgiveness, or as mercy, with 'mercy' mentioned for emphasis, and the 'rightly guided' as those who recite the formula and submit. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Qurtubi report that this formula was not given to any prophet before our Prophet, and cite Ya'qub's words 'Oh my grief for Yusuf' to support the point. Ibn Kathir and al-Samani also relay hadiths on the reward for reciting the formula, including the report of Umm Salama. On the meaning of fear and hunger, opinions differ: Ibn 'Abbas and Ibn Kathir take it as fear of the enemy and drought, al-Shafi'i as fear of God, fasting in Ramadan, zakat, illness and the death of children, and others as the hardships of jihad. Ibn 'Ashur notes that the word 'thing' (shay') is used to minimize the trial. Al-Razi observes that a calamity may come from God or from people, and the formula covers both cases. Like al-Baydawi, he adds that patience is not merely saying the words but reflecting in the heart while uttering them.

The commentators explain that this verse completes the description of the patient, those whom God tests with some fear, hunger, loss of wealth, lives and crops, and who, when a calamity strikes them, say: 'Indeed we belong to God and to Him we return.' The plain meaning is that such people receive from their Lord 'salawat', meaning forgiveness, praise and tenderness, accompanied by mercy, and that they are thereby the rightly guided, on the path of truth and right conduct. The scholars agree that God's prayer here denotes forgiveness, praise or compassion, that the mention of mercy after it reinforces and clarifies it, and that the plural indicates its abundance. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir note that prayer originally means supplication, and that when it comes from God it is mercy and kindness, citing the hadiths on the merit of the formula of return in calamity, such as that of Umm Salama. Al-Mawardi and Ibn al-Jawzi report, following Sa'id ibn Jubayr, that the prayer means forgiveness, and that guidance may mean guidance to Paradise and reward, or to truth and rightness. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Nasafi take the prayer to mean tenderness and affection, placed alongside mercy for emphasis. Ibn al-Qayyim, by contrast, holds that prayer and mercy are distinct, since God differentiates them in the verse. Al-Razi details the causes of misfortune and sees in the formula an acknowledgement of divine ownership and of resurrection. Most commentators conclude that patience here is not mere endurance but submission and acceptance of God's decree.

This verse states that al-Safa and al-Marwa, two small hills near the Ka'ba, are among the markers of God's religion, and that running between them is one of its rites. Whoever comes to the House for hajj or umrah commits no sin by doing so. Some Muslims were reluctant, because in the pre-Islamic period idols named Isaf and Na'ila stood on the two hills and people touched them while going round. The commentators report that this unease was the occasion of revelation, and that God lifted it by declaring the place part of Islamic worship. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir hold the running to be obligatory, relying on the hadith "God has prescribed the running, so run" and on the Prophet's saying "Take your rites from me"; al-Tabari adds that omitting it requires returning to perform it. Abu Hanifa, his companions and al-Thawri regard it as obligatory but repairable by a sacrifice, while al-Shafi'i, Malik and the prevailing view of Ahmad treat it as a pillar without which the pilgrimage is not valid. Ibn Abbas, Anas, Ibn al-Zubayr, 'Ata' and Mujahid consider it voluntary. Some read "that he should not run between them", a non-canonical reading that 'A'isha rejected and that most scholars explain by taking the particle 'not' as superfluous. The closing phrase "whoever does good voluntarily" is read by some as voluntary circumambulation or a further pilgrimage after the obligatory one, and by al-Hasan as any act of worship. God is grateful to His servants, rewards them, and knows their intentions and deeds.

This verse addresses those among the People of the Book who concealed the clear proofs and guidance God sent down, especially the signs pointing to the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ in the Torah and the Gospel, and so earned the curse of God and of those who curse. The commentators agree that it was revealed concerning Jewish scholars who hid the description of the Prophet and the ruling on stoning, as al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir report. Most extend its meaning to anyone who conceals knowledge of religion that people need, relying on the hadith about the one asked about knowledge who withholds it. On who the cursers are, opinions differ: Qatada and al-Rabi' ibn Anas say the angels and believers, the view al-Tabari prefers; Mujahid and Ikrima say the beasts and insects, which curse sinners when drought strikes; Ibn 'Abbas says all creatures except humans and jinn; and Ibn Mas'ud holds that the curse returns to the Jews when two people who curse each other do not deserve it. Al-Baghawi and Ibn Kathir explain that repentance is accepted on condition of stating what was hidden and repairing the harm done. Those who die in disbelief remain under the curse. Scholars differ on cursing a specific disbeliever, with the majority forbidding it and some permitting it. Al-Razi, al-Qurtubi and al-Baydawi also draw from the verse the duty to teach religious knowledge, the acceptance of a single reporter, and the prohibition of taking payment for teaching.

This verse states that God curses those who conceal the clear proofs and guidance He sent down after making them plain in the Book, and that those who curse also curse them. It then excepts those who repent, set right what they spoiled, and make clear what they hid. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir hold that the verse first addresses the Jewish rabbis, and that Abdullah ibn Salam and those who embraced Islam are included in the exception. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Nasafi understand setting things right as making up for what was missed, and making clear as openly declaring the repentance so that others may follow. Ibn 'Atiyya and Ibn Kathir take the verse to cover any scholar who withholds religious knowledge people need, citing the hadith of the one bridled with a bridle of fire for hiding knowledge. Al-Tabari and Ibn 'Atiyya identify the ones who curse as the angels and believers, while al-Baghawi and al-Shawkani record other views, including that all creatures, even animals, curse. Al-Razi explains that true repentance requires abandoning the wrong and doing what is right. Al-Qurtubi notes that most scholars forbid cursing a specific disbeliever, though cursing unbelievers in general is permitted. Finally, the commentators agree that those who die in disbelief bear the curse of God, the angels and all people, abide in the Fire, and receive neither reduction of punishment nor respite.

This verse states that those who disbelieved in the prophethood of Muhammad and died in disbelief incur the curse of God, the angels and the people. Al-Tabari holds that "the people" means all whose cursing counts, namely the believers and every person who curses the wrongdoer, so the disbeliever is included as a wrongdoer. Qatada and al-Rabi' say it refers to the believers alone, while Abu al-'Aliya places the cursing on the Day of Resurrection, when the disbeliever is first cursed by God, then by the angels, then by people. Several commentators, including al-Razi and al-Qurtubi, explain how the disbeliever can be cursed by humanity although his own community does not curse him in this world: the cursing occurs on the Day of Judgment when people curse one another, or the disbelievers curse themselves without realising it, or everyone curses the wrongdoer.

The exegetes agree that the curse is tied to dying in disbelief, and whoever repents is freed from it. Al-Razi notes that for those who hold the doctrine of the final state, the verse shows the curse attaches to dying in denial. Jurists differ on cursing a specific named disbeliever: some forbid it because no one knows his final state, while Ibn al-'Arabi and al-Qurtubi permit it in general. Ibn Kathir records this disagreement without preferring either view. As for "abiding therein", Ibn 'Atiyya and Abu Hayyan take it to mean lasting in the curse or in the fire. Al-Razi lists three features of the punishment, eternity, no lightening, and no respite, which together mean that all hope is cut off for the disbeliever.

This verse states that those who die in disbelief without repenting are under the curse of God, of the angels and of all people. They remain forever under this curse and in the Fire that follows from it, their punishment is not lightened, and they are given no respite to make excuses. Al-Tabari reads the phrase as a statement of the perpetual, untimed continuance of punishment, and understands 'nor will they be respited' as meaning they are neither delayed nor given time to offer an excuse, a view he attributes to Abu al-Aliya. As to 'abiding therein', most commentators, including al-Tabari, al-Razi, al-Baydawi and Ibn Kathir, take the pronoun as referring to the curse; al-Razi prefers this because the pronoun then has an explicit antecedent. Ibn 'Atiyya, al-Qurtubi and Abu Hayyan take it to refer to the Fire, implied by the curse. On the meaning of 'all people', Qatada, al-Rabi' and Ibn Mas'ud hold that only believers are meant; Abu al-Aliya holds that on the Day of Resurrection disbelievers curse one another; al-Suddi holds that everyone curses the wrongdoer, so the disbeliever is cursed by all. Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi relate that the disbeliever is first cursed by God, then by the angels, then by people. Most scholars permit cursing disbelievers in general, but they differ on cursing a specific individual: some forbid it since one cannot know how a person will end, while Ibn al-'Arabi permits it. Al-Zamakhshari and Abu Hayyan mention a reading in the nominative for 'the angels and the people', but the accepted reading is in the genitive.

This verse declares that the true God is one, with no partner or equal, and that there is no one worthy of worship but Him, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate. The commentators explain this oneness in several ways. Al-Tabari reports that 'one' means that He has no like and no equal, while others understand it as indivisibility and the absence of parts; Ibn 'Atiyya defines it as the denial of any likeness, equal or rival, and Abu al-Ma'ali as the denial of any division. The phrase 'there is no god but He' is, according to al-Baydawi and Abu Hayyan, an affirmation of oneness that removes the idea of a god who exists but does not deserve worship. Al-Razi and al-Qurtubi see it as a negation of divinity in general followed by its affirmation. As for 'the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate', al-Zamakhshari and al-Nasafi explain that He is the source of all blessings, primary and secondary, so that everything else is either a blessing or one who receives it; al-Razi adds that mentioning mercy after majesty calms the hearts. Most works give the occasion of revelation as a question from Quraysh asking the Prophet to describe his Lord, and mention the three hundred and sixty idols around the Ka'ba. Ibn Kathir cites a hadith that the Greatest Name of God is in this verse and in the Verse of the Throne, while noting weakness in its chain. Al-Jaza'iri and modern exegetes place the six cosmic signs that follow, the creation of the heavens and earth, the alternation of night and day, ships at sea, rain, winds and clouds, as proofs of this oneness. The commentators do not settle these views, presenting them side by side.

Verse 2:164 lists the signs of God in creation that point to His oneness: the creation of the heavens and the earth, the alternation of night and day, the ships that sail the sea for the benefit of people, the water God sends down from the sky by which the dead earth is brought to life, the scattering of living creatures across the earth, the turning of the winds, and the clouds held between heaven and earth. Commentators present these signs as the proof for the preceding statement, 'Your God is One God.' Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir link the verse to the disbelievers' demand for a sign, and report that the Quraysh were shocked that one God could suffice for all people. Other traditions say they asked the Prophet to turn Safa into gold. Al-Tabari judges that both accounts may be true and does not prefer one over the other. Al-Baghawi and al-Zamakhshari explain that the plural of heavens reflects their different natures while the singular of earth reflects its single nature. The word fulk, used for ships, serves as both singular and plural. Readers differ on whether winds should be singular or plural, and Ibn Kathir cites the prophetic supplication to make the wind a mercy and not a punishment. Al-Razi, al-Baydawi and Ibn Kathir stress that these signs reveal God's power, wisdom and mercy, and that only those who reflect perceive them.

This verse states that some people take rivals besides Allah, that is, equals, which in most readings are the idols they worshipped. They love them as they love Allah, meaning they venerate them and submit to them as they would to God. Most commentators hold that believers love Allah more intensely than these people love their idols, because their love is pure and shares nothing with Him. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn al-Jawzi report that the disbeliever turns away from his deity in hardship, whereas the believer never turns away from Allah.

The commentators differ on who the rivals are. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi take them to be idols, while al-Suddi and Ibn Abbas take them to be the leaders whom people obeyed in disobedience to God. Al-Wahidi and al-Baydawi adopt a broader sense that includes both. Al-Zamakhshari understands the love as veneration and submission, al-Razi connects it with the will, and Ibn al-Qayyim distinguishes love set alongside Allah, which is polytheism, from love for the sake of Allah, which belongs to the perfection of faith.

As for the clause about those who did wrong seeing the punishment, it is read in the second person by some and the third person by others. Its answer is left unstated; most hold that they would then know that all power belongs to Allah and that Allah is severe in punishment. Commentators note that this omission heightens the sense of dread.

This verse describes the Day of Judgment, when the leaders disown those who followed them after seeing the punishment, and every bond that joined them in this world is cut. The commentators agree that this refers to leaders who led people into idolatry and to followers who imitated them, and that the severing concerns everything they had clung to in hope of salvation. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir understand the 'bonds' (al-asbab) as the connections and mutual affection they had in the world, while Ibn Zayd and al-Suddi take them to be their deeds. Al-Tabari holds that the verse covers every leader who is upon disbelief. Al-Suddi says the 'leaders' are the devils who disown humans, whereas Qatada, 'Ata' and al-Rabi' mean human chiefs and leaders, a view that al-Razi and Ibn al-Jawzi prefer, since command and prohibition fit only beings who can speak. Al-Razi and al-Qurtubi report that the bonds may be love, kinship, covenants, dwellings or deeds, and al-Razi considers it most likely that all of these are included. Ibn al-Qayyim explains that every attachment made apart from God dissolves on the Day of Judgment, leaving only the servant's bond with his Lord. The followers wish to return to the world to disown their leaders, but this wish will not be granted and will only add to their regret, as God shows them their deeds as sources of anguish, and they will never leave the Fire.

This verse describes the fate of the followers on the Day of Resurrection: their leaders, whom they obeyed in disobedience to God, disown them, and the followers wish for a return to the world to disown them in turn. The commentators explain that this wish cannot be granted, that God will show them their deeds as sources of regret, and that they will never leave the Fire. As to who the "followed" are, al-Tabari, al-Rabi', Qatada, 'Ata' and al-Razi take them to be the chiefs and leaders among human associators, whereas al-Suddi takes them to be the devils who misled them; al-Wahidi, Ibn al-Jawzi and Ibn Juzayy report both views. Al-Razi judges the first more likely, since commanding and forbidding does not fit idols. On the deeds that cause regret, al-Rabi' and Ibn Zayd understand the evil deeds committed, which earned them the Fire, while Ibn Mas'ud and al-Suddi understand the good deeds neglected, whose loss deprives them of Paradise; al-Tabari favours the first view, while al-Razi and Ibn Kathir report both. The "severed ties" are read by Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid and Qatada as affections, by Ibn Jurayj as kinship, by Ibn Zayd and al-Suddi as deeds, and by Abu Rawq as covenants. The closing negation is taken by Sunni jurists as proof that unbelievers remain in the Fire forever; al-Razi draws from it that sinful believers do leave, al-Zamakhshari sees only emphasis and not exclusivity, and Ibn Kathir reads it as the eternal damnation of associators.

God addresses all people, permitting them to eat of what is on the earth, provided it is lawful and good, and warns them against following in the footsteps of Satan. The commentators agree that the verse permits good things and forbids making unlawful what God has made lawful. Most report that it was revealed concerning people of Thaqif, Khuza'a and Banu Mudlij, who had forbidden for themselves certain livestock and crops, such as the bahira, sa'iba, wasila and ham, as al-Tabari, al-Mawardi, al-Baghawi and Ibn Kathir relate. The word lawful is understood by most as what the law has permitted. As for good, Malik takes it as emphasising the sense of lawful, while al-Shafi'i understands it as what the soul finds pleasant, which excludes filthy animals. Al-Zamakhshari and Ibn 'Atiyya take it to mean pure from any doubt. The word for steps originally refers to the space between the two feet. Ibn 'Abbas explains it as Satan's deeds, Mujahid as his sins, al-Sudi as obedience to him, and Abu Mijlaz as vows made in disobedience. Al-Tabari observes that these views are close in meaning, since all of them forbid following the traces and works of Satan. The commentators conclude that his enmity toward mankind is clear, which makes the warning necessary.

This part of the verse says that Satan commands people to do evil, meaning any sin that harms the one who commits it, and indecency, meaning what exceeds all bounds of ugliness, as well as to say about God what they do not know. The commentators agree that evil (su') covers all acts of disobedience, with indecency (fahsha') being its most serious form. They differ on how to define each term. Ibn 'Abbas, through the report of Badhan, as well as al-Wahidi and al-Qurtubi, holds that evil is what carries no prescribed legal penalty and indecency is what does, while al-Sudi and Muqatil take indecency to mean adultery, and 'Ata' takes it to mean stinginess. Al-Tabari understands evil as sin and indecency as whatever is too shameful to mention. As for saying about God what one does not know, al-Tabari explains it as the prohibition of the bahira, sa'iba and similar practices they had made into law, while others read it as declaring things lawful or unlawful without knowledge, or as ascribing partners to God. Al-Razi and al-Qasimi take the phrase to cover every false statement about God, including that of the one who follows authority blindly. Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Alusi note that a jurist's conclusion reached by reasoned effort becomes knowledge through the consensus that it must be acted upon, so it is not the forbidden following of conjecture. Ibn Kathir reports that Qatada and al-Sudi consider every disobedience to God to be among Satan's steps.

This verse describes those who, when told to follow what God has revealed, reply that they will follow what they found their fathers doing. God answers that their fathers understood nothing and were not guided, so they should not be followed blindly. The commentators agree in condemning the blind imitation of people who have neither knowledge nor insight, whether in matters of belief, worship, or the forbidding of what is lawful, such as the baheera and the saiba. They differ on who is addressed. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and most exegetes take it to be the polytheist Arabs, while others, including al-Razi and Ibn al-Jawzi, relate a report that it concerns Jews invited to Islam by the Prophet. Al-Zamakhshari and Ibn 'Atiyya link the pronoun to the people mentioned in the preceding verse. Al-Razi, al-Nasafi and al-Baydawi explain the argument as setting proof against imitation. Al-Alusi and Abu al-Su'ud hold that the verse forbids imitation to one able to reason, while following someone whose rectitude has been established is not blameworthy. Ibn al-Jawzi, al-Qurtubi and Ibn 'Atiyya treat the wording as rejecting imitation in creed, and Ibn 'Ashur notes that the verse is directed at those who refuse the revelation rather than at the scholarly question of juristic taqlid. Ibn 'Uthaymin draws a warning against blind partisanship, and al-Sha'rawi observes that imitating parents is natural in childhood but must yield to revelation.

This verse compares the disbelievers, when they are called to follow what Allah has sent down, to a flock that hears its shepherd's shout and call without understanding what is meant. Commentators such as Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi and al-Baydawi agree that the disbeliever hears the admonition as mere sound, without grasping its meaning or benefiting from it. They are deaf to the truth, mute in proclaiming it, and blind to its path, so they do not reason.

According to reports traced to Ibn 'Abbas, the verse was revealed about Jews whom the Prophet invited to Islam and who replied that they would follow what their fathers had found. Al-Tabari adopts this reading, though he acknowledges difficulties in his own argument. Ibn Kathir and Ibn 'Atiyya, by contrast, consider that the passage continues to address the pagan Arabs and the Quraysh.

The scholars differ on how to read the image. Al-Farra', Sibawayh, Ibn Qutayba and al-Zajjaj assume an omitted element, namely the one who calls, or treat the comparison as concerning the livestock; al-Razi and al-Qurtubi record these readings. Ibn Zayd, whose view al-Tabari also notes from another angle, instead likens the disbelievers' calling upon their idols to someone shouting into a mountain and hearing only an echo. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Baydawi and al-Nasafi find this last reading weak, since idols hear nothing.

Al-Razi, Ibn al-Qayyim and Ibn Sa'di draw a moral lesson: the image diminishes the blind follower and warns others against imitating him. Ibn 'Uthaymin sees in it above all a criticism of blind conformity.

In this verse God addresses the believers, telling them to eat of the good things He has provided and to give thanks to Him for them, if they truly worship Him alone. Most commentators understand the "good things" to mean what is lawful and pleasant, and they take the provision of God to include what is lawful. Ibn 'Atiyya notes that the partitive "min" implies that some provision may be unlawful; az-Zamakhshari replies that this is a Mu'tazili view, while Sunni scholars accept that something God provides may be forbidden. At-Tabari and Ibn Kathir explain that the purpose is to cancel the prohibitions the polytheists had imposed on certain foods. Ibn Kathir adds that eating what is lawful helps the acceptance of supplication and worship, and cites the hadith of Abu Hurayra for this. As for gratitude, Ibn 'Uthaymin defines it as acting righteously, while al-Razi asks whether gratitude is obligatory at all and distinguishes between the heart, the tongue and the limbs. The conditional clause "if you truly worship Him" is taken by most to mean that gratitude is part of worship; others read it as knowledge of God or as the intention to worship Him. The following verses list the prohibitions: carrion, flowing blood, the flesh of swine, and what has been slaughtered for other than God.
