All agree that these are permitted in cases of necessity, provided one is neither rebellious nor transgressing. They differ, however, on the meaning of those two conditions. Mujahid and Sa'id ibn Jubayr understand them as referring to highwaymen and those who rebel against the ruler; al-Hasan and Qatada take them to mean eating without necessity or beyond what is needed. Jurists such as Abu Hanifa, al-Shafi'i and Malik disagree on how much carrion the one in necessity may eat.

The commentators agree that this verse lists the forbidden foods right after the command to eat good things, and that the word "innama" restricts the prohibition to the items named. Carrion (al-maytah) means an animal that died without lawful slaughter, the forbidden blood is flowing blood, the pig's flesh covers the whole animal, and what was dedicated to other than God refers to an animal offered to idols. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Abu Hayyan explain that the prohibition concerns eating. The word for carrion is general, but fish and locusts are excluded by the Sunna and by the verse on game of the sea; most scholars hold that liver and spleen are permitted and that blood left in the veins after slaughter is not forbidden. As for necessity, most commentators allow eating only without rebelling or transgressing. Al-Tabari, al-Shafi'i and others understand the rebel as one who revolts against the ruler and the transgressor as one who robs travellers or travels in sin, whereas Abu Hanifa and Malik take them to mean exceeding what is needed or seeking pleasure; al-Hasan and Qatada limit eating to what stills hunger, while Malik allows eating one's fill and taking provisions. Scholars also differ on the threshold of necessity, on eating human flesh, on using wine as medicine, and on taking another's food, matters developed in the legal works cited by al-Qurtubi and Ibn al-'Arabi. The verse closes with God's forgiveness and mercy, which explain why the sin is lifted.

This verse describes the fate of those who conceal what God has revealed in the Book and trade it for a small worldly price. The commentators explain that what they consume as bribes and payment for hiding the truth will turn into fire in their bellies, that God will not speak to them on the Day of Resurrection in a way that pleases them, will not purify them, and that a painful punishment awaits them. Most commentators, including Ibn 'Abbas, al-Rabi' and Qatada, say it refers to Jewish rabbis who concealed the description of the Prophet ﷺ found in their scriptures, fearing loss of leadership and the gifts they received. Al-Razi adds that concealment can mean twisting verses away from their true meaning, and that the small price may be wealth or status. Regarding eating only fire, al-Zamakhshari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baydawi read it as a figure: what they took leads to fire, while others, such as al-Hasan and Ibn Jarir, hold that it will be literal fire in the afterlife. On God not speaking to them, most scholars take it as an expression of His anger, while Ibn Juzayy and others understand it as the absence of pleasing words, not a total denial of speech, since other verses describe Him addressing the disbelievers. The verse thus warns scholars against hiding the truth for worldly gain.

The commentators explain that the verse refers to Jewish scholars who concealed what their scriptures said about the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ and the truth of his mission, in exchange for worldly gain or bribes. They traded guidance for misguidance and forgiveness for punishment, that is, they abandoned what leads to forgiveness and chose what leads to punishment. Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi add that what they eat of that gain becomes fire in their bellies.

The phrase "how patient they are over the Fire" has several readings. Most exegetes, including al-Hasan, Mujahid, Ibn Jubayr and Qatada, take it as an expression of wonder at their audacity in doing what leads to the Fire. Al-Kisa'i reports that the Arabs say "how patient you are toward God" to mean "how bold you are toward Him". By contrast, 'Ata', al-Suddi and Ibn Zayd read it as a rebuking question: what made them endure the Fire? Al-Mubarrad sees a warning rather than a true expression of wonder.

The commentators agree that those who conceal the truth deserve punishment, and that God will not speak to them on the Day of Resurrection in a word of approval nor purify them. They differ on the meaning of this absence of speech: al-Tabari, al-Baghawi and Ibn Kathir understand it as an expression of His anger, while others take it to mean that He will not speak to them of what they love. As for those who disputed the Book, al-Suddi and al-Tabari identify them with Jews and Christians, while others point to the Quraysh, some of whom called the Qur'an sorcery, poetry or fables. The "far-reaching schism" is generally understood as a long-lasting enmity and a distance from the truth.

The commentators explain that "that" (dhalika) refers back to the preceding threat against those who conceal what Allah has revealed of the Book: the punishment they receive is because Allah sent down the Book with truth, which they then hid and rejected. Al-Tabari and others note several grammatical readings, in which the word may be a subject or predicate, or an accusative governed by an implied verb. For al-Tabari the address is to the Jewish rabbis; Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Qurtubi hold that the meaning may extend to anyone who hides the truth. As for the second part, "those who differ about the Book are in far-reaching dissension," most commentators, including al-Tabari, al-Baghawi and al-Baydawi, take it to mean the Jews and Christians, who disagreed over the Torah and the Gospel, accepting some parts and rejecting others. Al-Wahidi and al-Sam'ani instead understand it as the Meccan polytheists who called the Quran sorcery, poetry or fables. The word shiqaq, they explain, means opposition and enmity, each party standing on its own side. Ibn Kathir and Ibn Sa'di stress that such division leads far from the truth, while those who hold to the Book in its entirety remain united. The commentators generally agree that the verse warns against concealing the truth and against divisions that lead to hostility.

This verse teaches that true righteousness does not consist merely in turning one's face toward east or west in prayer, since the prayer was previously directed toward Jerusalem. The commentators differ on who is addressed. Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid and al-Dahhak take it as addressed to the believers: righteousness is not limited to prayer. Qatada, al-Rabi' ibn Anas and Abu al-'Aliya take it as addressed to the Jews and Christians, each of whom claimed that righteousness lay in its own direction of prayer. On the substance they agree that complete righteousness is belief in God, the Last Day, the angels, the Scriptures and the prophets, giving wealth out of love for it to relatives, orphans, the needy, the wayfarer, those who ask, and for freeing captives, establishing prayer and paying the obligatory zakat, keeping covenants, and being patient in hardship, illness and battle. Ibn Kathir and al-Tabari explain that giving 'out of love for it' means giving while healthy, covetous and fearing poverty. Al-Zamakhshari and Ibn 'Atiyya tie the pronoun to the wealth, while others tie it to God. On whether there is an obligation in wealth beyond zakat, al-Sha'bi and al-Suddi affirm it, citing the verse and the hadith of Fatima bint Qays, whereas the majority restrict it to zakat or voluntary charity. Some take 'the wayfarer' to be the guest, others the stranded traveller; 'those in bondage' are understood by some as slaves buying freedom, by others as captives. The verse ends by describing these people as truthful and God-fearing.

This verse prescribes retaliation for deliberate killing: the killer is to be punished in kind, a free man for a free man, a slave for a slave, a woman for a woman. The commentators differ on its scope. Al-Tabari holds that retaliation is a right granted to the victim's heirs rather than an obligation, and that its purpose is to prevent harm falling on anyone other than the killer; he cites several accounts of the occasion of revelation, including tribal feuds of the pre-Islamic era, transmitted through al-Sha'bi and Qatada. Al-Mawardi and al-Wahidi list four opinions, among them that of Ibn Abbas that the verse was abrogated by the words "a life for a life". Ibn Atiyya argues that that later verse reports the law given to the Children of Israel and therefore cannot abrogate this one. Abu Hanifa and his followers hold that a free man may be killed for an slave, whereas Malik and al-Shafi'i reject this. The majority holds that a Muslim is not killed for a non-Muslim. As for the words "if anything is remitted to him by his brother", most exegetes take it to mean pardon in exchange for blood-money, to be claimed kindly and paid without delay. The verse calls this a lightening and a mercy, since the Jews were bound to retaliation and the Christians to pardon, while this community may choose between retaliation, blood-money, and pardon. Whoever transgresses after this will suffer a painful punishment, and scholars differ on whether this means death, punishment in the hereafter, or the ruler's judgment. The verse ends by saying that retaliation brings life, because it restrains people from killing.

This verse states that retaliation (qisas) brings life to people, and it addresses those of sound intellect so that they may guard against killing. The commentators explain that the prospect of execution deters the would-be killer: knowing he will be killed in return, he refrains, and so both his life and that of his intended victim are preserved. Al-Tabari, Mujahid and Qatada take this as a deterrent and a warning, a means by which God restrains people from harming one another. Al-Zamakhshari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn 'Atiyya see a broader meaning: executing the killer ends feuds and prevents one murder from leading to the deaths of many, as pre-Islamic Arabs used to do. Al-Razi, Ibn al-Qayyim and others discuss the eloquence of the wording, which makes retaliation the place of life and sets two opposites side by side. Al-Nasafi and al-Baydawi regard this phrasing as superior to the Arab saying that killing prevents killing. Most commentators understand the life in question as life in this world, while Ibn Kathir and others report that it may also refer to the life to come for one who has borne the penalty here. Al-Qurtubi holds that only the authority may enforce retaliation, and that a ruler who wrongs someone must submit to it himself. According to the majority, a free man is not executed for a slave, nor a Muslim for a non-Muslim, whereas Abu Hanifa allows the first of these. The verse ends with 'so that you may be godfearing': Ibn Zayd takes this to mean fearing to kill lest you be killed, Ibn 'Abbas to mean avoiding bloodshed, and al-Zamakhshari and al-Nasafi to mean refraining from murder out of fear of retribution.

This verse makes bequest to parents and close relatives an obligation for one who, as death approaches, leaves property. It must be made fairly, without excess or favouritism, and it is a duty for the God-fearing. Al-Tabari reports that this obligation was abrogated for heirs by the inheritance verses, the view of Ibn Abbas, al-Hasan, Qatada, Tawus and al-Dahhak. Al-Tabari and others hold that the verse remains valid, its general wording meaning in fact the relatives who do not inherit. Ibn Zayd and many others consider the whole verse abrogated, leaving bequest as a recommendation. Al-Razi and Ibn Kathir cite Abu Muslim al-Isfahani, who argues that the verse does not contradict the inheritance shares but clarifies them. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Baydawi read "with what is fair" as equity among the beneficiaries. On the amount concerned, opinions differ: al-Zuhri holds that bequest applies to any sum, while Ali and Qatada set the threshold at a thousand dirhams, and al-Nakha'i at between five hundred and a thousand. Aisha and Ibn Abbas judge that a small sum should not be bequeathed. The hadith "a third, and a third is much" leads many to limit bequest to a third. The following verse adds that whoever alters the bequest after hearing it bears the sin himself, and that whoever, fearing a wrong by the testator, restores fairness between heirs and legatees incurs no blame.

This verse states that whoever alters a bequest after hearing it bears the sin of that alteration himself, not the deceased who made it, and that God hears and knows all. The commentators agree that the pronouns in 'changed it' and 'heard it' refer to the bequest or the act of bequeathing. Al-Tabari, Ibn Abi Najih and Qatada read it as changing the instruction itself, while Ibn Kathir adds that adding to, reducing, or concealing the will are all included. Al-Razi gives two readings: one aims at the executor, the witness, or anyone who blocks the property from reaching its rightful heir, and the other aims at the testator himself when he departs from the people God designated as beneficiaries, a view he attributes to al-Asamm. Al-Qurtubi and Ibn al-Arabi add that an unlawful bequest may be altered, and that any portion exceeding a third should not be executed. Ibn Kathir and Ibn Sa'di note that scholars differ over whether this recommendation to bequeath to close relatives was abrogated by the inheritance verses. Most understand the closing phrase, God hears and knows, as a warning to those who corrupt the deceased's wishes. The next verse makes an exception for one who, fearing injustice in a will, sets matters right between the parties.

This verse says that whoever fears from a testator a deviation from justice, whether by error or deliberately, and reconciles the parties, meaning the legatees and the heirs, by bringing the bequest back to fairness, commits no sin, for God is forgiving and merciful. The commentators understood the verb 'fear' either as apprehension or as knowledge, and distinguished janaf (unintentional deviation) from ithm (deliberate wrong). Mujahid, 'Ata' and Ibn Zayd take the conciliator to be someone present while the testator dictates in his final illness, who urges him toward justice and forbids him from wronging others. Ibn 'Abbas, Qatada, al-Rabi' and Ibrahim hold that reconciliation happens after death, restoring the bequest to what is right between heirs and legatees. Al-Tabari concludes that janaf and ithm mainly concern a bequest to close relatives beyond the third or a preference shown to some heirs, and that reconciliation means reminding the testator of what God has permitted, especially the third. 'Ata' reports that it concerns giving some heirs during life to the exclusion of others in the final illness. Tawus mentions a bequest to a son's or a daughter's child or husband intended to benefit the daughter. Al-Suddi and Ibn Zayd see the verse as governing bequests between parents and relatives. Al-Baghawi and Ibn al-Jawzi define janaf as deviation and ithm as injustice, a view echoed by al-Zajjaj. Al-Tabari argues that fear here means apprehension, since a wrong already done no longer calls for fear. The commentators do not decide among these views, and note that reconciliation may occur either before or after death, with forgiveness and mercy presented as the reward of the conciliator or of a testator who returns to justice.

This verse prescribes fasting for the believers. Linguistically, sawm means abstaining, and in law it is abstaining from food, drink and marital relations from dawn to sunset with intention. The commentators agree that the verse refers to the fast of Ramadan, but differ on the comparison with earlier peoples. Al-Tabari, citing al-Sha'bi, al-Suddi and Asbat, takes it to mean the Christians, who reportedly extended their fast to fifty days; Qatada and Mujahid take it to mean the People of the Book or all nations. Al-Tabari concludes the comparison concerns the timing and duration of the fast. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Razi and al-Nasafi hold instead that it concerns the very obligation of worship, practised by every community since Adam. Nearly all explain that its purpose is taqwa, since fasting subdues desire and restrains the appetites. Most identify the 'counted days' with Ramadan, while others mention three days a month and Ashura, later abrogated. The verse also addresses the sick and the traveller, who may break the fast and make up the days. Most jurists require making up the missed days, though Ibn Abbas holds that an elderly person unable to fast should feed a poor person for each day. The majority regards the verse on feeding as abrogated for those able to fast. All agree that fasting is better than paying the ransom for one who is able.

This verse states that fasting was prescribed for the believers as it was for earlier peoples, so that they may attain piety, and that it applies to a limited number of days, which most commentators identify as the month of Ramadan. The sick and the traveller may break the fast and make it up later by an equal number of days. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir report that most scholars hold that the make-up days need not be consecutive. Those who can fast only with great hardship, such as the aged man and the aged woman, and those whose illness will not be cured, break the fast and feed a poor person for each day. The commentators differ on this fidya. Ibn Abbas, Ibn Umar, Ibn Kathir and most scholars consider it abrogated by the verse requiring fasting from whoever witnesses the month. Al-Bukhari, Ibn Abbas in another report, Sa'id ibn Jubayr and Al-Qurtubi hold that it remains valid for the elderly and for the pregnant or nursing woman. The readings differ between yuṭīqūnahu, meaning they are able to do it, and yuṭawwiqūnahu, meaning they are burdened by it. Al-Razi, Al-Baydawi and others specify the amount of food as a mudd or half a sa', according to the schools. Finally the verse says that whoever gives more does better, and that fasting is better than the fidya for whoever knows its worth.

This verse names the month of Ramadan as the one in which the Qur'an began to be revealed, a guidance for people and clear proofs that distinguish truth from falsehood. Most commentators, following Ibn Abbas, explain that the Qur'an was first sent down all at once to the lowest heaven on the Night of Decree and then revealed in portions according to events; others take the phrase to mean that it was revealed concerning the fasting obligation or its virtue. All agree that whoever is present, healthy and resident must fast. They differ over one who is resident at the start of the month and then travels: Ali, Ibn Abbas and Ubayda al-Salmani hold that he must complete the fast, while the majority of scholars permit him to break it while travelling. The sick person and the traveller must make up the number of days missed. Opinions differ on which illness permits breaking the fast: for some any illness that is called illness, for al-Shafi'i one whose worsening is clear, for al-Hasan one that prevents praying standing. On fasting while travelling, it is agreed to be permitted, but scholars debate which is better: some prefer fasting, others breaking it, and others choose whichever is easier. The verse states that God desires ease for you and not hardship. It adds that making up the days serves to complete the number of days of the month, and that God should be magnified at the end of the month, generally from the sighting of the new moon of Shawwal until the festival prayer, with thanks for the guidance received.

This verse affirms that God is near to His servants, hearing and answering the one who calls upon Him. The commentators give several accounts of its occasion. Al-Hasan al-Basri reports that people asked the Prophet ﷺ whether their Lord is near, so they might speak to Him privately, or far, so they must call out. Other reports, transmitted by Ata', Qatada and Mujahid, concern the time, the manner or the place of supplication. As to nearness, al-Mawardi and Ibn al-Jawzi understand it as nearness of response or of hearing. Al-Zamakhshari sees it as an image of how readily God grants what is asked, like someone close at hand who answers at once. Al-Razi explains it as nearness of knowledge and awareness rather than of place, a view that Ibn Kathir and al-Tabari also favour, quoting hadiths on the merit of supplication. Regarding the answer, many scholars make it conditional on God's will, on consistency with His decree, or on the absence of transgression in the prayer, as Ibn Juzayy and al-Shawkani do. Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi note that the answer may take the form of immediate granting, of a reward stored for the Hereafter, or of harm averted, relying on a hadith of Abu Sa'id al-Khudri. The Mu'tazila hold that the answer is reserved for believers, a view Ibn Kathir rejects as contrary to the sense of the praise. Several interpreters take istijaba to mean obedience and submission, and the faith that follows it to mean steadfastness, while rushd is rightful guidance.

This verse permits sexual relations and eating during the nights of Ramadan, a permission that had been withheld in the early days of Islam, when a fasting person who slept before breaking the fast, or who had prayed the night prayer, was forbidden food and intercourse until the following night. The commentators explain that "rafath" refers to intercourse, and that spouses are a garment for one another, covering and protecting each other; others take it to mean rest and comfort. According to al-Tabari and most exegetes, some companions, including Umar ibn al-Khattab, had broken the prohibition out of weakness; God forgave them and lifted the ban with the words "now, lie with them." As for "what God has prescribed for you," most understand it as offspring, Qatada as God's own permission, and Ibn Abbas as the Night of Power. Most scholars take the white thread as the light of dawn and the black thread as the darkness of night, relying on the hadith of Adi ibn Hatim, while a minority permitted eating until sunrise. The fast continues until nightfall; the man in spiritual seclusion in the mosque must abstain from his wife, and these rulings are God's limits that must not be approached, so that people may be mindful of Him.

This verse forbids believers from consuming one another's wealth unjustly, that is, by any means the law does not permit, such as seizure, theft or gambling. The commentators read the phrase 'and bring it before the judges' in two ways. Al-Tabari, al-Razi and Ibn Kathir understand it as pleading for property one has no right to while knowing one is in the wrong, using the courts to obtain it. Ibn 'Atiyya, al-Zamakhshari, al-Baydawi and Abu Hayyan take it rather as bribery, offering money to judges to obtain an unjust ruling, and Ibn 'Atiyya prefers this reading because judges are prone to accept bribes. Most explain that the 'sin' includes false testimony, false oaths and bribery. Many cite the hadith of Umm Salama, 'I am only a human being... whatever I award of a brother's right, let him not take it, for it is a piece of Fire', and conclude that a judge's ruling does not make lawful what is unlawful before God, though it binds outwardly. Al-Alusi reports that Abu Hanifa allowed an exception in certain cases, which others dispute. Ibn 'Ashur adds that a judge who takes payment for a just verdict also commits an unlawful taking. Al-Qurtubi stresses that taking any wealth unlawfully is a sin, whatever its amount.

The commentators explain that this verse answers the question about the crescent moons and their changes: God made them markers of time by which people set their dates and acts of worship, first of all the pilgrimage and its times, but also fasting, the waiting periods, debts and rental terms. On the phrase 'Piety is not entering houses from their backs', the exegetes report that the Ansar and other Arabs, once in ihram for hajj or 'umra, would not enter through the door of their house but would break through the back wall or climb over, considering this a good deed. The verse forbids this and commands entering through the doors. All agree that true piety is fearing God by doing what He commands and avoiding what He forbids, and that success is its fruit. Al-Tabari, al-Baghawi and Ibn Kathir keep the report of al-Bara' about an Ansari who entered by his door and was reproached. Al-Razi gives several possible causes and a figurative reading in which entering from the back means taking a crooked path. According to Ibn Abbas, Qatada and al-Rabi', the questioners were Companions; other reports name Mu'adh ibn Jabal and Tha'laba ibn Ghanm. Ibn Uthaymin holds that the question concerned the wisdom behind the moon's phases rather than their cause. Abu 'Ubayda sees the verse as a parable meaning that matters should be approached by their proper route, while al-Zamakhshari reads it as a call to accept God's wisdom in His acts without doubt. The commentators finally note that the verse links the markers of time with the rejection of innovation in worship and with the call to piety.

This verse commands believers to fight in the cause of God, meaning to raise God's word and support the religion, against those who fight them, while forbidding aggression such as killing non-combatants or exceeding the bounds of war. Commentators agree it is among the first verses revealed on fighting in Medina, when Muslims had earlier been ordered to hold back, and that the Prophet fought those who fought him and spared those who refrained. They differ on whether it remains in force. Al-Rabi, Ibn Zayd, al-Nahhas and Ibn al-Jawzi hold that it was abrogated by Surat al-Tawba and the verse 'fight the polytheists all together'. Ibn Abbas, Mujahid and Umar ibn Abd al-Aziz hold that it is still valid, applying only to those fit for combat and excluding women, children, the elderly and monks. Ibn Kathir and al-Sa'di read it as an exhortation that describes the reality of the enemy. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Razi and al-Baydawi understand the prohibition of aggression to include starting the fighting without warning, breaking a treaty, mutilation, and killing those who must not be killed. The following verses order that fighters be killed wherever they are found, except near the Sacred Mosque, and explain that persecution in religion is worse than killing. The scholars conclude that hostilities must cease once aggression ends, and that the aim of fighting is to remove polytheism and secure freedom of worship.

This verse commands the believers to fight the polytheists who fight them wherever they meet them, and to expel them from the place from which they expelled the Muslims, Mecca, and states that fitna, meaning associationism and turning people away from the faith, is worse than killing. The commentators explain that "thaqiftumuhum" means finding them and being able to kill them, and that fitna may mean disbelief itself, as Ibn Abbas, al-Rabi and Qatada held, the apostasy of a believer into idolatry, as Mujahid said, or persecution that pushes people to renounce their faith, as al-Kisa'i reported. On fighting near the Sacred Mosque the scholars differ: Qatada, al-Rabi and Ibn Zayd hold the ruling abrogated, while Mujahid, Tawus and Abu Hanifa hold it binding, so the fight there begins only if the enemy starts it. Ibn Kathir and al-Sa'di note the prohibition against harming women, children, the elderly and monks. The reading of Hamza and al-Kisa'i, "wa la taqtuluhum", is explained as meaning they kill some of you. Forgiveness is tied to ceasing disbelief and fighting, and it follows that one who desists should not be attacked, except the wrongdoers.

This verse says that if the unbelievers cease fighting the Muslims and turn away from their polytheism, God forgives them what has passed and shows them mercy. Most commentators understand "ceasing" as both giving up the fighting and giving up disbelief: al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi take the forgiveness to cover shirk and earlier sins, while al-Sam'ani and al-Jalalayn link it to conversion to Islam. Ibn al-Jawzi notes that some read it as stopping only the fighting, and al-Razi argues that forgiveness cannot be tied merely to giving up war.

The verse follows the command to fight those who fight you in God's way. On whether that command still stands, opinions differ. Al-Mawardi, Ibn al-Jawzi and Ibn Kathir report that al-Rabi', Qatada and Ibn Zayd held it abrogated by the later verses of Surat al-Tawba, while Mujahid, Ibn Abbas and Abu Hanifa considered it still binding, and al-Qurtubi sided with that view. Ibn Juzayy and Ibn Sa'di note that the word "those who fight you" refers to fighting men, excluding women, children and the elderly.

The commentators agree on the core meaning: enemies who stop hostilities and embrace Islam receive God's pardon, and ending hostility removes the basis for fighting. They differ on abrogation, on how broadly "ceasing" should be read, and on the precise nature of the forgiveness, some seeing in it a call to pardon the defeated. These differences shape how the passage is understood.

In this verse God commands the believers to fight those polytheists who fight them, until strife (fitna) ends, meaning associationism and the persecution it brings upon believers, and until religion belongs wholly to God. On the general meaning the commentators agree: Ibn Abbas, Qatada, al-Rabi' and al-Suddi take fitna to be associationism, and religion to be exclusive worship and obedience to God. As for "if they desist", most understand it as abandoning disbelief and entering Islam, while al-Zamakhshari, Ibn 'Atiyya and Abu Hayyan add that for People of the Book it may mean paying the poll tax. The phrase "there is no hostility except against the wrongdoers" means that those who have given up polytheism must not be attacked; the wrongdoers are, for some, those who persist in disbelief, and for others those who began the aggression. The word "aggression" is used for the retribution by way of correspondence, as in "whoever attacks you, attack him in the same way".

Scholars differ on the scope of the verse. Al-Rabi', Ibn Zayd, Qatada, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi consider it abrogated by the verses of the sword, whereas Mujahid, Ibn Abbas and Umar ibn Abd al-Aziz hold it to be still in force, restricting hostility to fighters and excluding women and children. Al-Zamakhshari, Ibn Juzayy and Ibn Kathir explain that the wrongdoers are polytheists who refuse to say "there is no god but God", as Ikrima and Qatada state. Al-Razi and al-Qurtubi draw from the verse that disbelief is the cause of fighting, relying on the hadith ordering people to be fought until they profess faith. Ibn 'Ashur notes that fitna is used here in a general sense, that its end is achieved either through Islam or through the death of the adversaries, and that reading it as polytheism concerns the intended aim rather than the strict meaning of the word.

This passage establishes that fighting in the sacred months and in the sacred precinct follows a rule of equal retaliation. The most widely reported occasion, given by al-Tabari, Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, Qatada, al-Rabi' and al-Dahhak, is the 'umra of the year six: the Prophet ﷺ set out in dhu al-qa'da, was prevented by the Quraysh from reaching the Ka'ba, and performed his 'umra in the same month the following year, so the sacred month in which he was barred corresponds to the sacred month in which he entered. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir favour this reading. Al-Hasan al-Basri, followed by al-Zajjaj, understands it instead as the case where the polytheists permit fighting in a sacred month, so the believers may respond in kind. Ibn al-Jawzi and Ibn Kathir report that some scholars considered the verse abrogated by the verse of the sword, while Mujahid held it to be valid and allowed fighting in the sacred precinct only after being attacked. The commentators agree that 'the sacred things are subject to retaliation' means every violated sanctity may be answered in kind, that the word 'aggression' is used for the response by verbal correspondence, and that God-consciousness sets the limit of the response, God being with those who fear Him through help and support. On recovering property the opinions differ: al-Shafi'i permits taking one's due secretly in clear cases, whereas Malik in one narration and Abu Hanifa hold that such matters rest with the judges. Some report the verse was revealed in Mecca before the Muslims had power and was later abrogated; Mujahid calls it Medinan, after the 'umra of substitution, a view al-Tabari adopts.

This verse calls on believers to spend in the way of God, warns them not to throw themselves into ruin, and then urges them to do good, since God loves the good-doers. The commentators agree on the main meaning: the spending meant is giving wealth for good causes, above all for jihad and equipping fighters, and tahlukah means destruction. They differ, however, on what this ruin consists of. Hudhayfa, Ibn Abbas, al-Hasan, Ata, Ikrima and most exegetes take it to be refraining from spending out of fear of poverty; Ibn Abbas adds that one should give even if one has only a single arrow. Abu Ayyub al-Ansari understood it as abandoning fighting in order to tend one's property, and Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi report that he held the verse was revealed about the Ansar. Al-Bara ibn Azib and others read it as despair of God's mercy after a sin, while some see it as extravagance in spending or reckless charging into battle with no effect on the enemy, as al-Zamakhshari and al-Qurtubi relate. As for ihsan, most take it to mean perfecting one's deeds, Ikrima as thinking well of God, and Ibn Zayd as kindness to the needy. Al-Tabari adopts a general reading covering everything that leads to ruin, a view al-Shawkani and al-Qurtubi also endorse.

The commentators explain that this verse commands believers to complete the hajj and the umrah for God alone, fulfilling them in full. They differ on the meaning of completion: Ibn Abbas, Alqama and Mujahid take it as performing the rites with their prescribed features; Ali, Ibn Mas'ud, Sa'id ibn Jubayr and Tawus take it as entering the state of consecration from one's home; al-Thawri takes it as setting out for these two alone, not for trade; Qatada takes it as performing the umrah outside the months of hajj. The verse then addresses the one who is prevented (ihsar): he should sacrifice whatever offering is within his means, and not shave his head until the offering reaches its place. Scholars differ on what counts as prevention. Malik, al-Shafi'i and Ahmad read it as the hindrance of an enemy, while Abu Hanifa extends it to illness and other causes, relying on the hadith of Hajjaj ibn Amr about the lame and the wounded. As for the offering, most commentators say a sheep, while Ibn Umar and Aisha restrict it to camels and cattle; the stronger view is that it is whatever is easily available among what is called an offering. A man troubled in his head may shave it, but must pay a ransom: a three-day fast, feeding six poor people, or a sacrifice, as in the hadith of Ka'b ibn Ujra. Finally the verse treats tamattu': whoever performs umrah and then hajj owes an offering; if he cannot, he fasts three days during the hajj and seven when he returns, making ten complete days. This applies to those who do not live in Mecca. The verse closes with a call to piety and a warning of severe punishment.

This verse states that the pilgrimage takes place in months known to the Arabs: Shawwal, Dhu al-Qa'da, and ten nights (or ten days) of Dhu al-Hijja. Whoever binds himself to the pilgrimage in these months must refrain from rafath, from wickedness (fusuq) and from quarrelling. The commentators agree that rafath means sexual relations and their verbal preliminaries; Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn Mas'ud, Ibn 'Umar and others take it as intercourse, while 'Ata' and Tawus include allusions made to women in their presence. Ibn 'Umar understands fusuq as the transgressions specific to the state of ihram, such as hunting game, whereas Ibn 'Abbas and al-Hasan take it as all sins; some read it as insult, citing a hadith. Quarrelling is explained as contending with a companion until he is angered, and others as disputes over the places and times of the rites.

Jurists differ on the length of these months. Ibn 'Umar, Ibn Mas'ud, 'Ata', Mujahid and Malik hold that all of Dhu al-Hijja is included, while Ibn 'Abbas, al-Sha'bi, Abu Hanifa and al-Shafi'i count only the first ten days. Al-Shafi'i concludes from the verse that one may not enter ihram for the hajj before these months, whereas Abu Hanifa and Malik permit it, the latter with reservation. On the intention, al-Shafi'i holds that intention alone suffices, while Abu Hanifa requires the talbiya or the garlanding of the offering.

The verse then orders the believers to take provisions for the journey. According to Ibn 'Abbas it was revealed concerning people of Yemen who set out without provisions and begged from others, though several commentators also read it as the provision of piety for the hereafter. Piety is called the best provision, and the address ends with the people of understanding.

This verse lifts any blame from pilgrims who seek provision from their Lord through trade during the pilgrimage, and then bids them, when they leave Arafat for Muzdalifa, to remember God at the Sacred Landmark, glorifying Him as He guided them, after having been astray before. The commentators agree that the 'bounty' here means profit from trade and hire, and that the verse was revealed to remove a scruple some Arabs felt about buying and selling during the pilgrimage. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir report Ibn 'Abbas on the markets of 'Ukaz, Majanna and Dhu al-Majaz, and Ibn 'Umar's answer to those who hired out their mounts for the pilgrimage, that their hajj is valid. Al-Tabari also notes that Ibn 'Abbas and Ibn al-Zubayr read the verse with an added phrase 'during the seasons of the hajj', a reading outside the standard text. On the outpouring from Arafat, most take it to mean the mass departure after the standing, and al-Tabari explains that the Hums of Quraysh stood at Muzdalifa rather than Arafat, hence the command to join the people. As for the Sacred Landmark, Ibn 'Abbas and Sa'id ibn Jubayr place it between the two hills of Muzdalifa, Ibn 'Umar takes it to be all of Muzdalifa, and others identify it with the hill of Quzah where the imam stands. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir favour the first view and state that all of Muzdalifa is a place of standing except the valley of Muhassir. The remembrance commanded is, for most, the talbiyah, tahlil and supplication, while one view takes it to be the maghrib and 'isha' prayers. The repetition of the command to remember God is explained in several ways: some distinguish remembrance of the heart from that of the tongue, others see the second as thanks for guidance. For many, the straying mentioned is idolatry and the corruption of the rites of the hajj.

In this verse God orders the pilgrims to depart from Arafat together with the rest of the people and to ask their Lord for forgiveness, for He is Forgiving and Merciful. Most commentators understand the address to be to the Quraysh and those who followed their religion, known as the Hums, who would stay at Muzdalifa instead of going to Arafat out of pride in the sanctity of the Haram; they are commanded to stand at Arafat and depart from it like everyone else. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi report, on the authority of 'A'isha, Ibn 'Abbas and others, that the Prophet, before his mission, used to stand at Arafat unlike his tribe. Al-Baydawi, al-Nasafi and Abu al-Su'ud explain that the word 'thumma' here expresses the gap in value between the two departures, one correct and the other mistaken, rather than a sequence in time; Ibn 'Atiyya sees it merely as linking two statements. Al-Dahhak, and al-Tabari who leans toward him, understand the address to be to all Muslims and 'the people' to mean Abraham, so the departure would be from Muzdalifa toward Mina; al-Tabari adopts this view were it not for the consensus against it, and Ibn Kathir reports it from al-Dahhak alone. Others, such as al-Qurtubi and Abu Hayyan, note that 'al-nas' may refer to Adam or to the Arabs other than the Hums. The commentators stress that seeking forgiveness is recommended in places where mercy is hoped for, and that the passage calls for humility and equality among pilgrims.

After completing the rites of pilgrimage, such as the stoning, the sacrifice, the circumambulation and the stay at Mina, God tells the pilgrims to remember Him often and praise Him, just as the Arabs used to boast about their forefathers, and even more. The verse then contrasts two kinds of supplicants: the one who asks only for the goods of this world and so has no share in the Hereafter, and the one who prays, "Our Lord, give us good in this world and good in the Hereafter, and protect us from the torment of the Fire." Commentators explain the remembrance in different ways. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and others take it to mean glorification and takbir, since the Arabs used to boast of their fathers at these gatherings, while Ata and al-Dahhak compare it to a child calling out to his father and mother. Al-Sudi reports that some people asked only for wealth and abundance. As for the two goods, the commentators differ: Ali and Qatada mention a righteous wife or health in this world and the houris or Paradise in the next, al-Hasan names knowledge and worship here and Paradise there, and several scholars see the prayer as encompassing all the good of both worlds. Al-Baghawi and Ibn Kathir note that the Prophet repeated this supplication often. On the phrase "a share of what they have earned", Ibn Kathir understands it as a reward, while al-Zamakhshari suggests that the supplication itself may count as an earning. Finally, God is swift in reckoning, which the exegetes explain as speed in judgment, ease in counting deeds, or the nearness of the Hour.

This verse distinguishes two kinds of prayer after the rites of the pilgrimage are completed. On the phrase, 'Our Lord, give us good in this world and good in the Hereafter, and protect us from the punishment of the Fire,' al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi and al-Qurtubi, along with most scholars, take the two 'goods' to mean the good of this world and the good of the next together, since the word is indefinite and can cover whatever benefit suits the believer. They agree that the good of the Hereafter is Paradise. For the good of this world, al-Tabari includes health, sustenance, knowledge and worship, while others narrow it: a righteous wife according to Ali, knowledge and worship according to al-Hasan, and wealth according to al-Suddi and Ibn Zayd. Ibn Kathir reports that the Prophet often recited this supplication, that Anas used it too, and that it is recommended between the Yemeni corner and the Black Stone. Those who ask only for worldly things, according to al-Zamakhshari, al-Razi and Ibn Kathir, have no share in the Hereafter; al-Razi adds that some of these askers may be believers, yet their request is confined to this world. All commentators agree that each group receives a share of what they earned, and that God is swift in reckoning. They differ on what this swiftness means: some say it is like the blink of an eye, others the time it takes to milk a goat, and others that God needs neither counting nor reflection. Al-Razi notes that this prayer combines both goods, and that one should not insist on a specific good but ask for whatever accords with God's decree and wisdom.

This verse, in the context of the rites of Hajj, describes how people, once they have completed their rites, differ in what they ask of God. Some ask only for the good of this world, while others ask for the good of both this world and the Hereafter. The commentators agree that the promise of the verse concerns this second group, who will receive a share of the reward for what they have earned through their deeds and supplications, and that God is swift in reckoning. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir explain that the remembrance commanded replaces the pre-Islamic custom of boasting about one's forefathers at Mina. Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi regard the supplication 'Our Lord, give us good in this world and good in the Hereafter' as a complete prayer that encompasses every blessing. The meaning of 'good' is disputed: Ali ibn Abi Talib takes it as a righteous wife in this world and the houris in Paradise, al-Hasan as knowledge and worship in this world and Paradise in the next, al-Suddi and Ibn Zayd as wealth, and Qatada as health and well-being. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Baydawi read 'a share of what they earned' as a share of the same kind as their deeds, while Ibn Abbas and al-Alusi take 'what they earned' to refer to the supplication itself, since it is a form of action. Ibn Abbas also reports that the verse applies to one who performs Hajj on behalf of a deceased person. As for swift reckoning, al-Razi and al-Nasafi explain it as God's capacity to reckon all of creation in an instant, citing the report of a reckoning as brief as the milking of a sheep, while al-Qurtubi notes that it means the reckoning is near and one should hasten to good deeds.

God commands the believers to remember Him during the numbered days, the three days of tashriq after the day of sacrifice, by takbir after the prayers and at the stoning of the pillars. He states that whoever hastens his departure from Mina on the second day incurs no sin, and whoever stays until the third day incurs no sin either. The commentators agree that the numbered days are the days of tashriq, although Ibn Abbas and others also reported other views, such as the first ten days of Dhu al-Hijjah. On the meaning of the absence of sin, opinions differ. Ata and al-Nakha'i take it as a choice between leaving early or late. Ibn Mas'ud, Ali, Ibn Abbas and Ibrahim take it as forgiveness granted to the pilgrim in either case, citing the hadith of the one who performs the pilgrimage without obscenity or wickedness. Mujahid understands it as lasting until the following year, and Abu al-Aliya as covering the rest of one's life if one fears God. Ibn Abbas and Qatada tie the forgiveness to fearing God during the pilgrimage, especially by abstaining from hunting. Al-Tabari holds that the most sound reading is forgiveness for the one who completes the pilgrimage fearing God. The verse closes with a call to fear God and a reminder that all will be gathered before Him.

This verse describes a man whose words charm listeners when he speaks of worldly matters, who calls God to witness that his heart agrees with his tongue, yet who is in fact the most contentious of disputants. The commentators agree that it describes a hypocrite, but they differ on who is meant. Al-Suddi, Muqatil and others say it was revealed about al-Akhnas ibn Shariq al-Thaqafi, who professed Islam and then burned the crops and slaughtered the donkeys of Muslims. Ibn Abbas, as transmitted by Ibn Ishaq, links it instead to hypocrites who mocked the companions killed at al-Raji'. Qatada, Mujahid and many others hold that the verse is general, applying to anyone who conceals disbelief, hypocrisy or falsehood while showing the opposite; Ibn Kathir considers this the sound view. On the phrase 'calls God to witness what is in his heart', Tabari and Ibn Kathir take it to mean he swears his heart matches his words, while others read it as God knowing what he hides. Al-Hasan reads 'the most contentious' as the most lying, Ibn Abbas as the most argumentative, Mujahid and al-Suddi as the one who does not stay upright in dispute, and Qatada as the one hard in disobedience. All agree that the destruction of crops and offspring signifies the extent of his corruption, that God does not love corruption, and that whoever is told to fear God and is seized by pride in sin will have Hell as his dwelling.

This verse describes the man who speaks eloquently in the presence of the Prophet ﷺ and swears to the sincerity of his heart, yet who, once he turns away, spreads corruption on earth. The commentators agree that corruption (fasad) includes every act of disobedience, that the tilth (harth) means crops and vegetation, and that the offspring (nasl) means living beings that reproduce, and that God does not love corruption. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir report that the verse was revealed concerning al-Akhnas ibn Shariq, who burned the crops of the Muslims and slaughtered their donkeys, while al-Zamakhshari, al-Razi and Ibn 'Atiyya take it as a general description of anyone who shows outwardly what he conceals within. Al-Tabari prefers, as closest to the apparent wording, the meaning of highway robbery and terrorizing travellers, though he allows other meanings. Mujahid explains that a wrongdoer in authority causes rain to be withheld and the harvest to perish, whereas Ibn Jurayj, Ibn Abbas and al-Hasan take the verb tawalla to mean being angry, departing, or holding authority. Several commentators, including al-Razi, draw from the verse that corruption is not willed by God, and the Sunni scholars reply that love and will are not the same thing. Ibn 'Ashur stresses that such destruction is grave because material life depends upon the fields and the livestock.

This verse describes a man whose words impress people when he speaks of worldly affairs, and who swears by God that his heart matches his tongue, yet who is in fact fiercely contentious. Once he leaves the Prophet ﷺ, he spreads corruption on earth, destroying crops and offspring, and God does not love corruption. When he is told to fear God, the pride and tribal honour of the age of ignorance seize him and drive him into further sin, so his due is Hell, and a wretched resting place it is. The commentators differ on who is meant. Al-Tabari, al-Suddi, Ibn Juzayy and al-Wahidi report that it is al-Akhnas ibn Shariq, whose raid on the Thaqif, burning their crops and killing their livestock, is cited as the corruption. Ibn 'Abbas, al-Hasan and al-Dahhak take it to be hypocrites who mocked the companions killed at al-Raji'. Qatada, Mujahid and Ibn Kathir favour a general meaning covering all who share this character, while al-Razi argues the verse does not necessarily imply hypocrisy. Ibn 'Atiyya notes it is never established that al-Akhnas converted. Mujahid takes the destruction of crops and offspring to be drought caused by sin, Ibn Kathir to be the withholding of rain, while others read it as direct destruction. The second half, on the one who sells his soul seeking God's pleasure, is linked by several scholars to Suhayb, and more broadly to fighters and those who enjoin good.

This part of the verse describes the person who gives up his very self seeking the pleasure of God, that is, who stakes his life for Him. The commentators agree on the basic sense: the verb yashri means here to sell, so the believer sells his soul to God. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Qurtubi and al-Baydawi note that most exegetes apply it to the fighter in God's cause, while others extend it to the one who enjoins good and forbids evil even at the cost of his life. Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi also point out that the verse echoes the language of exchange, with God presented as the buyer in a nearby verse of the same sura. On the occasions of revelation the reports differ: Ibn Abbas, Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab and Ikrima say it was revealed about Suhayb ibn Sinan al-Rumi, who gave his wealth to the Quraysh to be allowed to emigrate to Medina, and the Prophet told him that the bargain had been profitable. Others connect it to the rescue of Khubayb from the cross, or to men who commanded good and were killed for it. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir judge that the wording reaches beyond these particular events and includes everyone who sells himself to God. Finally, the closing phrase, that God is compassionate towards His servants, is read by Ibn Kathir and al-Baydawi as a divine kindness, since God laid down the path that leads to the reward of the martyrs.

In this verse God commands the believers to enter fully into Islam, meaning into all its laws and teachings without picking some and leaving others, and not to follow the steps of Satan, that is, his traces, his whisperings and his ways of making sins look attractive and wrong things seem acceptable, since he is a clear enemy to them. The commentators agree that the verse calls for complete submission to the rules of Islam, but they differ on the meaning of salm. Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, al-Dahhak, Qatada, al-Suddi and Ibn Zayd take it to mean Islam, al-Rabi' and Abu al-'Aliya take it to mean obedience, and Qatada takes it to mean peace. The readings also differ on the vowel of the sin: Abu 'Amr ibn al-'Ala gave the kasra form the sense of Islam and the fatha form the sense of peace, a distinction al-Mubarrad rejected. As for kaffa, most read it as meaning 'all', while al-Zamakhshari and al-Baydawi make it a circumstantial term referring to salm or to the believers. They also disagree on who is addressed: Ibn 'Abbas and 'Ikrima say it concerns believers among the People of the Book, such as 'Abdallah ibn Salam, who wished to combine honouring the Sabbath and avoiding camel meat with Islam; Mujahid and Qatada say it addresses all Muslims, and some say it addresses the hypocrites. Al-Tabari holds that the path of Satan is whatever contradicts Islamic law, whereas Ibn Kathir understands it as performing all acts of obedience and avoiding all sins. Al-Razi mentions several interpretations, including one that reads the verse as a call to persevere in Islam without departing from it.

The plain meaning of the verse, as the commentators explain it, is that God addresses the believers: if you stray from the truth and go astray after the clear proofs have come to you, know that God is mighty, no one can prevent Him from punishing you, and He is wise in what He decrees. The commentators agree that zalal means straying from the straight path, and that the verse carries a stern warning to anyone who turns from the truth after the proof has been established. They differ on what the clear proofs are. As-Suddi, Mujahid, Ibn Jurayj and Ibn Kathir take them to be Muhammad ﷺ, the Qur'an and Islam, while al-Tabari, though accepting this, prefers to read them as God's arguments that silenced the addressees, including what the Torah and the Gospel said about the Prophet. On the meaning of zalal, Ibn Abbas takes it as associationism, as-Suddi as going astray, while az-Zamakhshari and al-Razi see it as a deviation from what is required. Az-Zamakhshari relates the preceding command to the whole of Islam's laws, while Ibn Kathir holds that one must follow all of its rites and laws without picking and choosing. The exegetes explain that al-Aziz is the one who prevails and nothing escapes him, and al-Hakim the one who acts with perfect precision. Ibn al-Qayyim explains why might precedes wisdom in the phrase. Al-Razi, al-Nasafi and Ibn Atiyya report the story of the Bedouin who rejected the reading "forgiving, merciful" in this context, since the Wise does not mention forgiveness at the moment of error.

The commentators explain that this verse is a rebuke to those who delay entering Islam after the proof has been made clear. God asks them, in a tone of reproach, what they are waiting for: only that God come to them, or the Day of Judgement arrive, in canopies of cloud with the angels, so that the matter is decided, for all affairs return to God alone. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Qurtubi, al-Baghawi and Ibn 'Ashur agree that this refers to the Day of Recompense and God's coming to judge between people, though Qatada, cited by Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi, held that the coming of the angels may refer to the moment of death. Regarding the attribution of 'coming' to God, the early scholars affirmed it without specifying how, as Ibn Kathir, al-Jaza'iri and al-Shinqiti report, while al-Razi, Ibn 'Ataiya and Ibn 'Ashur read it as a figure for the arrival of God's command, His punishment, or His manifestation. Ibn 'Ataiya notes that the common reading makes the angels a subject, while some read the word in the genitive. As for 'the matter is decided', the commentators take it to mean that judgement is complete and the punishment executed. Al-Baghawi reports that the preceding verses were revealed about believers among the People of the Book who wished to keep the Sabbath and abstain from camel meat, a tradition attributed to Ibn 'Abbas and 'Ikrima.

This verse tells the Prophet ﷺ to ask the Children of Israel, in a tone of rebuke, about the many clear signs God gave them, such as the parting of the sea, the shading cloud, the manna and quails, and how they rejected them. Most commentators understand the 'grace of God' as God's signs or Islam; whoever replaces it with disbelief or distortion after knowing it and after the proof has reached him will face God's severe punishment. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi take the replacement to mean rejecting the grace, while al-Zamakhshari and Abu al-Su'ud also include distorting the scriptures. Scholars differ on who is addressed by the question: some say the Prophet, others anyone able to be addressed. Mujahid and al-Hasan identify the signs as Moses' miracles, while others see them as evidence for Muhammad's prophethood in their own scriptures. In the next verse, according to al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and others, the life of this world was made attractive to the disbelievers, who mocked the poor believers; the God-fearing will be above them on the Day of Resurrection in rank and place. God gives provision to whom He wills without reckoning, meaning without measure or accounting, as Ibn Kathir and Ibn 'Ashur explain.

The verse says that worldly life was made attractive to those who disbelieved, so they clung to it and mocked the poor believers who had renounced its goods to obey God. It states that on the Day of Resurrection the God-fearing will be above the disbelievers in rank and position, through faith and Paradise, while the latter will be in the Fire. On who makes it attractive, al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir take God Himself to be the one who created beautiful things and the inclination towards them, while al-Zamakhshari, al-Baydawi and al-Nasafi mainly attribute it to Satan's whisperings, with al-Zamakhshari adding that God permitted it by abandoning these people. The Mu'tazila, as reported by al-Razi, read it as respite or abandonment and deny that it comes from God. Regarding the mockers, al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir name the leaders of Quraysh such as Abu Jahl, al-Wahidi and al-Baghawi name Jewish leaders, and Muqatil names the hypocrites such as Abd Allah ibn Ubayy. The believers mocked are, according to Ibn Abbas, Ibn Mas'ud, Ammar, Suhayb and Bilal. Al-Tabari and al-Baghawi take 'above' to mean in rank, while al-Razi and al-Qurtubi also accept a spatial sense, since Paradise is in heaven. As for 'without reckoning', Ibn Abbas and al-Baghawi understand abundance without limit, al-Dahhak understands no accountability, and Ibn 'Ashur sees gift without measure. In the preceding verse, al-Tabari and al-Baghawi read the question to the Children of Israel as a rebuke, and all agree that the blessing rejected is Islam or the signs received, whose punishment is severe.

The commentators explain that mankind was originally one community, and then they split; God then sent the prophets as bearers of good news and warners and sent down the Book with them to judge between people on what they differed about. They disagree on when this unity existed. Ibn 'Abbas and Qatada place it between Adam and Noah, ten centuries upon guidance, after which disagreement arose and Noah was the first messenger. Al-Rabi' and Ubayy ibn Ka'b place it when Adam's offspring were brought forth from his loins and acknowledged servitude to God. Mujahid understands the people to mean Adam alone. Al-Tabari judges that the soundest reading is that the unity was in the religion of truth, without fixing a date, while Ibn al-Qayyim upholds the first view and considers the view of general disbelief before Noah or Abraham weak. As for the words 'and none disputed it except those who were given it, after clear proofs had come to them, out of envy among themselves', most scholars see envy and the pursuit of leadership and worldly gain, aimed at Jews and Christians. Al-Farra' and al-Tabari propose an inversion of the sentence: God guided the believers to the truth on what they disputed. All agree that God guided the community of Muhammad to the truth on matters the People of the Book disagreed about, such as Friday, the direction of prayer, Abraham and Jesus, citing Abu Hurayra's hadith about this community preceding others. Finally, the commentators affirm that guidance rests on God's will and permission and is a grace from Him.

God rebukes the believers for assuming they would enter Paradise without being tested as those before them were. Those earlier believers suffered hardship (al-ba'sa'), meaning poverty and want, and distress (al-darra'), meaning illness and injury, and they were shaken by fear and trials, to the point that the Messenger and those who believed with him asked impatiently, 'When will God's help come?' The answer came: 'Surely God's help is near.' The commentators agree that the trial means enduring hardship for the sake of the religion, and that Paradise is not earned by mere claims. Most, including Qatada, al-Suddi, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi, say the verse was revealed during the Battle of the Trench, while others link it to Uhud or to emigrants who had left their property behind; the commentators do not settle between these reports. They also differ on reading 'yaqula': most read it in the subjunctive, as an end point, while Nafi' reads it in the nominative, as a past situation being described. Al-Tabari, al-Razi and al-Qurtubi explain each reading. Al-Tabari and al-Razi take the Messenger's words as an expression of impatience, while others take the second sentence as God's own speech. The verse ultimately promises that patience through trial leads to both victory and Paradise.

The Companions asked the Prophet ﷺ what they should spend and on whom. The answer is that whatever good wealth they give should first go to parents, then to close relatives, orphans, the needy and the traveller left without means, and that every good deed is known to God, who will reward it. Tradition names the questioner as 'Amr ibn al-Jamuh, and the word 'good' is understood as wealth. Most commentators take the verse as encouragement to voluntary charity. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn Juzayy hold that it is not abrogated. Al-Suddi, followed by al-Mawardi, al-Wahidi and al-Baghawi, says it was revealed before zakat and was abrogated by it, while Ibn Jurayj and Ibn Zayd regard it as a recommendation distinct from zakat, so there is no abrogation. Al-Razi rejects abrogation by the verse of inheritance and offers several readings that keep the ruling, including a duty to support needy parents and relatives. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Baydawi and al-Nasafi explain that the question concerned the giver while the answer concerns the recipients, since spending counts only when it reaches its right place. Al-Tabari adds that the order of recipients runs from the nearest to the most needy, and that most scholars read the verse as urging giving rather than imposing it.

This verse makes fighting obligatory for the believers while acknowledging that it is naturally disliked, because it puts lives and property at risk. Yet the commentators explain that it is good for them in its outcome, whether through victory and booty or through martyrdom and paradise. The verse also warns that loving to stay away from it can be a harm, bringing humiliation and loss of reward. Al-Tabari, al-Razi, al-Qurtubi and Ibn Kathir agree that this aversion is a natural human reaction which does not contradict submission to God's command, and that God knows what is good for them while they do not. The scholars differ on the legal status of jihad. 'Ata' and al-Thawri hold that the verse concerns the Companions or that fighting is voluntary, while the majority, as al-Tabari and Ibn Juzayy report, consider it a collective obligation which lapses once enough people undertake it. Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab held it to be an individual duty for every Muslim, as al-Mawardi relates. The following verses are linked by the exegetes to the expedition of Abdullah ibn Jahsh and the killing of Ibn al-Hadrami in a sacred month. Al-Zuhri and 'Ata' ibn Abi Maysara consider the prohibition on fighting in the sacred months abrogated, whereas others maintain it is still in force. Al-Tabari sees it as abrogated by the verses of Surat al-Tawba. The passage concludes that barring people from God's path and leading them into disbelief is graver in God's sight than killing.

The believers ask the Prophet ﷺ about fighting in the sacred month. The answer is that fighting in it is a great sin, but that the disbelievers have committed something graver in God's sight: barring people from God's path, denying Him, barring access to the Sacred Mosque and expelling its people, and the persecution that pushes believers away from their faith, which is worse than killing. The commentators relate that the occasion was the expedition of Abdullah ibn Jahsh, who killed Amr ibn al-Hadrami at the end of Jumada or the start of Rajab, and the Quraysh mocked the Muslims for it. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Nasafi hold that the prohibition on fighting in the sacred months was abrogated by the verses commanding war, while 'Ata' maintained that it remains valid, and others, such as Ibn 'Ashur, held that offensive fighting remains forbidden there while defence is permitted. The verse goes on to say that the unbelievers will not cease to fight the believers until they turn them from their religion, if they are able, though this is presented as unlikely. It then warns that whoever apostatises and dies a disbeliever has his deeds voided in this world and the next and becomes an inhabitant of the Fire forever. Jurists differ on the effect: al-Shafi'i held that deeds are voided only if one dies in disbelief, whereas Abu Hanifa and Malik held that apostasy itself voids them, a question tied to whether pilgrimage must be repeated. The following verse reassures those who fought unaware of the sanctity of the month: those who believed, emigrated and struggled in God's path hope for His mercy, for God is Forgiving and Merciful.

This verse states that those who believed, emigrated, and struggled in the way of God hope for God's mercy, and that God is Forgiving and Merciful. Most commentators report that it was revealed concerning 'Abd Allah ibn Jahsh and his companions after they killed 'Amr ibn al-Hadrami on the last day of Jumada or the first of Rajab. The Quraysh reproached them, and some Muslims feared they would have no reward. The verse reassures them that faith, emigration, and struggle are deeds through which one hopes for mercy. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir explain that emigration means leaving homes and tribes, and struggle means exerting effort to support the religion. Al-Razi, al-Nasafi and Abu al-Su'ud note that the word 'hope' rather than 'receive' shows that the deed does not oblige God and that the outcome is unknown. Ibn al-Qayyim distinguishes true hope, which is joined with action, from idle wishing, which neglects the means. Al-Qurtubi and Ibn 'Atiyya also report that the word raja' can mean fear. Ibn Sa'di stresses that hope presupposes that the good works have been done. The commentators agree that the ending, with forgiveness and mercy, affirms God's goodness toward those who act in this way.

This passage explains that wine and gambling both contain a great sin, because they corrupt the mind, ruin wealth, cause enmity and hatred, and divert from the remembrance of God and from prayer, yet they also bring some benefits to people, such as commercial gain, pleasure and easy wealth; but their sin outweighs their benefit. The commentators explain that khamr is whatever covers the intellect and that maysir is gambling in all its forms. The majority holds that every intoxicant is khamr and is forbidden in small or large amounts, while Abu Hanifa restricts khamr to fermented grape juice and permits some drinks short of intoxication; he also holds that this verse preceded the definitive prohibition, which came through other verses in Surat an-Nisa and al-Ma'ida. It is reported that 'Umar, on hearing the verse of al-Ma'ida, said: we have ceased. The passage then turns to the question of spending: al-'afw means what exceeds one's needs, and most commentators understand it as voluntary charity, some considering it abrogated by zakat and others holding it valid. The verse ends by stating that God makes His signs clear so that people may reflect on this world and the next. The verse on orphans answers the concern of Muslims who separated the orphans' food from their own; it is established that improving their property is better, that mixing it with one's own is permitted since they are brothers, and that God knows the corrupter from the reformer.

This verse, together with the one before it, addresses two matters bearing on the welfare of the community: wine and gambling, and then the care of orphans. The commentators explain the general principle as seeking what improves both this world and the next, and they note that a person is urged to reflect on matters touching both abodes. Regarding orphans, earlier revelation had warned against devouring their wealth unjustly, so people, out of fear, separated their food and drink from theirs. This caused them great hardship, and they asked the Prophet ﷺ. The answer was that improving the orphan's condition is better, and that mixing with them is permitted because they are brothers in faith. The exegetes agree that the aim is to work at improving their property and their persons, and that God knows the corrupter from the reformer, so that each is repaid according to intent.

The meaning of 'mixing with them' is disputed. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir understand it as sharing food, drink, lodging, service and beasts of burden; Ibn 'Abbas, in one report, takes it as drinking from their milk and eating from their dish. Abu Muslim al-Isfahani, followed by al-Razi in his preference, takes it to mean marriage, although al-Razi ultimately favours the first reading, while al-Alusi counts as mixing anything that benefits the orphan. Al-Qurtubi draws from the verse the principle that managing an orphan's property by sale, purchase and profit-sharing is permitted when beneficial, and jurists differ on whether a guardian may buy from the orphan's property for himself.

As for 'Had God willed, He would have burdened you', Ibn 'Abbas and Mujahid take it to mean constraint and hardship, Ibn 'Abbas in another report takes it to mean that what you took from the orphans' wealth would have been a ruin for you, and Abu 'Ubayda takes it to mean destruction. The verse closes by affirming God's might and wisdom.

This verse forbids believers to marry idolatrous women until they believe, and states that a believing slave woman is better than a free idolatrous woman, even if the latter pleases you. It likewise forbids giving believing women in marriage to idolaters until they believe, and that a believing slave is better than a free idolater. The reason given is that idolaters call to the Fire, while God calls to Paradise and forgiveness by His permission. The commentators agree that 'idolatresses' originally means worshippers of idols, and that the women of the People of the Book are excepted by the verse of the Table, 'and the chaste women of those given the Book'. Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, Sa'id ibn Jubayr and others report this reading, and al-Hasan, Qatada and al-Dahhak are cited in similar terms. Some, including Ibn 'Umar, hold instead that the verse of the Cow abrogated that of the Table, a view others reject because the Table was revealed later. Al-Tabari reports that 'Umar disliked the marriages of Talha and Hudhayfa to Jewish and Christian women, but he judges this report weaker than the version in which 'Umar only feared that people would turn away from Muslim women. Exegetes link the revelation to the story of Abu Marthad al-Ghanawi and 'Anaq, and to the case of Ibn Rawaha and his black slave-woman. There is consensus that a Muslim may not marry an idolatress, nor marry a Muslim woman to an idolater. Some derive from the verse the requirement of a guardian in marriage. The commentators explain that 'calling to the Fire' means that association and alliance lead one away from Islam, while God calls to faith and the deeds that lead to Paradise.

Verse 2:222 is a rule about menstruation. The Companions asked the Prophet about it, and God answers that it is harmful, so men must avoid intercourse during menses until the bleeding stops and the women bathe. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn Juzayy agree that intercourse is forbidden, while the wider contact is permitted, as shown by Aisha and Maymuna's reports. Ibn Abbas and Mujahid hold that the wording 'hatta yatahharna' requires ritual bathing, and Abu Hanifa allows intercourse after the blood stops if it ended late in the period. Al-Razi and al-Qurtubi explain the two readings and their legal consequences for when a wife may be approached again. Ibn Kathir reports that the verse 'fa-'tuhunna min haythu amarakum Allah' means the front passage, and that the Prophet forbade anal intercourse. Al-Razi, al-Qurtubi and Ibn Kathir agree this is the sound view. The verse ends by saying that God loves those who repent and those who purify themselves.

This verse describes wives as a tilth for their husbands, so a man may come to his tilth in whatever manner he wishes, provided the union takes place in the place where children are produced. Commentators read the phrase 'as you wish' in different ways. The majority, including Ibn 'Abbas, 'Ikrima and Mujahid, take it to mean 'in any manner', from the front or from behind, as long as it is in the proper place. Al-Dahhak reads it as 'whenever you wish', while Nafi' reports from Ibn 'Umar a reading that allows intercourse in the back passage. Most scholars reject this view, and Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi say it was wrongly attributed to Malik. The occasion of revelation given by several authorities is that Jews claimed a child conceived this way would be squint-eyed, and the verse refutes them; other reports describe companions asking the Prophet about intercourse during menstruation, and his reply that everything except intercourse itself is allowed. On 'Send ahead for yourselves', al-Suddi understands good deeds, Ibn 'Abbas and 'Ata' understand invoking God's name at intercourse, and others understand seeking righteous offspring. The verse ends with a call to fear God, a reminder that believers will meet Him, and the good news for the faithful.

This verse forbids making the oath by God an obstacle that prevents doing good, being mindful of God, and reconciling people. According to al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi and most of the commentators cited, it refers to a person who swears not to do a good deed, such as keeping ties of kinship or helping someone, and then uses the oath as an excuse to refrain. The recommended course is to break the oath, do the good deed and make expiation. They cite the hadith: whoever swears an oath and sees something better should expiate his oath and do what is better. Al-Razi, al-Baydawi and Abu al-Su'ud add that oaths should not be multiplied, since frequent swearing by God makes His name common and weakens trust in the one who swears, so he cannot be relied on as a mediator. Al-Zamakhshari and Ibn 'Ashur discuss the grammar of 'an tabarru', as a purpose clause or as implying 'not'. Both readings, they note, lead to the same prohibition against treating God's name lightly. The occasion of revelation is reported as Abdullah ibn Rawaha and his brother-in-law Bashir ibn al-Nu'man, or Abu Bakr vowing to stop supporting Mistah; the commentators relate these without deciding between them. The verse ends with God being All-Hearing and All-Knowing, meaning He hears the oaths and knows the intentions behind them.

This verse states that God does not hold people accountable for oaths that slip from the tongue without any intention to swear, but He holds them accountable for what their hearts have deliberately bound themselves to. The commentators agree that 'what the hearts have earned' means what the heart intended. The meaning of 'idle oath' (laghw), however, is disputed. Ibn Abbas, Aisha, al-Sha'bi, Mujahid, Abu Salih and al-Shafi'i, as cited by Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi, understood it as phrases such as 'no, by God' or 'yes, by God' said without intent to swear. Abu Hurayra, another report from Ibn Abbas, al-Hasan, Qatada, Makhul and Abu Hanifa, as al-Tabari and al-Razi relate, took it to be an oath sworn on a belief that later proves mistaken. Ali and Tawus linked it to oaths made in anger, citing the saying that there is no oath in anger. Sa'id ibn Jubayr and Masruq applied it to oaths to commit sin. Al-Dahhak took it to mean an oath that is expiated, and Zayd ibn Aslam a curse one calls down on oneself. Al-Tabari concludes that expiation applies to deliberate oaths, while al-Shafi'i uses the verse to require expiation for the deliberate false oath, which Malik and others deny. God is forgiving and forbearing, not hastening punishment.

This verse addresses the husband who swears not to approach his wife, known as ila'. He is granted a period of four months. If he returns to his wife within that time, God is forgiving and merciful toward him. The commentators explain that the return (fay') means resuming marital relations; for a man prevented by illness or travel, some accept a declared intention and witnessed statement instead. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir report that this practice was once used to harm the wife, who was left neither widowed nor married, and Islam set a fixed limit. Scholars differ on what counts as ila'. Ibn Abbas, Malik and Abu Hanifa hold that any oath preventing intercourse qualifies, while al-Shafi'i, in one opinion, restricts it to an oath by God. Most scholars say oaths under four months are not ila', while Ishaq and others include them. When the period ends, Malik, al-Shafi'i and Ahmad hold that the husband must be made to either return or divorce, whereas Abu Hanifa and his followers hold that an irrevocable divorce takes effect automatically. On expiation, the majority requires it from one who returns, while al-Hasan and al-Nakha'i do not. Ultimately the choice rests with the husband, under pressure from the judge.

This verse addresses the husband who swears not to approach his wife, known as îlâ'. The commentators explain that he has a period of four months; if he returns to his wife, by intercourse or, if unable, by words, God is Forgiving and Merciful. If he persists in refusing and resolves on divorce, God hears and knows his intention. The exegetes agree that îlâ' is an oath to abstain from intercourse, but differ on what follows. Ali, Ibn Mas'ud, Ibn Abbas and Uthman, along with many Companions and Successors, as transmitted by al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir, held that divorce takes effect at the end of the four months, as an irrevocable divorce in their view, while Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab, al-Zuhri and, in one report, Malik held it to be revocable; Abu Hanifa adopted the irrevocable view.
