Another position, held by Umar, Uthman, Ali, Abu al-Darda' and Ibn Umar in other reports, is that the husband is halted at the end of the period and made to either return or divorce, with the judge pronouncing divorce if he refuses; this is the view of Malik, al-Shafi'i and Ahmad. Opinions also diverge on the nature of the oath, on whether anger is required for the îlâ' to count according to Ibn Abbas and Ali, and on the expiation owed after a return, which most scholars require, whereas al-Hasan and al-Nakha'i waive it.

The commentators explain that this part of the verse concerns divorced women who menstruate, who must wait three periods before remarrying. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and others report that the word qur' may mean either menstruation or the state of purity between two menstrual periods. The Companions Umar, Ali and Ibn Mas'ud, together with Abu Hanifa and his followers, take it to mean menstruation, whereas Aisha, Ibn Umar, Zayd ibn Thabit, Malik and al-Shafi'i take it to mean purity. Al-Tabari observes that the word is ambiguous in Arabic. A pregnant divorcee's waiting period ends with childbirth; a woman past menopause or not yet menstruating waits three months; and a slave woman observes two periods according to the majority. All agree that a woman must not conceal what God has created in her womb, whether a child or menstrual blood, and that the husband has the prior right to take her back during this period if he intends reconciliation and not harm. Wives have rights comparable to their duties according to what is customary, yet men hold a degree of precedence, which commentators explain as leadership, financial maintenance, inheritance, the right to divorce, or responsibility. The verse ends by affirming God's might and wisdom.

This verse sets the limit on revocable divorce at two pronouncements. After the second, the husband must either take his wife back in kindness and good treatment, or release her graciously without harming her. Most commentators understand the release to mean the third divorce, and note that the verse came to end the pre-Islamic practice, and the early Muslim practice, of divorcing and taking back without limit, which harmed women. Al-Tabari observes that the verse both fixes the number of divorces that allow reconciliation and describes the proper manner of divorce. The Hanafis regard pronouncing several divorces together as a blameworthy innovation, while others hold that a triple divorce at once takes effect. The verse then forbids the husband to take back anything he gave his wife, unless both fear they will not keep within God's limits; in that case khul' (divorce for compensation) is allowed. Reports link this to Jamila, daughter of Ibn Ubayy, and her husband Thabit ibn Qays, who returned his garden to him and was released. Scholars differ on whether more than the dowry may be asked; the majority allow it, while others refuse. The verse concludes that these rules are God's limits, which must not be crossed, and whoever transgresses them wrongs himself.

This verse sets out the rule for a third divorce. If a man divorces his wife for the third time after two divorces, she is not lawful to him again until she marries another husband in a valid marriage, and that husband consummates it. If the second husband divorces her or dies, there is no blame on her or her former husband if they remarry, provided they think they can keep God's limits. The commentators agree that nikah here means a valid marriage, but differ on whether consummation is required. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi hold that it is required, relying on the hadith of the wife of Rifa'a, while Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab accepted the contract alone, and al-Hasan al-Basri required ejaculation. They also condemn the marriage of intended legal re-marriage (tahlil), which the Prophet is reported to have cursed. On the meaning of 'zanna', some take it as 'knew' and others as 'hoped', since the future is unknown. As for khul', Ibn 'Abbas and Tawus treat it as a dissolution rather than a divorce, while Malik, Abu Hanifa and al-Shafi'i in his later view count it as an irrevocable divorce. The verse closes by saying that God makes these limits clear to those who know, meaning those who benefit from them.

This verse sets out the rules of taking a wife back after a revocable divorce. When a divorced woman nears the end of her waiting period (iddah), the husband may either take her back in a fitting manner, meaning with the intention of treating her well and giving her what is due, or release her kindly until her waiting period ends. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and others explain the prohibition of taking a wife back to harm her as divorcing and reconciling repeatedly to prolong her waiting period, or to pressure her into ransoming herself with her dower. Those who do this wrong themselves by exposing themselves to God's punishment. The commentators agree that a proper reconciliation requires witnesses. They differ on the phrase 'reach their term': most take it to mean near the end, while Ibn Kathir favours the sense of actually completing it. As for not taking God's signs in jest, Abu al-Darda and al-Hasan link it to the man who divorces or frees a slave and then claims he was joking, whereas al-Razi and al-Zamakhshari extend it to any disobedience of God's commands. The verse then calls the believers to remember the blessing of Islam, the Book and wisdom, to fear God and to know that He has knowledge of all things. Most commentators understand wisdom as the Sunna or the admonitions of the Quran.

This verse addresses a divorced woman whose waiting period has ended without her husband taking her back. It forbids those who hold guardianship over her from preventing her from remarrying her former husband by a new contract, when both agree in a fair manner. Most commentators, including al-Tabari, al-Razi, al-Qurtubi, al-Baydawi, al-Nasafi and Ibn Kathir, take the address to be to the guardians, relying on the occasion of revelation reported about Ma'qil ibn Yasar and his sister, which al-Bukhari transmits. Al-Tabari also cites a report from al-Sudi about Jabir ibn 'Abd Allah, but does not choose between the two accounts and holds that the general meaning is the same either way. Al-Razi prefers that the address is to the husbands who used to harm their wives by prolonging the waiting period, and al-Zamakhshari holds that it is addressed to people in general. Ibn 'Abbas, al-Dahhak and al-Zuhri said it covers anyone who prevents his wife from remarrying. Many scholars take the verse as evidence that a guardian is required in marriage, while Abu Hanifa held that a woman may contract her own marriage; al-Razi and al-Baydawi discuss this without treating the verse as decisive. As for the words that this is an admonition to those among you who believe in God and the Last Day, most explain that only the believer benefits from it, and that refraining from obstruction is purer and better for everyone, for God knows what is good while you do not know.

This verse sets out rules for breastfeeding after divorce. Mothers are to nurse their children for two full years, for those who wish to complete the nursing, and the father must provide them with food and clothing in a fair manner according to his means, since God does not burden a soul beyond its capacity. Neither parent may harm the other through the child. According to most commentators, the heir bears a similar duty toward the nursing mother, while others read it as a prohibition on harm. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir hold that the two years are the limit of nursing for an infant, with no legal effect afterward, whereas others tie the period to the child's gestation. Weaning before this term is allowed when both parents agree after consultation. The father may also hire another woman to nurse the child, provided he pays her the agreed wage fairly. The commentators conclude with the call to piety, since God sees all that people do.

This verse states that a woman whose husband has died must wait four months and ten days, refraining from remarriage, and that once her waiting period is over, there is no blame on the guardians for what she does with herself in a proper manner, for God is aware of your deeds. The commentators agree that this waiting period is obligatory for a widow, and that a pregnant woman's period ends with the birth, as the chapter of Divorce says, while a slave woman observes half the period, the view of the majority. Al-Tabari reports that Ibn Abbas and Ali held that the longer of the two periods applies, but the majority relied on the hadith of Subay'a al-Aslamiyya, who was allowed to remarry after giving birth, which limits the general sense of the verse. On mourning (ihdad), all agree it is required, and the hadiths forbid the widow adornment, perfume, kohl and dyed clothes, while allowing some exceptions such as kohl at night or white garments. Al-Hasan al-Basri held mourning not obligatory, while Ibn Abbas and Abu Hanifa said she may spend the night wherever she wishes, whereas Malik and the majority require her to remain in the marital home. The majority hold the period applies whether or not the marriage was consummated. Allusive proposals are allowed while explicit ones are forbidden, and a marriage contract during the waiting period is void. Some commentators explain the choice of this number, such as the breathing of the soul into the fetus according to Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab, or as a precaution regarding the fetus's movement according to Ibn Kathir.

This verse establishes that it is not sinful to hint at a wish to marry a woman who is in her waiting period after the death of her husband or an irrevocable divorce, nor is it sinful to keep such an intention in one's heart, since God knows that such thoughts will arise. Al-Tabari explains allusion (ta'rid) as speech whose intended meaning is understood without being stated outright. Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, Sa'id ibn Jubayr and al-Sha'bi give examples such as "I wish to marry" or "you are lovely", while most commentators exclude revocably divorced women, who are treated as wives. The scholars differ on the prohibition of "secret promises": al-Hasan, Qatada, Abu Mijlaz, Jabir ibn Zayd, al-Dahhak and Ibrahim take it to mean fornication, the view al-Tabari favours; Ibn 'Abbas, al-Sha'bi, Mujahid and Sa'id ibn Jubayr take it to mean taking the woman's pledge not to marry anyone else; al-Kalbi and al-Shafi'i take it to mean describing one's sexual prowess; Ibn Zayd takes it to mean concluding the marriage in secret and announcing it later. All agree that the contract itself must not be concluded until the waiting period ends. On whether a marriage contracted during this period becomes permanently forbidden, 'Umar, Malik, al-Layth and al-Awza'i say yes; 'Ali, Ibn Mas'ud, Abu Hanifa and al-Shafi'i say no, the couple being separated and the woman completing her waiting period before she can be proposed to again. The verse closes with a warning against disobeying God, followed by mention of His forgiveness and forbearance.

This verse states that there is no blame on a man who divorces his wife before touching her or fixing a dower for her, and that he should then give her a provision (matá') according to his means, rich or poor, in a fair manner, as a duty upon the good-doers. The commentators agree that touching means intercourse. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and others report that Ibn Abbas set the highest provision as a servant, then silver, then clothing, while al-Sha'bi and 'Amir described the middle level as a woman's garments, and al-Hasan and Malik held that each gives according to his means without a fixed limit. Abu Hanifa set it at half the usual dower in case of dispute, while al-Shafi'i left it to the judge and found thirty dirhams a good measure. Scholars differ on whether it is obligatory: al-Hasan, Abu al-'Aliya, 'Ali and al-Zuhri held it due to every divorced woman, whereas Ibn 'Umar and Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab limited it to a woman not touched and without a fixed dower; Malik considered it recommended, and Shurayh treated it as mere exhortation. On the phrase 'the one who holds the knot of marriage', Ibn Abbas and Malik took it to mean the guardian, while Ali, al-Shafi'i in his earlier view and others took it to mean the husband, a view some prefer since he alone holds both the contract and its dissolution. The verse adds that pardon is closer to piety, and that both parties should not forget the favour between them.

This verse addresses divorce before consummation when a dowry has already been fixed. In this case the divorced woman is entitled to half of the agreed dowry, and she may waive it, or the one who holds the marriage tie may pardon it. The commentators agree that the obligation is half the dowry, but they differ on who holds the marriage tie. Ali ibn Abi Talib, Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab, Shurayh, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, Mujahid, al-Sha'bi and Qatada hold that it is the husband, whose pardon means paying the full dowry; al-Tabari, al-Razi and al-Zamakhshari favour this view, as do Abu Hanifa and, in his later opinion, al-Shafi'i. By contrast, Ibn Abbas in one report, 'Alqama, al-Hasan, Tawus, 'Ata', al-Zuhri and Malik say it is the guardian, and Malik specifies the father of a virgin daughter and the master of a slave-woman. Al-Tabari holds that the address "that you pardon is closer to piety" covers men and women alike, while al-Sha'bi restricts it to the husband. The exegetes also stress that spouses should not forget kindness between them. A general reader should take away that the text sets a fair rule and encourages forgiveness, while the identity of the pardoner has long been debated among scholars.

The plain meaning is a command to believers to guard the obligatory prayers at their proper times, to complete their conditions and pillars, and to stand before God in prayer, humble and obedient. The commentators note that the "middle prayer" is singled out after being included among the prayers, to honour it. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi and Ibn 'Atiyya hold, relying on authentic hadith such as Ali's report from the day of the Confederates, that it is the afternoon prayer (al-'asr), and they see support in the readings of 'A'isha, Hafsa and Umm Salama that add "and the afternoon prayer". Zayd ibn Thabit, Ibn 'Umar, Abu Sa'id al-Khudri and Usama ibn Zayd identify it as the midday prayer (al-zuhr). Others choose the dawn prayer, because it lies between the night and day prayers and because the qunut is recited in it, a view attributed to Ibn 'Abbas in one report and held by Mu'adh, Jabir and al-Shafi'i. Qabisa ibn Dhu'ayb names the sunset prayer, others the night prayer, Friday, or leave it undetermined. On qunut, most read it as obedience and humility; Zayd ibn Arqam and Ibn Mas'ud read it as keeping silent during prayer, while Mujahid links it to restraint of hands and gaze. On fear, Ibn 'Abbas and Jabir say the worshipper prays on foot or mounted, facing wherever he can, and once safe completes the prayer as God taught.

This part of verse 2:239 addresses how to pray in times of fear. God says that if you fear an enemy or any other threat to your life, pray on foot or on horseback, in whatever way you can. Once the fear has passed and you are secure, perform the prayer in its full form and remember God in gratitude for what He has taught you of the religious laws. The commentators agree that the fear includes the threat of an enemy, a wild beast or a flood, and that the verse permits movement and riding in such a situation. They differ on the manner. Ibn Umar, Mujahid and most exegetes hold that the worshipper gestures with the head wherever he faces, whether or not he faces the qibla, bowing lower for prostration than for bowing. Al-Hasan and Qatada say a single rak'a is enough. Al-Shafi'i permits prayer even during close combat, while Abu Hanifa holds that the one walking should not pray until he stops. Malik advises repeating the prayer when the danger was not from an enemy, whereas most jurists of the major cities treat the two cases alike. As for the words 'remember God as He taught you', some read them as the prayer as it was taught, others as thanks for the knowledge received. On the middle prayer, the commentators offered many views; most identify it as the asr prayer on the basis of the reported hadiths, while others propose fajr, dhuhr or maghrib, and no single view has been agreed upon.

This verse concerns the bequest a husband should make to his widow: that she remain in his house for a full year, be provided for from his estate, and not be driven out by the heirs. If she chooses to leave before the year is over, the guardians of the deceased bear no blame for what she does with herself in a proper manner. The commentators differ on how to read the word wasiyya: some read it in the accusative, meaning that they should make a bequest, while others read it in the nominative, meaning that a bequest is prescribed for them. Al-Tabari prefers the nominative. On the ruling itself, most exegetes hold that it has been abrogated. Ibn Abbas, Qatada, al-Dahhak and Ibn Zayd report that the widow was entitled to lodging and maintenance for a year, and that this was replaced by the inheritance share of a quarter or an eighth, and the year by the waiting period of four months and ten days. Ibn Kathir reports that Uthman, asked why the verse was kept in the Qur'an, replied that he would not move anything from its place. Mujahid, however, holds the verse to be unabrogated: the legal waiting period is four months and ten days, to which a year of residence is added as a bequest that the woman may accept or reject. Ibn Taymiyya chose this view, while others, including Ibn Atiyya, disputed it. Abu Muslim al-Isfahani argues that the husband did make a bequest, so there is no abrogation, and al-Razi follows him. On whether residence rights continue after the waiting period, the Hanafis hold they end with the husband's death, while the Shafi'is maintain them on the basis of the hadith of Furay'a.

This verse states that every divorced woman has a right to a provision (mata'), meaning clothing, maintenance, a servant or whatever she may benefit from, given in a fair and customary manner according to the husband's means and her situation, and that this is a duty upon the God-fearing. The commentators agree that this provision is encouraged and tied to piety and good conduct, and that 'in a fair manner' refers to what is customary and suitable to the circumstances. They differ on whether it is obligatory for every divorced woman or only some. Sa'id ibn Jubayr, Abu al-'Aliya and al-Zuhri hold that it is owed to every divorced woman, a view chosen by al-Tabari, while Abu Thawr considers the verse general and unabrogated. 'Ata' ibn Abi Rabah says it concerns women who have been consummated, Malik excludes the woman who obtains divorce by khul', and al-Shafi'i limits it to the woman divorced before consummation with no dowry fixed. Many commentators report that the verse came after the phrase 'a duty upon the doers of good', when a man said he would give only if he wished, so God made it binding on the pious. Ibn Kathir and others see a general principle, most scholars treating it as recommended. On the meaning of mata', some take it to be maintenance during the waiting period. The commentators differ and none settles the question definitively.

In this verse God states that He explains His signs in this way, meaning that the rules just laid out serve as a model for the clarifications to come, so that believers may understand His limits and grasp what benefits their religion and their worldly and eternal life. The commentators agree that the verse closes the preceding legislation on divorce, the waiting period and provision, and that it urges reflection on these rules and their application, presenting this clarity as a blessing from God. The main disagreement concerns the verse before it, on provision for divorced women. Sa'id ibn Jubayr, Abu al-'Aliya, al-Zuhri and Abu Thawr hold that it is owed to every divorced woman. Others restrict it to a woman divorced before consummation with no dowry fixed, while Ata' ibn Abi Rabah limits it to women who have been consummated, and Ibn Zayd sees it as reinforcing the obligation stated earlier. Ibn al-Qasim and Zayd ibn Aslam argue that the verse on divorce before touching abrogated this generality, and al-Shafi'i restricts it to the woman who has received no dowry. Most scholars, such as Ibn Kathir, hold that the one-year maintenance ruling for widows was abrogated by the four months and ten days verse, though Mujahid and others regard the one-year residence provision as still valid, a view Ibn Taymiyya supports and Ibn Abd al-Barr rejects. Some understand the provision to mean maintenance during the waiting period, which removes the apparent repetition.

This verse recounts the story of a large group, said by the commentators to number in the thousands, who left their homes in fear of death. God made them die and then brought them back to life, to show that life and death belong to Him and that fleeing His decree is of no avail. The exegetes agree on the exhortative purpose of the passage: it urges fighting and warns against cowardice, since fleeing death does not postpone it. They also agree that the revival is a grace from God toward people. The differences begin with the number. Ibn 'Abbas and Sa'id ibn Jubayr say they were four thousand, Ibn 'Abbas also reports eight thousand or forty thousand, al-Suddi and Abu Malik speak of about thirty thousand, and 'Ata' ibn Abi Rabah of seventy thousand. Al-Tabari, al-Baghawi and Ibn 'Atiyya prefer the view that they exceeded ten thousand, since the word alluf is not used for fewer. As for why they fled, two views are prominent: al-Hasan, 'Amr ibn Dinar and al-Suddi say it was the plague, while 'Ikrima, al-Dahhak and al-Kalbi say they fled from the jihad to which they had been summoned. Ibn Kathir and others report that the revival came through the supplication of a prophet, named Hizqil by some and Shim'un by others, while some exegetes hold that God revived them directly. A few treat the account as a parable rather than an actual event, and Ibn 'Atiyya replies that nothing in the verse excludes its being real. Many commentators draw from the passage the prohibition of fleeing a plague once it has struck a land, citing the hadith recorded in the two Sahihs.

This verse commands believers to fight in the cause of God, meaning for His religion and against His enemies who block the path to Him, and reminds them that God hears what they say and knows what they intend. Most commentators, including al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Razi and al-Baydawi, understand the address to be to the community of Muhammad, and place it after the story of those who left their homes fleeing death: flight does not avert the appointed term. Ibn Abbas and al-Dahhak instead hold that the command is addressed to those whom God revived among the Children of Israel, so that the meaning is that He then ordered them to fight. Al-Tabari rejects this reading outright, while Ibn Atiyya and Abu Hayyan judge the first view more apparent. On the meaning of the path, al-Razi and al-Qasimi explain that jihad defends and strengthens the religion, and they cite the hadith narrated from Abu Musa that whoever fights so that God's word is supreme is in the path of God. Ibn Uthaymin adds that both intention and conduct must follow the Sharia. He also treats the command as a collective obligation in general and an individual one in certain cases, a detail few other commentaries develop. The attribute of hearing is mentioned before knowledge because much of combat is audible, while knowledge also covers inner states such as fear and the urge to hold back.

In this verse God urges believers to spend in His way, calling what a believer gives seeking His reward a "goodly loan" that He will multiply many times over. The commentators agree that a goodly loan means lawful wealth, given willingly and sincerely for God's sake, without reproach or harm to the recipient. They differ on the scale of the multiplication. Ibn Zayd and Ibn Kathir report seven hundred times, while al-Suddi and others say that only God knows its extent, a view al-Tabari favours and Ibn Kathir mentions elsewhere. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Baydawi take the verse as a call to fight and to spend, al-Asamm limits it to voluntary charity, and others include obligatory giving. Al-Hasan reports that Jews, on hearing it, said God was poor and they were rich; the word loan is a figure meant to bring the idea within human understanding, since God is the Rich and the Praiseworthy. On the phrase "He withholds and He extends", al-Hasan and Ibn Zayd speak of provision being narrowed or widened, al-Zajjaj speaks of God accepting charity and rewarding it, and others speak of God's control over hearts. The verse closes by reminding that all return to God, who repays each person according to their deeds. The commentators agree that the verse encourages the believer to give without fearing poverty, since provision lies in God's hand.

The verse recounts how the notables of the Children of Israel, after Moses' death, asked their prophet to appoint a king to lead them in fighting in God's cause so they could recover their homes and children, from whom their enemy had expelled them. The prophet asked whether they would refuse fighting if it were prescribed, and they replied that nothing prevented them from fighting. The commentators differ on the prophet's identity: Wahb ibn Munabbih, Ibn Ishaq, Ibn Kathir and Mujahid name Samuel (Shamwil), as-Suddi names Shim'un, and Qatada names Joshua ibn Nun, which Ibn 'Atiyya and Ibn Kathir consider weak given the long gap before David. Al-Tabari, al-Baghawi and Ibn al-Jawzi relate that their request was prompted by defeat at the hands of the Amalekites under Goliath, who captured the sons of their kings and took their Torah. Most read 'nuqatil' as an answer to the imperative, while some read 'yuqatil' with a yaa. On the particle 'an' in 'alla nuqatil', al-Kisa'i takes an omitted preposition, al-Farra' a sense of prevention, al-Akhfash considers it superfluous, and many reject that view. All agree that most of them turned away, and that the small faithful group were those who crossed the river with Talut, some counting them as three hundred and thirteen. Modern exegetes draw a warning against turning back once fighting has been prescribed, and describe such desertion as wronging oneself by abandoning an accepted duty.

The Quran reports that the prophet of the Israelites told his people that God had sent Saul (Talut) to them as king. The notables objected that he was neither from the royal tribe nor from the prophetic tribe, that he was poor, and that they themselves had a better claim to kingship. The prophet replied that God had chosen him over them and increased him in knowledge and bodily stature, and that kingship is in God's hand, given to whom He wills. The commentators explain that the objection rested on lineage and wealth, while the answer rests on knowledge and strength, qualities that matter for leading a war. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir, citing Wahb ibn Munabbih, explain that the Israelites had two tribes, one for prophethood and one for kingship, and that Saul belonged to the tribe of Benjamin, which had neither. Wahb and al-Suddi say Saul was a tanner or water carrier, while Ibn Zayd holds that his added stature came after he became king, and Wahb and al-Suddi hold that it came before. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Razi draw from the verse the view that leadership is not inherited. Mujahid takes kingship here to mean command of the army. Some read the knowledge as knowledge of war and others as knowledge of religion, and al-Sam'ani prefers the first. The verse closes by affirming that God is Vast and All-Knowing, who knows who deserves kingship.

Their prophet told them that the sign of God's appointing Talut as king would be the return of the Ark, which their enemies had seized, a chest that held relics of the family of Moses and Aaron and that they carried into battle to find calm in their hearts. The commentators agree that the Ark contained remnants of the prophets' legacy, but they differ on what these were. Ibn Abbas, Qatada and as-Suddi name the shattered tablets and Moses' staff, Ikrima adds the Torah, al-Thawri mentions the sandals, the turban and a measure of manna, while ad-Dahhak says it was the struggle in God's cause. As for the sakina, Ali ibn Abi Talib describes it as a gentle wind with a human face, Mujahid as a creature like a cat with wings, and Ibn Abbas as a golden basin from Paradise in which the hearts of prophets were washed, whereas Ata, Qatada and al-Kalbi understand it as tranquillity and dignity. At-Tabari and Ibn Atiyya prefer the view that it is whatever known signs calm the souls. The reports say the Ark returned to them, some describing how angels carried it on cows, others how it had been left in the wilderness with Joshua and angels brought it to Talut's house. At-Tabari holds that the angels truly carried it and that the sign is its return. Other exegetes see the miracle as a means of reassuring hearts and leading them to accept Talut, and draw a lesson for the believers.

The Qur'an relates that when Talut set out with his troops, he told them that God would test them with a river they would cross. Whoever drank from it directly was not of his company, whoever refrained was, except one who took a single handful. Commentators differ on the river: Ibn 'Abbas and Qatada placed it between the Jordan and Palestine, while al-Sudi identified it as the river of Palestine; al-Tabari reports that the soldiers complained of thirst and asked God for a river. All agree the trial revealed who was steadfast: most drank until thirst overcame them, and few remained firm. On the number of the small group that did not drink, scholars disagree. The majority, including Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi, say it was three hundred and thirteen, matching the companions at Badr, while 'Ikrima and al-Sudi said four thousand. They also differ on who said, we have no strength against Jalut today. Ibn 'Abbas and al-Sudi understood them as the hypocrites who had withdrawn, while al-Hasan, Qatada and Ibn Zayd took them to be believers whose certainty was weak. Those who expected to meet God, that is those whose conviction was firm, replied that many a small company has overcome a great one by God's permission, and that God is with the patient. The commentators agree that patience and certain faith bring victory, and that the test before battle separates the steadfast from the rest. Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi note that a single handful of water sufficed each man's need.

This verse describes the prayer that Talut and his believing companions raised when they came out to face Jalut and his forces. They asked God to pour patience over them until it filled their hearts, to make their feet firm in the battle so that they would not flee, and to help them against the disbelieving people. The commentators agree that patience means restraining oneself from panic and retreat, and that firm feet is an image of a steady heart. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi and al-Nasafi explain that the request for victory was for God's help against unbelievers, not for personal revenge. Ibn al-Jawzi and al-Qurtubi note that Jalut was the leader of the Amalekites and that his army was very large, which led the believers to turn to their Lord. Al-Razi raises a theological point: patience is an act of the servant, yet its firmness comes from God, and he cites al-Qadi's view that this refers to putting in place the causes of steadfastness. Al-Qurtubi also mentions a report from al-Bara' that the companions of Badr were equal in number to Talut's companions. Al-Alusi and al-Qasimi praise the order of the supplication, which asks first for patience, then for firmness, then for victory. All the commentators see in this passage a model of turning to God before battle.

This verse describes how the believers in Talut's army defeated Goliath's forces by God's permission. David killed Goliath, and God gave him kingship and wisdom and taught him what He willed. The commentators explain that the defeat was by God's decree and will, and that David struck Goliath with a sling and a stone. Some take 'wisdom' to mean prophethood, others the Psalms. Al-Tabari reports many detailed accounts of the battle, including the story of three stones that spoke to David; Ibn Kathir and Ibn 'Atiyya regard much of this material as weak or drawn from Israelite narratives and do not rely on it. The commentators agree that David was the first among the Children of Israel to be given both kingship and prophethood together, but they differ on the timing: al-Tabari and al-Qurtubi place it after the deaths of Talut and Samuel, while others say it came seven years later. The second half of the verse states a general principle: were it not for God repelling some people by means of others, the earth would be corrupted. Ibn 'Abbas and Mujahid understand this as God repelling the unbelievers by the Muslim armies, others as the protection of the righteous from the wicked, and others as the protection provided by the revealed laws. Nafi', Abu Ja'far and Ya'qub read 'difa'', the rest 'daf'', and al-Tabari holds that both readings carry the same meaning. The verse ends by affirming that God is full of bounty to all the worlds.

This verse states that the stories of the Children of Israel just related, the death and revival of thousands, the appointment of Talut, the coming of the Ark, and David's killing of Goliath, are signs and proofs from God, which He recites to His Prophet Muhammad ﷺ in truth, and that he is among the messengers. The commentators agree that "those" refers to the preceding narrative and that "in truth" means a certain report, matching what the People of the Book have in their scriptures. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Razi and al-Baydawi note that these accounts could not have been known without reading books or hearing them from people, so the Prophet's telling of them is evidence for his prophethood.

Al-Razi also sees in the verset a consolation for the Prophet: all messengers were sent to convey the message, not to compel belief, and some were rejected by their peoples, so he should not grieve over the disbelief of his contemporaries. Ibn Kathir and Ibn al-Jawzi add that whoever believes him will share the fate of those who believed earlier messengers, and whoever disobeys him will share the fate of their opponents.

Ibn 'Ashur explains that the emphasis with inna and the lam answers those who deny his mission, and that the phrase "among the messengers" shows he brings nothing new compared with the messengers before him. Al-Shinqiti clarifies that "in truth" describes a report that matches reality, and al-Sha'rawi argues that knowing these events without study proves they were revealed to him. Ibn 'Uthaymin and others add that the story teaches patience and trust in God in battle.

This verse states that God preferred some of the messengers over others, granting them different ranks and distinctions. Among them is the one to whom God spoke directly, Moses, and the one He raised in rank, whom most commentators identify as Muhammad, peace be upon him, because of the universality of his mission, the abundance of his signs and the seal of prophethood. God gave Jesus, son of Mary, clear signs, such as healing the blind from birth and the leper and raising the dead, and strengthened him with the Holy Spirit. Many identify this as Gabriel, while others take it as the revelation or the name by which Jesus raised the dead. The verse then says that the divisions among the peoples after these messengers, some believing and some disbelieving, leading to fighting, would not have happened had God willed it, yet He does what He wills, guiding whom He wills and leaving astray whom He wills. Most commentators understand this will as a will of decree and creation rather than a will of approval, and they attribute belief, disbelief and fighting to His decree. The question of ranking prophets troubled some, since hadiths forbid comparing them. Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi answer with several points: the prohibition concerns preferences made out of passion or dispute, no one but God can rank them in detail, and prophethood itself does not admit degrees, only the additional favours and miracles do. Some suggested that the one raised in rank might be Abraham, Idris or the messengers of firm resolve, but the prevailing view is Muhammad.

The verse calls believers to spend from what God has provided before a day comes when there will be no trade, no useful friendship, and no intercession. Commentators differ first on what kind of spending is meant: al-Hasan and as-Suddi take it as the obligatory zakat, Ibn Jurayj and Sa'id ibn Jubayr include voluntary charity as well, and Ibn 'Atiyya calls this view sound while leaning, given the surrounding talk of fighting, toward spending in God's cause. Al-Asamm reads it as spending for jihad, while al-Razi notes that most scholars include both obligatory and recommended giving. On the word 'trade', Ibn 'Abbas and others understand ransom, and al-Tabari understands it as acting before the time for deeds has passed. 'Friendship' is generally taken as a helpful affection that gives aid, and Qatada adds that only the friendship of the pious will remain that day. On intercession, most commentators hold that the denial addresses unbelievers or applies unless God permits it, and that permitted intercession remains; al-Baydawi and al-Zamakhshari report the Mu'tazili view limiting it to increase in reward, whereas Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi extend it to lightening punishment. Readers differ on the case of the three nouns: Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr and Ya'qub read them with fatha, while the others read them with damma and tanwin. Finally, the closing phrase, which 'Ata' ibn Dinar praised for its precision, identifies the unbelievers as the wrongdoers par excellence; al-Zamakhshari sees in it an expression of the seriousness of withholding charity.

This verse affirms that God is the only deity, the Living who subsists by Himself, the Self-Subsisting who sustains all things; neither drowsiness nor sleep overtakes Him. To Him belongs whatever is in the heavens and on earth, and none may intercede with Him except by His permission. He knows what lies before people and what is behind them, and they grasp nothing of His knowledge except what He wills. The commentators agree on the general meaning: these phrases establish monotheism and the perfection of God's attributes, and most report that this is the greatest verse of the Quran, as several hadiths of the Prophet ﷺ state. On the Kursi, opinions differ: Ibn Abbas, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, Mujahid and al-Tabari take it to mean God's knowledge; Abu Musa al-Ash'ari, al-Suddi and al-Dahhak say it is the place of the two feet; al-Hasan al-Basri identifies it with the Throne; Ibn Kathir and Ibn al-Qayyim, followed by most, see a vast created thing, smaller than the Throne yet wider than the heavens and earth; others see an image of God's greatness rather than a real seat. On height and greatness, some understand loftiness of rank, others a real elevation above creation. Some Mu'tazilites denied several of these attributes, while the people of the Sunna affirm them without specifying how.

The commentators explain that the verse affirms that no one may be compelled into religion, because faith cannot rest on coercion, and that right guidance has been distinguished from error through clear proofs: rushd is faith and ghayy is disbelief. Most also hold that the tāghūt includes Satan and whatever is worshipped besides God, while others take it to mean the soothsayer, the sorcerer or the idol; whoever rejects the tāghūt and believes in God has grasped the firmest handhold, which cannot break. As for the occasion of revelation, Ibn 'Abbas, Sa'id ibn Jubayr and Mujahid relate it to sons of the Ansar who had been made Jews or Christians, whom their fathers wanted to force into Islam, and God forbade this. Al-Tabari sees it as a specific cause with a general ruling. Scholars differ on abrogation: Ibn Mas'ud, Sulayman ibn Musa and Ibn Zayd consider it abrogated by the verses on fighting, whereas Qatada, al-Hasan, al-Sha'bi and al-Dahhak hold it to be valid and limited to People of the Book who pay the jizya. Some read the negation as a prohibition, others as a plain statement. Al-Tabari judges the view that it concerns People of the Book and Magians to be the most correct, while al-Zamakhshari and al-Razi stress that God built faith on free choice rather than compulsion. On the 'firmest handhold', Mujahid understands faith, al-Suddi Islam, and Ibn 'Abbas the declaration of monotheism; nearly all agree that it is an image of holding fast to a stable truth that cannot be broken.

This verse states that God is the protector (wali) of the believers: He brings them out of darkness into light, that is, from disbelief and error into faith and guidance. Those who disbelieve have as their allies the tyrants (taghut), namely the devils, idols and anything that turns people from the truth, and these lead them out of the light into darkness. The verse concludes that these are the companions of the Fire, where they will abide forever. The commentators agree that light and darkness here mean faith and disbelief, the plural 'darknesses' pointing to the many paths of error and the singular 'light' to the one straight path. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi report that the verse first concerned people who believed in Jesus and then rejected Muhammad, relying on Mujahid and 'Abda ibn Abi Lubaba. Al-Tabari also notes that it may mean hindering someone from entering faith, in the same way that a son says his father expelled him from an inheritance he never held. Al-Mawardi, al-Zamakhshari and al-Razi offer broader readings: the light may be the natural disposition (fitra), clear proof or the light of reward, and the darkness doubt, desire or punishment. Ibn 'Atiyya holds that the wording is general and applies to every disbelieving nation. Al-Razi and the Mu'tazilites discuss whether bringing people out of darkness is God's direct act or results from sending prophets and proofs. All agree that eternal punishment is reserved for the disbelievers.

God relates the story of the tyrant Nimrod who disputed with Abraham about his Lord, because God had given him kingship and he grew arrogant. When Abraham said, "My Lord is the One who gives life and causes death," Nimrod replied that he too gives life and causes death, by pardoning or by killing. Several commentators report that he summoned two men, killed one and spared the other. The commentators agree that giving life and death means creating life and death in bodies, and that Nimrod's answer was deception or stubborn denial. Abraham then moved to a clearer argument that his opponent could not contest: "God brings the sun from the east, so bring it from the west." The unbeliever was confounded. Scholars differ on the nature of this step. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Baydawi see it as a move from one proof to a clearer one, while Ibn Kathir and Ibn al-Qayyim see it not as a change of argument but as holding the opponent to the consequences of his own claim. Some read "fabahata" and understand it as abuse or slander. The verse ends by saying that God does not guide the wrongdoers, those who put things in the wrong place, including one who denies the truth after it has become clear. Many scholars take from the passage the permissibility of debate to establish belief, provided one does not persist in obstinacy.

This verse gives another example of God's power to bring the dead back to life: the man who passed by a town in ruins, its roofs fallen in, and who wondered how God could restore it after its destruction. God caused him to die for a hundred years and then raised him. The commentators agree that this account is a sign, but they differ on the man's identity and on the town. According to Qatada, 'Ikrima, al-Rabi', al-Dahhak, al-Suddi and Ibn 'Abbas, as reported by al-Tabari, he was Uzayr; according to Wahb ibn Munabbih and 'Abd Allah ibn 'Ubayd ibn 'Umayr he was Jeremiah; Ibn Ishaq identified him with al-Khidr; Mujahid saw him as a disbeliever in resurrection, an opinion al-Zamakhshari adopts by linking the verse to the story of Nimrod. As for the town, most identify it as Jerusalem after its destruction by Nebuchadnezzar, while Ibn Zayd thought of the town from which thousands fled for fear of death. The commentators report that his food, figs and grapes, and his drink, grape juice, had remained unchanged, and that his donkey had been reduced to bones before being restored before his eyes. On the verb 'nunshizuha', the reading with zay means raising and assembling the bones, and the reading with ra' means reviving them. Regarding who asks 'how long have you remained?', opinions differ: God Himself, an angel, or a prophet. When it became clear to him, he said: I know that God is capable of all things; the reading 'qala i'lam' in the imperative is attributed to Hamza and al-Kisa'i.

The Qur'an recounts Abraham's request that his Lord show him how He gives life to the dead. God asks whether he does not believe, and he replies that he does, but wants his heart to be at rest. The commentators agree on the plain meaning: Abraham wished to see resurrection with his own eyes to increase his certainty. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi report that Abraham never doubted God's power and sought direct observation, since reports are not like witnessing. Al-Tabari relies on the hadith of Abu Hurayra in which the Prophet said that we have more right to doubt than Abraham, and he takes this as a denial of doubt itself. They differ on the cause of the request. Al-Hasan, Qatada and Ibn Jurayj mention a carcass torn apart by beasts and birds; Ibn Ishaq links it to Abraham's dispute with Nimrod; al-Suddi and Sa'id ibn Jubayr connect it to the announcement of his friendship with God. The birds are usually given as the rooster, peacock, crow and dove, with some variation in reports. All agree that he cut them up, scattered the pieces on mountains, and called them, and they came to him swiftly, but the number of mountains differs: four, seven or ten. The meaning of the verb sur-hunna is also debated, between cutting them and drawing them close. Abu Muslim denied the whole story and read the verb as training the birds to answer, a view rejected by the majority. Al-Tabari prefers the damma reading, the two senses being close, and notes that the verse displays God's might and wisdom.

In this verse God gives an image of those who spend their wealth in the way of God, a phrase the commentators usually understand as struggle in God's cause, though some extend it to every form of good work. They explain that their spending grows and multiplies like a single grain that produces seven ears, each bearing one hundred grains, that is seven hundred grains. Al-Tabari, al-Baghawi and Ibn Kathir link this multiplication to the tradition that a good deed is multiplied tenfold, and up to seven hundred times for spending in God's way. Most agree that the reward varies according to the giver's sincerity and intention and the nature of what is spent.

Scholars differ over the phrase "God multiplies for whom He wills." Al-Tabari, and a report from al-Dahhak, take it as a confirmation of the seven hundred figure with no further increase. Ibn 'Atiyya, Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi hold that God may give more to whom He wills, citing the hadith from Ibn Umar in which the Prophet asked God to increase his community's reward. A report attributed to Ibn Abbas speaks of multiplication reaching two million, but Ibn 'Atiyya notes that its chain of transmission is not established. Al-Razi and Ibn Juzayy leave this possibility open.

The commentators also discuss whether an ear with one hundred grains really exists. Al-Tabari and Ibn 'Atiyya say it may be found in wheat or other grains, al-Zamakhshari points to millet and sorghum, while al-Razi stresses that the image serves as an illustration rather than a claim about what grows. Ibn Kathir adds that such an image strikes the soul more forcefully than a bare number.

This verse states that those who spend their wealth in the way of God, which includes fighting and all good works, and who do not follow their giving with reminders of their favour or with hurt to the recipient, will have their reward with their Lord, with no fear or grief for them. The commentators agree that al-mann is recounting the favour and boasting of it, and that al-adha is reproach or words that wound the needy person's dignity, both of which nullify the reward of charity. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi report that the verse was revealed about 'Uthman ibn 'Affan and 'Abd al-Rahman ibn 'Awf in equipping the army of hardship, while Ibn Zayd holds that it concerns those who give while staying home rather than going out to fight, a view Ibn 'Atiyya considers arbitrary. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Baydawi read 'thumma' here as marking a difference in rank rather than a delay, so that refraining from reminders and hurt is better than the giving itself, whereas Ibn al-Qayyim holds that a later reminder also undoes the charity, and al-Razi holds that the condition is the absence of both. Some extend the scope of adha to include things like a greeting that burdens the recipient, following a saying attributed to Zayd ibn Aslam. Al-Qurtubi counts al-mann among the major sins on the basis of hadiths, and Ibn Kathir cites several that forbid it.

This verse teaches that a kind word to a beggar, together with forgiveness of whatever in his demand may irritate the giver, is better than a charity followed by reproach or hurt. The commentators generally understand that charity is spoiled when it is followed by reminding the recipient of one's favours (al-mann) or by harm (al-adha), that God is self-sufficient and needs no gifts from His servants, and that He is patient, not hastening to punish those who wound the needy. There is wide agreement that the 'kind word' means a gracious refusal, a prayer for the asker, or words of encouragement. The 'forgiveness' is understood by most as concealing the poor man's need and not exposing it, or overlooking his rudeness. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Sa'di take this line, while al-Razi lists several readings, including that the asker himself pardons the giver's refusal, or that God forgives in return for a fine refusal. Ibn al-Qayyim judges the last reading weak, since the address is to the giver and not the recipient. On 'mann', Ibn Abbas takes it as reproach directed at God, whereas most scholars take it as reminding the recipient of the favour. On whether the aumônes are truly annulled, the Mu'tazilites, as Ibn al-Jawzi and al-Razi report, hold a real loss of reward, while Sunni commentators, as al-Razi and Ibn Juzayy record, read it as a charity performed without sincerity and therefore void from the start. The parable of a smooth rock covered in soil, which the rain strips bare, illustrates this. Ibn Atiyya and al-Baghawi note that any reproach about the pauvre's poverty counts as harm, and the hadith says a kind word is itself a charity.

In this verse God warns believers not to nullify their charity by reminding recipients of their favours and by harming them. He compares such a giver to one who spends his wealth to be seen by people while not believing in God or the Last Day. His case is like a smooth rock covered with dust: a heavy rain strips the dust away and leaves it bare, so the giver gains nothing from what he gave. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi, al-Zamakhshari and al-Qurtubi agree that reminding of favours and harming the recipient cancel the reward, and that showing off does the same; such a person will find nothing of his deeds on the Day of Judgment. Al-Tabari clarifies that the cancellation concerns the reward rather than the act itself, and he supports this with a hadith forbidding reminders of favours. Ibn Atiyya and al-Alusi note the difficulty of saying an accomplished act can be cancelled; the Sunni answer is that an act is not accepted when accompanied by reminders and harm, and that sins do not erase good deeds in general. The commentators differ on the meaning of the reminder: most say it is the reminder made to the poor, while Ibn Abbas understands it as reminding God. Al-Razi and al-Qurtubi take the word for 'like' as linked to an omitted term, and the comparison targets the hypocrite or the open disbelieving show-off; Ibn Ashur sees the image as describing the unbeliever who gives for display. Al-Baydawi and Ibn Atiyya link ostentation with hypocrisy. Al-Wahidi, al-Baghawi and Ibn Kathir report that the verse was revealed about Uthman and Abd al-Rahman ibn Awf during the expedition to Tabuk, an account several exegetes cite as the occasion of revelation.

This verse offers an image for those who spend their wealth seeking God's pleasure and to firm up their own souls: their spending is like a garden on a height which, when struck by heavy rain, yields twice its usual crop, and when it receives no heavy rain, is satisfied with a light drizzle. The commentators explain that "ibtigha'" means seeking God's pleasure. On "tathbitan", al-Sha'bi, al-Suddi, Ibn Zayd and Abu Salih take it to mean certainty and conviction in God's promise, a reading al-Tabari adopts, while al-Hasan and Mujahid take it to mean carefully choosing where to give charity, and Qatada takes it to mean seeking the reward. Ibn 'Atiyya considers the first view the soundest. As for the "rabwa", Mujahid and Ibn 'Abbas describe it as an elevated place, al-Hasan as level ground that does not rise above the water, and Ibn 'Abbas specifies a place without flowing rivers. Al-Razi reads it as fertile soil that swells and grows with rain. The "di'fayn" is generally understood as twice the yield, though Ibn Kathir and others relate it to annual harvests and some to four times. The "tall", according to Ibn 'Abbas and others, is a light rain or dew. The overall meaning is that sincere spending is accepted and multiplied by God, whether large or small, and that God sees what people do, which encourages sincerity and warns against showing off.

On its plain reading, the verse offers a parable: would any of you wish for a garden of palms and vines, with rivers flowing beneath it and every kind of fruit, then reach old age with weak offspring, only to see the garden destroyed by a fiery whirlwind just when he needs it most? The commentators broadly agree that it depicts a deed that is annulled, but they differ on who is meant. Al-Tabari reports al-Suddi's view, which he prefers, that it describes the one who spends to be seen, and Ibn Zayd's view that it describes the one who follows his charity with reproach. Mujahid, Qatada and al-Rabi' say it concerns the one who neglects obedience to God until death. Ibn Abbas, as transmitted by al-Bukhari through a report from 'Umar, says it refers to the man who did good deeds and then spoiled the end of his life with sin. Al-Hasan extends it to anyone who will need his deeds when this world is taken from him. All agree that the image is of grief at losing something exactly when one needs it most. On the word i'sar, al-Zajjaj describes a wind rising from the earth like a pillar; Ibn Abbas, al-Suddi and Ibn Zayd say it is a scorching wind, while al-Hasan and al-Dahhak say it carries bitter cold. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Baydawi take the particle wa in 'wa asabahu al-kibar' as introducing a circumstance, whereas al-Farra' and others take it as coordinating with the sense of the preceding verb. Ibn Kathir concludes that the passage shows the need for sincere deeds and the consequences of corrupting them.

This verse tells believers to spend from the good things they have earned and from what the earth yields for them, and forbids them to aim at the bad, which they would not accept themselves except by overlooking its flaws. Most commentators understand the good as the best and choicest, and the bad as the inferior, though Ibn Zayd takes the good as the lawful and the bad as the unlawful. On the nature of this spending, Ali, Ubayda al-Salmani and Ibn Sirin take it to be the obligatory zakat, holding that a counterfeit dirham is better than a date given in charity, while al-Bara ibn Azib, al-Hasan and Qatada take it to be voluntary charity, in which one is only encouraged to give the finest. The phrase "unless you overlook it" receives several readings: tolerating a loss on one's due, accepting a reduced price, or accepting a poor gift out of shame. Many report the occasion of revelation, in which some Ansar hung bunches of dates in the mosque that included spoiled dates. The verse concludes that God is self-sufficient and worthy of praise. Some scholars draw from it the obligation of zakat on trade goods, crops and minerals, while others point to the thresholds and conditions set by jurists.

This verse says that Satan frightens believers with poverty if they spend, and urges them toward indecency, while God promises them forgiveness from Him and bounty, and He is all-encompassing and all-knowing. The commentators agree that Satan 'promises' poverty in the sense that he frightens people into holding back their wealth from charity. Most, including al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Zamakhshari and al-Razi, take the indecency here to mean stinginess and withholding zakat, though some, such as Ibn Juzayy and al-Qurtubi, note that it may refer to any act of disobedience. The forgiveness is generally understood as the covering of sins through charity, and the bounty as a replacement in this world or a reward in the next, with some speaking of multiplied reward. Al-Razi gives several readings of the indecency, including the idea that Satan leads a person step by step from fear of poverty to miserliness and then to neglect of duties. Ibn Atiyya holds that the verse offers no decisive proof that poverty is better than wealth, although some have used it that way. Many commentators, including Ibn Kathir, connect the verse to the command to give from the best of one's wealth rather than from what is inferior. Al-Tabari also cites the hadith of Ibn Mas'ud on the whisperings of the angel and of Satan, which he accepts as traced back to the Prophet.

The verse says that God grants wisdom to whomever He wills among His servants, that whoever receives it has received abundant good, and that only people of understanding take heed of this. The commentators differ on what "wisdom" means. Ibn Abbas, Qatada, Mujahid and Abu al-Aliya understood it as the Quran and its understanding; Ibn Abbas specified knowledge of its abrogating and abrogated verses, its clear and ambiguous verses, its lawful and unlawful matters and its parables. Mujahid also understood it as rightness in speech and action. Malik, al-Hasan, Zayd ibn Aslam and Ibn Zayd defined it as knowledge of the religion, understanding of it, reason or scrupulous piety. Ibrahim al-Nakha'i took it to be understanding the meanings of things, al-Rabi' ibn Anas fear of God, and al-Sudi prophethood. Ibn Atiyya judged most of these views to be close to one another, since wisdom derives from the idea of perfecting an act or word. Al-Razi reports that some take it as theoretical knowledge of the truth and others as doing what is right, and that these meet. Al-Razi and Ibn Ashur connect the verse to the preceding contrast between the promise of pardon and bounty from God and the promise of poverty from Satan, wisdom itself being a gift from God. Ibn Kathir cites a hadith on envy being permitted only toward one given wisdom who teaches it. Ya'qub's reading "wa man yu'tihi" is noted alongside the common reading.

This verse states that God knows every charity and every vow that people make, and that He will reward them for it, while the wrongdoers have no helper against divine punishment. The commentators agree that God's knowing here means that He will recompense: Mujahid explains it as counting it, and al-Zajjaj as rewarding it. The verse therefore carries a promise for the sincere and a warning for those who spend to be seen, spend in disobedience, or withhold what God has required. Al-Tabari defines the wrongdoers as those who place something in the wrong place; Muqatil identifies them with the polytheists, while Abu Sulayman al-Dimashqi links them to those who follow their gifts with reproach, harm and show. Al-Qurtubi and Ibn Atiyya define a vow as an obligation a person imposes on himself; al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir hold that a vow of obedience must be fulfilled, whereas a vow of disobedience is not binding. The singular pronoun in 'knows it', though two things are named, is explained by Ibn Atiyya and al-Qurtubi as referring to what was mentioned, and by Abu Hayyan through the usage of the particle 'or'. On the following verses about giving openly or in secret, most scholars take them to concern voluntary charity, with Ibn Abbas holding that secret giving is more meritorious. Al-Mawardi and others consider that paying zakat openly is preferable to avoid suspicion. Al-Wahidi, Ibn Kathir and others mention that the verses were revealed about the giving of Muslims to their non-Muslim relatives or the poor, while Ibn Kathir records a report linking the passage to Abu Bakr and Umar.

This verse states that if almsgiving is made public it is good, but if it is given secretly to the poor, secrecy is better for the giver. Most commentators, including al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Qurtubi and al-Baydawi, hold that this refers to voluntary charity, since secrecy guards against showing off, while the obligatory zakat is better given openly to avoid suspicion. They cite Ibn Abbas that secret voluntary charity outweighs public charity seventy times, and that public obligatory charity outweighs secret charity twenty-five times. Al-Hasan, Qatada and Yazid ibn Abi Habib held that secrecy is preferable even for zakat. Al-Zajjaj said that openness became better in later times because people were quick to suspect. Al-Razi and al-Qurtubi note that openness may be better when the giver wishes to be imitated, and that secrecy suits the one not known for wealth. Readers differ on the verb yukaffiru, in the forms with nun, ya or ta, and in the mood, which depends on how the clause is read after the conditional answer. Most take min in min sayyi'atikum as partitive, since charity does not expiate every sin, while some consider it superfluous. All agree that the verse praises secret charity while leaving room for judgment according to circumstances.

This verse states that true guidance, meaning the granting of success and acceptance, belongs to God alone, so the Prophet ﷺ is not responsible for making people guided, only for delivering the message. The commentators understand the good spending to be that which benefits the giver, whose reward returns to him, and which is made solely seeking God's face. Most agree that the passage concerns voluntary charity, since obligatory zakat may not be given to a non-Muslim. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir report that Muslims refrained from giving to their polytheist relatives, or that the Prophet had forbidden giving to non-Muslims, and the verse came to permit it. Al-Qurtubi and Ibn 'Atiyya record other occasions of revelation, including the case of Asma bint Abi Bakr and her mother. Al-Razi discusses guidance as tied to human choice under God's will and answers Mu'tazilite arguments. Al-Zamakhshari reads the denied guidance as only the urging to avoid reproach and harm, while most take it as success in faith. The phrase 'you spend only seeking God's face' is read by some as praise for the companions' sincerity and by others as a command. The verse also affirms that the reward will be repaid in full and that God wrongs no one. Ibn 'Ashur notes that Abu Hanifa allowed giving the Eid alms to dhimmis, a view the majority rejected.

This verse identifies the best recipients of charity: the poor who confined themselves to the cause of God, unable to travel for trade or livelihood. The ignorant observer thinks they are wealthy because of their restraint and refusal to beg, yet those with insight recognise them by the marks of need on their faces and in their dress. They do not press people with insistence. The verse closes by reminding the reader that God knows whatever good is spent and will reward it.

The commentators agree that ihsar here means being restrained or prevented, but they differ on the cause. Qatada and Ibn Zayd, followed by Ibn Kathir, say they confined themselves to jihad and had no time to earn a living. Al-Suddi attributes the restraint to unbelievers who threatened them, Sa'id ibn Jubayr to wounds sustained in battle, and Ibn Abbas to poverty itself. Some extend the verse to all poor emigrants, while others restrict it to the People of the Bench, about four hundred men who lived in the mosque.

Opinions also differ on the meaning of the sign. Mujahid takes it as humility and lowered gaze, al-Suddi and al-Rabi' as the traces of hardship, Ibn Zayd as shabby clothing, and some as the mark of prostration. On the phrase 'they do not beg persistently', al-Tabari, al-Zajjaj and most exegetes read it as meaning they never ask at all, whereas al-Zamakhshari and Ibn 'Atiyya hold that they may ask, but gently and without importunity.

This verse promises that those who spend their wealth by night and by day, in secret and in public, will have their reward with their Lord, with no fear for them and no grief. The commentators broadly agree on the general meaning: giving is praised at every time and in every situation. They differ on the occasion of revelation. Many, including Ibn Abbas, report that it concerns Ali ibn Abi Talib, who gave away his four dirhams, one by night, one by day, one in secret and one in public. Others, such as al-Zamakhshari and al-Baydawi, link it to Abu Bakr, who is said to have given forty thousand dinars. Ibn Abbas, Abu al-Darda', Abu Umama, Makhul and al-Awza'i relate it to feeding horses kept for jihad, while Qatada takes it in the general sense of those who spend in God's cause without extravagance or stinginess. Ibn Kathir and al-Tabari consider spending on one's family to be included too. Several exegetes, including al-Razi and Ibn Uthaymin, observe that the placing of night and secrecy first points to the merit of discretion, though Ibn Uthaymin adds that open giving may be better when it serves a benefit. The verse thus offers a promise of tranquility, which Ibn Ashur understands as peace in this life and reward in the next.

The verse describes those who consume usury as rising on the Day of Resurrection only like one whom Satan has struck and driven mad. Most commentators, including al-Tabari, Mujahid, Qatada, al-Suddi and Ibn Zayd, take this literally as a sign that the usurer will be resurrected in a state of frenzy, and Ibn Abbas is cited as saying he is raised mad and choked. Ibn Atiyya and Ibn al-Jawzi also mention the view that it is a figurative picture of the usurer's frantic greed in pursuing gain in this life. The verse then gives the reason for this punishment: their claim that trade is just like usury. God answers that He has made trade lawful and forbidden usury. The commentators explain that trade involves a real exchange, while usury is an increase imposed on the debtor for delay. Whoever receives this admonition and desists keeps what he took before, and his affair rests with God. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir take the threat as directed at those who persist in declaring usury lawful, while Ibn Atiyya and al-Qurtubi see a share of it falling on sinful believers. Al-Razi and al-Baydawi stress that the eternal dwelling applies to unbelievers, and Zamakhshari's reading supporting the eternal punishment of grave sinners is contested by others. All agree on the prohibition of usury by the Quran, the Sunna and consensus, and the commentators note that God wipes out usury and makes charity grow.

God diminishes usury and makes charity grow, and He does not love any ungrateful sinner. The commentators explain that the verb yamhaqu means to reduce and destroy gradually, like the waning moon at the end of the month. Al-Tabari, citing Ibn Abbas, understands it as a decrease, while al-Mawardi and al-Wahidi say it removes the blessing from wealth, and Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi state that unlawful gain is wiped out in this world and punished in the next. As for the increase of charity, most scholars combine two meanings: a real increase in the wealth from which it was given, a blessing upon it, and a multiplication of reward. Al-Baydawi, al-Nasafi and Ibn Kathir hold both senses together, whereas al-Razi stresses the reward in the hereafter. Several of them, including Ibn Kathir, cite the hadith that God receives charity and raises it as one raises a foal. On the closing words, al-Zamakhshari, al-Razi and al-Baydawi see in kaffar and athim intensive forms describing the one who persists in usury and considers it lawful, while Ibn Atiyya prefers the reading that God does not love to grant him success. Ibn Kathir argues that the usurer, unsatisfied with what God has allotted him, is repaid with the opposite of his aim. The commentators agree that the verse combines a warning of loss for the usurer with a promise of growth for the giver, both in this life and the next.

This verse promises that those who believe, do righteous deeds, establish the prayer and pay zakat will have their reward with their Lord, with no fear for the future and no grief for the past. Al-Tabari connects it to the prohibition of usury: those who had practised riba in the pre-Islamic period, then repented and gave alms, will have their reward, and will feel neither fear nor grief, since on seeing the great reward they will be content with what they left behind. Ibn Kathir and Ibn Jarir read it as the counterpart of the warning before it: God destroys usury, removing its blessing and punishing its taker, while He makes alms grow. The commentators agree that prayer and zakat are singled out although they are included in good deeds, because of their rank: prayer is the greatest of bodily acts and zakat the most excellent of financial ones. They differ on the meaning of the denial of fear and grief. Ibn Abbas holds that fear concerns what lies ahead in the Hereafter and grief concerns what was left in this world; al-Asamm takes fear as dread of punishment and grief as missing an added bliss; al-Razi holds that such slight distress does not touch the people of reward. Al-Razi also records the debate over whether deeds belong to the definition of faith, and the answer that naming them after the good deeds is a matter of emphasis. For most commentators the verse carries no separate legal ruling; it closes the passage on usury with a promise to the righteous.

In this verse God addresses the believers, commanding them to fear Him and to give up whatever remains of riba owed to them, meaning the unpaid excess, now that riba has been forbidden. Commentators read the phrase "if you are believers" in two ways: some take it as a real condition, since true faith demands obedience, while others take it as a rhetorical emphasis showing that abandoning usury is a sign of genuine belief. Al-Tabari, al-Baghawi, Ibn Kathir, Ibn Atiyya and al-Qurtubi largely agree that the verse was revealed concerning Thaqif and the Banu al-Mughira, or concerning al-Abbas and Uthman, or al-Abbas and Khalid ibn al-Walid, about usurious debts from the pre-Islamic period. They were told to drop what remained of these debts after Islam, whereas what had already been collected before the prohibition was forgiven, as al-Tabari, al-Razi and Ibn Juzayy note.

The commentators also agree that whoever persists in usury after this warning declares war on God and His Messenger. Ibn Abbas explains that the ruler should first call the offender to repent and, if he refuses, execute him; others read the threat as a severe warning rather than a literal call to fight. Hamza and Asim (in Abu Bakr's transmission) read the long form "fa-ādhanū", while most read the short form "fa-idhnū"; some prefer the long form as more emphatic, others the short form because it addresses the listeners directly.

A person who repents keeps his principal: he neither takes any excess nor suffers a reduction of his capital. If the debtor is in hardship, he must be given time until he is able to pay, and remitting the debt as charity is better, as Ibn Kathir, al-Baydawi and Ibn Ashur maintain. The passage closes with a reminder of the day when all will return to God, which Ibn Abbas and Said ibn Jubayr regard as the last verse revealed.

This verse states that whoever does not give up what remains of riba after its prohibition has declared war on God and His Messenger, while whoever repents may take back only his principal, without interest. The commentators differ on who is addressed. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi report occasions of revelation involving the Banu al-Mughira of Thaqif, or al-Abbas and Uthman, and take the addressees to be believers who still held usurious debts from before Islam. Al-Razi and Ibn 'Atiyya also allow that the address may be to disbelievers who considered riba lawful, though Ibn 'Atiyya finds the reading about stubborn believers more probable. All agree that any gain above the principal is forbidden and that the creditor takes only his capital, neither more nor less. On the threatened war, Ibn 'Abbas and others hold that the usurer should first be asked to repent and otherwise be put to death, while some read the phrase as strong warning only. Hamza and 'Asim read «fa-adhanu» with an alif, meaning to inform others, while the rest read it without, meaning to be certain, a reading al-Tabari prefers. On granting time to an insolvent debtor, al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir treat it as an obligation based on the text; some restrict it to riba debts and others extend it to every debt. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Baydawi prefer remitting the debt altogether to merely granting time. Several commentators regard this verse as among the last revealed.

This verse addresses the debtor in hardship: if a debtor cannot repay, the creditor must give him time until he is able to pay. The commentators explain that hardship means poverty and lack of means, and that ease means affluence. The verse then recommends something better: to remit all or part of the debt to the struggling debtor, which is better than merely granting time. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi and al-Qurtubi generally understand this charity as the forgiveness of the debt, while Ibn Atiyya and others report that some understood it as simply granting respite, citing the hadith that whoever gives respite to a debtor in difficulty receives a charity each day. As for the occasion of revelation, al-Baghawi and Muqatil link it to the clans of Thaqif and Banu al-Mughira who demanded their interest after the Prophet's time, while al-Suddi links it to al-Abbas and Khalid ibn al-Walid. On the scope of the rule, Ibn Abbas, Shurayh and Ibrahim al-Nakha'i hold that it concerns only usurious debt, while Mujahid, Abu Hurayra, al-Hasan, Ata', al-Dahhak and most jurists extend it to every debt. Al-Razi notes that granting time is obligatory once insolvency is established, while remission is a meritorious recommendation. The verse thus commands the creditor to wait, and invites him to do better by forgiving.

This verse calls believers to be mindful of God and to beware of a day on which they will be returned to Him. The commentators almost all understand it as the Day of Resurrection, when every soul is paid in full for what it earned, and no one is wronged. Al-Tabari explains that one must fear appearing before God burdened with ruinous sins, since that day is one of recompense, not of seeking to make amends. Ibn 'Abbas, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, 'Atiyya and others report that it was the last verse revealed, and Ibn Jurayj says the Prophet lived nine nights after it. The reported periods differ between transmissions, and al-Suyuti notes these differences. As for the day itself, Ibn 'Atiyya and Ibn Kathir take it to be the Day of Resurrection, while some hold it to be the day of death; Ibn 'Atiyya considers the first view more fitting to the wording. Readers differ on the verb: Abu 'Amr reads it with a fatha on the first letter, while the others use a damma. Al-Zamakhshari and Ibn 'Atiyya see it as a general admonition addressed to everyone. Many, including al-Qurtubi and Abu Hayyan, take it as proof that reward and punishment depend on what a person has earned, which answers the Jabriyya. Al-Razi adds that returning to God may mean that all affairs return to His command, or that one returns to the reward or punishment He has prepared, and he considers both readings compatible with the text.

This verse, the longest in the Qur'an, is the verse of debt. It instructs believers, when they contract a deferred debt, to put it in writing to safeguard rights and prevent disputes. Most commentators understand it to cover deferred sales, salam (advance purchase) and loans. Al-Tabari holds that writing is obligatory, while most scholars treat it as recommended; some consider it abrogated by the verse 'if one of you trusts another'. The commentators agree that the scribe must write with justice, adding nothing and omitting nothing, and must not refuse when asked. The debtor dictates what he owes, fearing God and reducing nothing. If he is feeble-minded, a minor, or unable to dictate, his guardian dictates with fairness. Most require two adult free Muslim male witnesses; failing that, one man and two women, so that one may remind the other if she forgets. Witnesses must not refuse when called, and people must not tire of recording a debt, small or large. This is more just in God's sight, more upright for testimony, and closer to removing doubt. Immediate exchanges settled on the spot are exempt from writing, though taking witnesses at sale is advised. Harming the scribe or witness is forbidden and is an act of transgression. The verse closes with a call to piety and the assurance that God teaches, for He is knowing of all things.

This passage of verse 2:283 addresses how a debt is secured when no scribe can be found on a journey: a pledge taken into possession stands in place of a written record, as al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baydawi and al-Nasafi explain. Most commentators hold that possession of the pledge (al-qabd) is required for it to be valid and binding, and they do not restrict the rule to travel alone, since the Prophet ﷺ pledged his armour in Medina, as al-Razi, Ibn Juzayy and al-Shawkani note. Mujahid and al-Dahhak maintain that a pledge is permitted only on a journey, whereas Malik considers the contract sufficient without possession and says the pledgor can be compelled to hand it over. On the phrase 'if one of you trusts another', commentators agree that the debtor who has been trusted without written proof or pledge must repay the trust and fear God; some report from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri that this verse abrogates what precedes it, while others treat it as an independent ruling tied to trust, with no abrogation.
