Concerning concealing testimony, all declare it forbidden and count it among the major sins; its guilt is ascribed to the heart, the seat of concealment and the source of the act. Finally, all remind that God knows well what people do and will repay them accordingly.

This verse states that all that is in the heavens and on earth belongs to God, and that whatever people reveal or conceal of what is in their souls will be reckoned by Him: He forgives whom He wills and punishes whom He wills, for He has power over all things. The commentators agree that God knows everything in the hearts and that the 'reckoning' means being made aware of it or being repaid, while forgiveness and punishment rest solely on His will. The precise meaning divides the scholars. Ibn 'Abbas, 'Ikrima, al-Sha'bi and Mujahid held that it primarily concerns concealing testimony, whereas most exegetes gave it a general scope covering any evil the person harbours. On whether it is abrogated, Ibn Mas'ud, Abu Hurayra, one report from Ibn 'Abbas, al-Sha'bi, 'Ata' and Qatada said it was abrogated by 'God burdens no soul beyond its capacity', citing the Companions who were distressed. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn 'Atiyya considered it unabrogated: being called to account does not necessarily mean being punished, as God informs believers of their inner thoughts and forgives them, while unbelievers and hypocrites are punished for what they hid. They relied on the hadith of the private conversation between God and the believer. Others held that punishment for inner thoughts concerns disbelief and hypocrisy, and the widely reported hadith of Abu Hurayra says God has overlooked what the souls of this community whisper unless they act or speak on it. In recitation, most readers use the jazm on both verbs as a continuation of the conditional answer, Ibn 'Amir and 'Asim read them with raf' as a fresh clause, and nasb is also attested.

The commentators explain that this verse describes the faith of the Messenger in what was sent down to him from his Lord, and the faith of the believers with him in God, His angels, His books and His messengers, as they say: we make no distinction between any of His messengers. They also say: we heard and we obeyed, and then they ask for forgiveness and turn back to God. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Qurtubi and al-Baydawi agree that the verse was revealed after the Companions were troubled by the preceding verse about God's reckoning of what souls conceal; they said 'we heard and obeyed', and God praised them. Several, including Ibn Kathir and al-Tabari, report that the following verse, 'God does not burden a soul beyond its capacity', abrogated or lifted what troubled them. Ibn 'Atiyya sees the praise as a reward for their submission. The readers differ on 'wa-kutubihi' and 'wa-kitabihi': Ibn 'Abbas, Hamza and al-Kisa'i read the singular, Ibn 'Abbas explaining that the Book denotes the genus; the majority read the plural. They also differ on 'la nufarriqu' in the first person or 'la yufarriqu' in the third. The exegetes clarify that not distinguishing means not believing in some messengers while rejecting others, as Jews and Christians did; al-Razi and al-Qurtubi take it as not distinguishing in the truth of the mission, not in preference. On 'God does not burden a soul beyond its capacity', Ibn 'Abbas and most exegetes understand the thoughts that pass through the soul, for which one is not held accountable, while al-Hasan and al-Rabi' understand that God reckons what souls conceal and then forgives whom He wills. Others take it as a general rule about burden according to capacity. The hadith in al-Bukhari and Muslim, that God pardons the thoughts of the soul as long as they are not spoken or acted upon, is cited on this point. Finally, the Prophet said that whoever recites these two verses at night is sufficiently protected, which some interpret as sufficing for the night prayer or as protection from the devil.

This verse affirms that God imposes on no soul a burden beyond its capacity: each person reaps the fruit of the good they have done and bears the consequences of the evil they have committed. God then taught the believers a supplication, asking that He not hold them to account for forgetting or erring, not lay upon them heavy burdens like those borne by the peoples before them, not impose on them what they cannot bear, and that He pardon them, wipe away their sins, have mercy on them and grant them victory over the disbelieving people. The commentators report that these verses were revealed when the Companions were troubled by the words, 'Whether you show what is in your souls or hide it, God will call you to account for it.' The Prophet told them to say, 'We hear and we obey,' and God then lightened their burden. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir explain that capacity means the real power of a person, and that passing thoughts are not held against one who has not resolved to act on them. Al-Razi and al-Baydawi draw from the verse that no charge exceeds what is possible, without deducing an absolute rational impossibility; the Mu'tazilites take it as proof that commanding the impossible is impossible. Al-Tabari distinguishes forgetfulness through negligence, for which forgiveness is sought, from forgetfulness through weakness of memory, for which the request has no meaning. The word 'isr' is glossed by some as a heavy covenant, by others as the severe obligations imposed on the Children of Israel. The hadiths on the merit of the last two verses of the sura, related by Muslim and others, are cited by most commentators.
